News.title: Newquay deaths: Dad and daughter die at Britain's top surfing spot as police search for handbag
News.content:
Beachgoers bravely tried to rescue a man and woman after they reportedly fell from rocks and died in the choppy sea at Britain's most popular surfing spot.

Police have urged the public to be on the lookout for an orange handbag containing items of 'great sentimental value' after a father and his daughter, in their 60s and 30s, died tragically at Britain's most famous surfing beach in Cornwall.

People at Fistral Beach, in Newquay, bravely attempted to rescue the pair after they fell from some rocks into water below on Sunday evening, with nine emergency vehicles and a helicopter rushing to the 750-metre long sands, known as the 'home of British surfing' , to assist in the doomed rescue effort.

The area is well-known for having extremely strong and dangerous rip currents, particularly during outgoing tides. Locals said the sea currents were "very strong" last night.

Following news of their deaths, police urged the public to look for a "leather-style" handbag approximately 30cm by 30cm in size worn by the woman at the time of her death. The bag, described as "orange or peach in colour", is said to contain a number of sentimental items that grieving family members "would take great comfort in being reunited with," police said in a statement.

The Mirror has launched the Save Lives For Sam water safety campaign to tackle the UK's growing drowning crisis. Backed by MPs, Olympic champions, national water safety organisations and bereaved families, the campaign is calling for urgent action to make our waters safer.

Find out more about the campaign and how you can support it here.

News.title: Hundreds of people turning up at A&E with eye complaints opticians would treat for free
News.content:
Hundreds of people turning up at A&E with eye complaints opticians would treat for free

Opticians on the high street provide free NHS clinics where you can be seen quicker for eye problems - but most people don’t know they exist and turn up in A&E instead

View 4 Images A host of eye injuries could be treated quickly without going to A&E (Image: Getty Images/Westend61)

Hundreds of thousands of people are turning up at A&E for eye complaints for which they could go to free clinics on most high streets.

‌



New analysis shows eye infections, such as conjunctivitis and dry eye, are among the conditions with which 400,000 people went to hospital with last year but could have been treated on the high street.

‌



The Association of Optometrists (AOP) estimates that between 62% and up to 78% of the 780,000 eye-related A&E visits in England could safely be managed by community opticians. It says up to 400,000 visits to over-burdened A&E departments could be saved by better use of those on the high street.

‌



View 4 Images A&Es are still struggling after a decade of funding cuts to services that keep people well (Image: Adam Gerrard / Daily Mirror)

The AOP is calling for better funding of urgent and minor eye care services in optometrists so all can offer the NHS clinics as an alternative to A&E.

Chief executive Adam Sampson said: “Emergency departments should not be the default destination to manage eye problems. What this research tells us is that hundreds of thousands of patients each year end up in A&E because they conclude it’s their only option, but they could be treated by the highly trained optometry workforce based in the community.”

‌



A&E waits have remained stubbornly high since Labour came to power despite some progress on the elective NHS waiting list.

Waiting time standards collapsed under various conservative governments and the NHS target for 95% of patients to be treated or admitted within four hours of arriving in A&E has not been achieved in any month since July 2015.

Eye problems are among the top 10 most common reasons people attend A&E. Less serious eye abrasions can also be treated at NHS-funded clinics at optometrists.

‌



View 4 Images Opticians say they could do more for the NHS if paid to do so (Image: Getty Images/Image Source)

Known as minor and urgent eye care services, they allow patients with conditions such as red eyes, infections, flashes and floaters, or sudden changes in vision to be assessed and treated for free. Patients can attend some on a drop-in basis but are usually advised to book ahead over the phone.

However not all opticians are funded by the NHS to provide these free NHS clinics and the industry body is calling for an end to this postcode lottery.

‌



AOP boss Adam Sampson added: “The challenge is not capability, it's consistency. It’s essential we have a service in place for everyone everywhere in England to treat eye problems in the community. The reality of the postcode lottery is that it deprives patients of access to care close to home.

“It is simply a no-brainer that the Government acts to ensure that every member of the public who has an eye problem should be able get the help they need on the high street, in the same way the public can go to a community pharmacy for a range of health issues, regardless of where they live.”

View 4 Images Adam Sampson, Association of Optometrists (AOP), has called an end to the postcode lottery

‌



A&E waits got steadily longer during over a decade of Conservative governments before which waits over 12 hours were unheard of. By December 2019 some 2,356 patients waited longer than 12 hours on a trolley until a proper bed became available and by December 2025 it was 50,775 patients.

Labour and NHS England have set an interim target of March 2026 for 78% of patients attending A&E to be admitted, discharged or transferred within four hours. Latest data shows 75.4% of patients in England were seen within four hours in A&Es and this has been improving in recent months.

Dr James Gagg, vice president of the Royal College of Emergency Medicine said: “It’s no secret that emergency departments in England are under immense pressure at the moment, and we know our patients are being let down due to overcrowding and unacceptably long waits.

Article continues below

“We would welcome better-resourced community eye care, which could help deflect demand from A&E, accompanied by further measures from government to tackle the root causes of overcrowding and corridor care elsewhere in the system.”

News.title: Elon Musk AI tool 'designed to create harmful content' according to court papers
News.content:
Elon Musk AI tool 'designed to create harmful content' according to court papers

EXCLUSIVE: Labour MP Jess Asato is taking legal action against Elon Musk's xAI, the platform behind Grok, after the chatbot created fake images of her in a bikini

View 2 Images Labour MP Jess Asato is taking legal action against xAI (Image: PA)

AI chatbot Grok was designed in a way that allowed it to generate harmful sexualised content, according to court documents filed against Elon Musk's tech company.

‌



Labour MP Jess Asato is suing xAI, the platform behind Grok, after the chatbot created fake images of her in a bikini, as well as an AI video appearing to show her being drugged and prepared for a sexual assault. Her legal claim alleges xAI breached data protection law and misused her private information by allowing Grok to use her image and create false images.

‌



Documents filed by her lawyers allege that Grok was instructed to operate with "no restrictions on adult sexual content or offensive content", to "assume good intent", and to offer "no restrictions on fictional adult sexual content with dark or violent themes".

‌



The claim also alleges the chatbot added explicit material when users had not asked it to.

View 2 Images Elon Musk's xAI faced a global backlash over the spread of non-consensual deepfakes of women and children (Image: AFP via Getty Images)

‌



Lawyers acting for Ms Asato argue that the company behind Grok should be held accountable for the design and training choices that enabled the abuse. If successful, the case will set a precedent for liability for AI system design.

Ms Asato was targeted after speaking out against Grok amid an explosion in non-consensual sexualized and "nudified" deepfake photos of women and children on Mr Musk's X platform earlier this year.

The Lowestoft MP told the Mirror: "It feels demeaning and degrading because that's what it's designed to do. Users have used Grok as a weapon to humiliate women, and so my first reaction was to feel that it was humiliating and targeting me specifically as an elected woman. But of course, this can happen to anybody."

‌



Ms Asato said the hyper-realistic photos, which included a fake image depicting her as pregnant, were disorientating. "It makes you start to question yourself," she said. "Mostly, I was just very angry that anybody would do this without my consent."

She said AI had been allowed to develop without clear guardrails, but some firms have put protections in place. Of Grok, she said: "This is a product that has been developed without any concern for the social harms it might create. This is a product for profit.

"This isn't a free exercise. This is the basis on which Elon Musk and his companies make their money. And there ought to be, I think, a real understanding that people cannot make money off the back of harm to women and children."

‌



In the four weeks after proceedings were issued on June 3, Ms Asato said she was subjected to more than 700 abusive posts on X, including explicit content, from users angered by her decision to take on Mr Musk's company.

Ravi Naik, Legal Director at AWO, the law firm which is representing Ms Asato, said: “Deepfake abuse isn't a rogue user exploiting a loophole. xAI built a tool that generated non-consensual sexual images of real women at scale, and it took lawyers to get those images taken down. The claim lays bare why xAI are and should be held responsible for the harm they caused.

“The case shows that Grok did not malfunction. Grok's training allowed it to generate harmful sexualised content. Grok behaved according to the choices its designers made. Those choices should carry legal consequences. The remedy our client seeks includes a court order requiring the systems be brought into compliance if xAI refuses to do so.”

‌



TV star Narinder Kaur, who has herself been the victim of AI-generated deepfake abuse, said: "I've experienced first-hand how AI can be weaponised.

"Fake videos and manipulated images of me have been shared online in an attempt to humiliate me and silence me. Technology companies can't keep blaming users while ignoring the way their own products have been designed and trained to abuse."

Keir Starmer's Government intervened earlier this year amid a global backlash over Grok. He told MPs at the time: “The actions of Grok and X are absolutely disgusting and shameful.” Technology Secretary Liz Kendall made it illegal to create or request non-consensual, intimate images.

Article continues below

Earlier this year, X said it would block the ability of users to use Grok to create images of real people in bikinis, underwear or similar attire, in countries where it was illegal. Mr Musk said at the time: "Anyone using Grok to make illegal content will suffer the same consequences as if they upload illegal content."

xAI was approached for comment.

News.title: Cold case cops face race against time to solve 40-year Suzy Lamplugh riddle as they reveal 'prime suspect'
News.content:
Cold case cops face race against time to solve 40-year Suzy Lamplugh riddle as they reveal 'prime suspect'

Scotland Yard's cold case homicide unit have issued a last-ditch plea for information which may help locate estate agent Suzy Lamplugh's body - exactly 40 years after she was abducted and killed

View 10 Images Suzy Lamplugh's heartbroken family released new pictures of the estate agent to make the 40th anniversary of her unsolved murder

Cold case detectives probing the murder of missing Suzy Lamplugh are convinced they know who killed her - but face a race against time to solve the 40-year riddle.

‌



Scotland Yard detectives today said John Cannan remained the "prime suspect" in the estate agent's 1986 abduction after years eliminating other suspects, including "Suffolk Strangler" Steve Wright. Convicted rapist Cannan took his secrets to his grave after dying in 2024 in his cell at HMP Full Sutton, in East Yorkshire, aged 70.

‌



Following Cannan's death, detectives sifted through his prison writings in the hope they would hold clues to unlock Suzy's disappearance. Despite failing to unearth any new evidence and a lack of forensics, it's emerged officers still believe circumstantial evidence makes Cannan the most likely suspect.

‌



View 10 Images In 2002, Scotland Yard detectives publicly named convicted rapist John Cannan as Suzy's killer but he died in 2024 in prison aged 70 (Image: SWNS)

Holly Willoughby reveals how she rebuilt her life after Gavin Plumb kidnap plot ordeal READ MORE :

It came as detectives also said they would begin winding down the 40-year investigation - one of the biggest missing persons investigations in UK history - and classify it as "inactive" over the next year. It means they have just months to trace 30 people who may have key information about the murder, in the hope of tracing Suzy's body.

Today, in a last-ditch plea for help, the Metropolitan Police's Detective Chief Inspector Teresa Foster said: "Please help us find Suzy's body." Referring to prime suspect Cannan, she added: "I think John Cannan is a very good suspect. I think he's a prime suspect. He has been a focus of the investigation, but he has not been the only focus. There have been other names put forward over the last few years, but again, each of them have been eliminated from the investigation."

‌



View 10 Images Estate agent Suzy Lamplugh vanished on July 18, 1986 in a case that made headlines across the globe (Image: Met Police/REX/Shutterstock)

Detectives admit they missed any opportunity to secure Cannan's confession before his death. Det Chief Insp Foster said: "Up until [his death] there were efforts made to speak to him again. So with him dying, we would not be able to bring justice anymore. And it's going to have to be forensics really to point to if he did do it. He's a good suspect, but I'm keeping an open mind."

View 10 Images Today, it is exactly 40 years since estate agent Suzy vanished after going to meet a 'Mr Kipper' in Fulham, London (Image: SWNS)

‌



Cannan - who when he died was serving a 35-year life sentence for the 1989 murder and rape of Shirley Banks, 29, in Bristol - always denied any involvement in 25-year-old Suzy's disappearance on July 28, 1986. She went to meet a client known as "Mr Kipper" in Fulham, west London, when she vanished. Her body was never found and in 1993 she was declared dead, presumed murdered. Cannan was given the nickname “Kipper” by people at a bail hostel where he lived at the time of the murder — due to his fondness for the fish and a habit of having a “kip”.

In 2002, Scotland Yard detectives named killer Cannan but the Crown Prosecution Service said there was insufficient evidence to charge him.

The cold case unit is sitting on a trove of evidence consisting of 3,000 documents and 80,000 pieces of physical material. Detectives are also still using the carousel card system with 26,000 entries from the original investigation - the only remaining Met investigation where this historic system remains in active use.

‌



View 10 Images Before his conviction for abducting and murdering Shirley Banks, Cannan filmed a dating video for prospective partners

Now, on the 40th anniversary of Suzy's murder, police have revealed they reviewed all DNA evidence from the abandoned white Ford Fiesta found less than a mile from where she was last seen. Seat tapings, fibres and DNA recovered from the vehicle during a forensics review in 2018 were sent for mitochondrial testing in the USA.

It was hoped the piece of evidence may throw up some familial link but it failed to identify any suspects. Detectives now hope advances in forensic testing and artificial intelligence may help crack the case. Police have also been unable to identify a smudged fingerprint found on the rearview mirror and are yet to match it to a DNA profile on their records. It did not match Cannan's DNA profile.

‌



View 10 Images New pictures show Suzy beaming as she poses for the camera before her 1986 murder

Digs have been carried out across the UK - including a 2018 excavation of Cannan's mother's home in Sutton Coldfield, West Midlands - but no trace has ever been found of Suzy. Detectives also reviewed evidence recovered during a huge dredge of the Grand Union Canal in London as part of a police probe into the murder of 14-year-old Alice Gross in 2014. However, nothing of significance was found.

View 10 Images Suzy's company car, a white Ford Fiesta, was found by cops in Stevenage Road at 10.01pm on the day she vanished (Image: Mirrorpix)

‌



Det Chief Insp Foster said: "It has been 40 years, we're not going to give up on trying to find Suzy. But it is difficult. It is going to take a change in forensics or technology, or a change of allegiance to someone with new information."

Police also say they have ruled out "Suffolk Strangler" Steve Wright as a suspect in Suzy's disappearance. The 68-year-old serial killer - who is serving a whole-life tariff for killing six women - was said to be besotted with the estate agent after they worked together during cruises on the QE2 in the 1980s.

View 10 Images Missing Suzy Lamplugh (right) with her siblings, (left to right) Lizzie, Richard and Tamsin (Image: Family Handout/PA Wire)

‌



But detectives say that since he was jailed earlier this for the 1999 murder of 17-year-old Victoria Hall hey have spoken to SEVENTEEN of his crew mates who denied he had a relationship with Suzy. And police say he was on board the ship on the day Suzy vanished - with it docking at Southampton at 4.30pm - hours after Suzy was reported missing. Det Chief Insp Foster said: "There's nothing to indicate any sort of relationship between [Suzy and Wright]. So we ruled him out."

View 10 Images Suffolk Strangler Steve Wright was probed over Suzy's disappearance but ruled out by cold case detectives earlier this year (Image: Copyright unknown)

Suzy's daylight disappearance made headlines across the globe and shattered the illusion of routine daytime safety. It permanently changed how British workplaces approach lone working and personal protection and the Suzy Lamplugh Trust - set-up to tackle stalking - was born. Det Chief Insp today said her officers remained "haunted" by the case.

‌



She said: "It does frustrate us. We've never found who did it. I think everybody who lives in London, can think, 'That could have been me'. I was 12 years old and I come from a small town in New Zealand. This was a huge story then, and it was just shocking. And I think we are invested in this, it upsets us because we're very close to the family as well." She added: "This was a big news story, a woman being snatched that from the street."

View 10 Images The disappearance of Suzy - pictured with her family in 1984 - shattered the illusion of routine daytime safety in the UK (Image: Carl Fox)

Det Chief Insp Foster said: "Obviously, the key thing is always to bring somebody to justice, but that's likely not going to happen if Cannan is the person who was responsible. Our priority is finding Susan. We are 40 years on, so if it wasn't Cannan and if it was somebody else, it's likely they would be dead too. So for us and for Susan's family, it is about finding her, finding her remains to bring her back."

Article continues below

In 2024, Cannan wrote to the Mirror insisting he did not kill Suzy and accusing police of prejudice against him. He claimed to have an alibi for the day she vanished and said police had pointed the finger at him to "divert attention from themselves". Cannan said that on July 28, 1986, the day Suzy disappeared, he had been in Birmingham “treating my mother to a spot of lunch”.

News.title: Women still face threat of stalking 40 years after Suzy Lamplugh disappeared
News.content:
Women still face threat of stalking 40 years after Suzy Lamplugh disappeared

Emma Lingley-Clark, the Interim CEO of the Suzy Lamplugh Trust, said it is "a really sad fact" that the charity is having to do the same work for women's safety 40 years on from the estate agent's disappearance

View 4 Images No trace of Suzy Lampligh has ever been recovered despite a series of police reviews into her disappearance in 1986 (Image: Mirrorpix)

The head of the Suzy Lamplugh Trust has said the threat facing women is as great today as it was in 1986 when the estate agent was murdered.

‌



In the wake of Suzy's disappearance, her mother, Diana, threw herself tirelessly into setting up the Suzy Lamplugh Trust. Its aim was to improve awareness of personal safety. Diana and husband Paul both received OBEs in 1992 but died without ever finding out what happened to Suzy.

‌



Today, on the 40th anniversary of Suzy's disappearance, Emma Lingley-Clark, the Interim CEO of the Suzy Lamplugh Trust, said: "It's something that is actually a really sad fact that 40 years on from Suzy's disappearance, we are still having to do the work that we do around campaigning and supporting victims.

‌



"Ideally, I think we'd all have hoped that by now, perhaps some of these issues might have gone away. But for us, the cause is still very much there."

View 4 Images Emma Lingley-Clark, the Interim CEO of the Suzy Lamplugh Trust, said stalking should be taken more seriously (Image: Suzy Lamplugh Trust)

The trust works to support stalking victims, including running the National Stalking Helpline, as well as campaigning on issues such as public sexual harassment and minimum safety standards for taxis and minicabs, and training employers to keep staff safe.

‌



The alarm was only raised six hours after Suzy, 25, was last seen at work in Fulham, west London. Detective Chief Inspector Teresa Foster, who leads the Metropolitan Police's cold case homicide squad, believes Suzy may have been targeted by a stalker after her employers made her sit in the window because she was attractive and could draw in customers.

She said: "I do think that she was targeted. She was put in the window because her employers thought she was attractive and would bring in people. I'm more inclined to believe that stalking side, that someone has seen her, a predator of some type, and then lured her into a false meeting."

View 4 Images Suzy's parents Paul and Diana Lamplugh set up the charity in the wake of their daughter going missing from her job as an estate agent in 1986 (Image: PA )

‌



There are an estimated 1.5 million victims of stalking in the UK, and the trust has seen an increase in the number of cases linked to domestic abuse.

Around 40% of stalking cases reported to the national helpline are not carried out by partners or ex-partners but by friends, colleagues or strangers.

Ms Lingley-Clark said: "From our perspective, it's about making sure that every victim is taken seriously when they do report. We would like to see more people come forward, we would like more support, so ideally, we would like everybody to have access to a specialist stalking advocate.

‌



View 4 Images Suzy Lamplugh disappeared 40 years ago today (Image: SWNS)

"Often, they can access support, but it's not somebody who actually understands stalking, understands the dynamic nature of the risk and how it changes.

"And I think more generally we would like to just have society believe that stalking is wrong. I think in some instances we're still seeing quite a lot of jokes made about stalking and and really not reflecting the serious nature of it and and how actually it has such a big impact on victims."

‌



Detective Superintendent Ian Martin, who leads on domestic abuse and stalking for the Metropolitan Police, said stalking has changed dramatically since the time of Miss Lamplugh's disappearance because of the technology now available.

He said: "That case had a profound impact on the community. The methodology is completely different now because of the technology that's available.

"We're seeing people tracked through online fitness apps, through social media, and through a number of methodologies that weren't even in existence back then. The impact that that has on victims cannot be underestimated."

‌



Officers use the acronym FOUR to help victims determine whether they are being stalked - behaviour that is fixated, obsessive, unwanted and repetitive.

Det Supt Martin said: "They should look out for people who are taking an interest in what may seem a mundane, day-to-day activity. Are there people that turn up at locations that they don't recognise and they repeatedly see them, or is it a partner? Is it an ex-partner who has tried to get back into their life?

"Stalking can take place in a domestic situation, but also in a non-domestic one, and equally as important. So it's about being vigilant and aware of that. Have people tried to befriend them online repeatedly, even though they might be blocked? Is there somebody who's in their workplace or a friendship club that's taking a particular interest?

Article continues below

"There's a number of different flags that they could look out for but, again, I'd reiterate: if it's fixated, obsessive, unwanted and repeated, and they're recognising that, then do notify the police."

He added: "Stalking can lead to significant events and physical harm. So, identifying stalking cases early on, reporting them to the police is hugely important in a way that we prevent that further impact of injury taking place."

News.title: Search continues for missing baby after bodies of woman, toddler pulled from ocean
News.content:
Search continues for missing baby after bodies of woman, toddler pulled from ocean

While police are “keeping an open mind about everything" they did not “hold out great hope” for the baby. “The child is less than one year old,” one officer told the press

View 4 Images Search continues for missing baby after bodies of woman, toddler pulled from ocean (Image: 9News)

A search remains underway for a missing infant with police expressing 'grave concerns' for the baby after the bodies of a mother and toddler were pulled from the sea. The state emergency service and police were called to a beach in South Australia on Monday (July 28) just after 11am local time after a car was found west of Port MacDonnell with its engine still running. Officers will resume their search for the missing baby in the coastal waters of the small town, 477 kilometres south-east of the state capital of Adelaide, on Tuesday morning.

‌



Superintendent Trent Cox said on Monday (July 27) that the baby was with the 36-year-old mum earlier in the day.

‌



View 4 Images Police hold grave fears for a missing baby after the bodies of a 36-year-old mum and a toddler were pulled from the water

‌



“The baby is known to have been with the mother earlier that day but as to whether the baby was still with her when the vehicle was left, that’s open to speculation,” Cox said, adding: “I honestly don’t know.” He said while police were “keeping an open mind about everything" they did not “hold out great hope” for the baby. “The child is less than one year old,” he told NCA. He added: “In any conditions, that would cause great concern about the child’s ability to survive, if not in the water.”

The search for the missing child was called off on Monday night after conditions became too dangerous to continue. The break at Port MacDonnell as per time of writing is producing five footers, or waves two times overhead. Water temperatures are 15C and the temperature out of the water is 12C - very cold conditions. SA Police will continue the search on Tuesday, as officers are determined "to find the missing child”, Superintendent Cox said.

‌



View 4 Images The search will resume today in the waters not far from Mount Gambier

“We wish incidents like this didn’t happen, but we’ve got to maintain the safety of not just emergency services, but we’ve been assisted by a number of volunteers as well with their boats. We need to be very much aware of their welfare," he said, “The conditions were not easy for the waterborne assets, and I’m led to believe that (Tuesday) is not going to be an easy day either.” He added the incident was “tragic” for everyone involved. I can’t imagine what the family are going through.

View 4 Images Police have since released an image of the car believed to belong to the woman; a white Isuzu MU-X, with the rego S592 BJR

Article continues below

“It’s tragic for them. It’s an awful thing for emergency services and the community to have to deal with.” Police have since released an image of the car that they say belonged to the woman. Anyone who may have seen a white Isuzu MU-X, with South Australian registration S592 BJR, in the Mount Gambier, Compton, or Port MacDonnell areas on Monday are urged to contact Crime Stoppers.

News.title: Police arrest 15-year-old after festival shooting which killed three at iconic Space Needle
News.content:
Police arrest 15-year-old after festival shooting which killed three at iconic Space Needle

Three people were killed and at least four others injured after a gunman opened fire in a crowd at a food festival over the weekend - a 15-year-old has been arrested in connect to the incident

View 3 Images Police have arrested a 15-year-old over a shooting at a festival (Image: Associated Press)

Police have arrested a 15-year-old over a shooting at a festival that killed three people.

‌



The shooting took place near Seattle's Space Needle over the weekend.

‌



At least four others sustained injuries at the crowded food festival, the city's mayor Katie Wilson said on Monday.

‌



View 3 Images The shooting took place near Seattle's Space Needle (Image: Associated Press)

"Shortly after 6pm last night, officers responded to the sound of gunfire," she said. "They... were on scene within seconds and took one suspect into custody."

Ms Wilson said that it is believed two people exchanged gunfire outside the Seattle Center Armory.

‌



A 19-year-old man, 44-year-old man and a 56-year-old woman lost their lives.

A 15-year-old was detained by police in connection with the shooting.

View 3 Images Police responded to the sound of gunfire shortly after 6pm (Image: Associated Press)

‌



"We believe this teenager opened fire in the crowd but details are still under investigation," said Ms Wilson.

The search for a possible second suspect is ongoing. Faith Adia Hunter said she and her friends had just got food from a crepe vendor when gunfire broke out.

Ms Hunter realised a gunman was near them.

‌



She and others found shelter in the nearby Seattle Children’s Museum.

“We were right next to him when it started so we took off running,” Ms Hunter said.

“So we took off running too into the building with the crowd.” Many vendors bolted towards the exits when the gunfire rang out, abandoning their food stands.

‌



Hours afterwards, some milled outside the police tape, wondering when they would be allowed to return to collect their tents, food and cooking gear.

Roberto Ramirez, a vendor at the event, said he heard what sounded like firecrackers before people began yelling “shooter” and frantically running.

“Suddenly everything was empty,” he said. “People were freaked out.”

News.title: France wildfires live: Inferno is country's 'most difficult situation since WW2' - Macron
News.content:
More than 220,000 people in south-west France's Gironde region have been evacuated as raging wildfires approach Bordeaux

French President Emmanuel Macron has claimed the raging wildfires are the 'most difficult situation' his country has dealt with since World War Two.

Fierce wildfires are currently burning seven miles from the French city of Bordeaux and its airport, with more than 220,000 people evacuated from their homes in the south-west of the country.

Firefighters are struggling to contain the flames, which have burned 42,000 hectares - an area four times the size of Paris - leaving two firefighters dead and 88 injured. Volunteers, including local farmers, are helping by towing huge water tankers to the scene.

France's Interior Minister Laurent Nuñez says the 'unprecedented' wildfires have developed a "life of their own," while Bordeaux's mayor has labelled the blaze the "fire of the century" that could take months to extinguish.

Meanwhile in Spain, 25,000 people have been ordered to evacuate and almost 40,000 have been told to stay indoors. Wildfires near Madrid "slowed their advance" overnight but remain active, the regional government said today.

News.title: Devastating European wildfires in maps - and how they're being tackled
News.content:
Wildfires are tearing through France and Spain, forcing more than 300,000 people to evacuate their homes.

France has seen its worst fires in two decades, while officials in the Spanish capital Madrid say they are the worst the region has ever experienced.

It follows a sweltering summer of heatwaves across Europe that have seen temperatures soar above 40C (104F) in many places.

Separate wildfires in the regions outside Madrid have together burned about 297 sq miles (770 sq km), authorities estimate - an area larger than Madrid itself.

News.title: Reform UK reports Zack Polanski to police over guillotine T-shirt post
News.content:
Reform UK have reported Green Party leader Zack Polanski to the police, after he shared an Instagram post including a photo of a man wearing a top featuring the name "Nigel" alongside an image of a guillotine.

One of several images showed a man in a black t-shirt with a large guillotine below the words "We're only making plans for Nigel".

Sharing a screenshot on X, Reform UK leader Nigel Farage said: "If I was to post anything as inciteful then I would expect to be arrested, and so should Polanski."

A Green Party spokesperson said: "Once this image was brought to [Zack's] attention he immediately unshared the post. He unequivocally does not support this type of dangerous message."

Polanski had shared the photo with his 713,000 followers in a post containing several pictures of a Green Party event on Sunday, having accepted a request to collaborate with another account.

In a post on X, the Metropolitan Police said: "We received a third-party report relating to an image shared on social media. We take reports of this nature extremely seriously, and officers are conducting enquiries into the matter."

The words "We're only making plans for Nigel" are the same as the lyrics of a 1979 song by band XTC, external.

The Green Party spokesperson said: "Zack condemns the image on the T-shirt. He was tagged in a post with 20 images and clicked accept without realising there was more to it than he had seen.

"The T-shirt is clearly in poor taste, especially at a time of heightened fears for the security of public figures, having experienced multiple threats himself.

"He and the Green Party call on everyone involved in public discourse to show kindness and not encourage more division."

The BBC understands Polanski has not been contacted by police.

News.title: New technical education routes to be offered at 14 in England
News.content:
Pupils will be able to study subjects like manufacturing and AI alongside core academic learning from age 14 under new government plans for education in England.

The government said the courses available from Year 10 would be linked to local jobs and industries.

The announcement comes after data published earlier this year showed more than one million young people across the UK were not in education, employment or training, or "Neet" - the highest level in more than 12 years.

School leaders' unions welcomed the government's ambition to improve technical education, but called for greater clarity on how and when the changes would be implemented, and how they would be paid for.

Prime Minister Andy Burnham said "for too long" students had been told to take academic subjects to "do well and be respected".

"My message to young people is this - whether you choose construction, coding or classics, or maths, manufacturing or mechanics, you'll get the skills you need and be given the respect you deserve," he said.

He said the government was delivering the "major shake-up" required to fix the youth unemployment crisis in Britain, starting with improving the availability and quality of technical education.

This would provide students with skills training, work experience and connections with employers, the government said.

It said students would have the chance to combine core academic subjects such as English and maths with a high-quality technical education linked to the jobs available in their area.

"They will be able to spend time with employers and gain real-world experience," it said.

The BBC understands that the government expects the new pathways into work to be up and running in some areas by 2028.

News.title: Man jailed for abduction and rape of girl, 15, in Edinburgh basement
News.content:
A masked rapist who abducted a 15-year-old girl from an Edinburgh city centre bus stop has been jailed under a lifelong restriction order.

Aaron Strachan, 21, pulled a knife on the girl on the city's Princes Street in May last year, before marching her to a basement storage area and raping her.

The High Court in Edinburgh heard that he also attacked a man with a hammer days later, and had a criminal record of violence, robbery and possession of weapons.

Strachan was jailed for a minimum of five years with an order for lifelong restriction (OLR). It means a parole board must decide if he is ever safe to be released.

Judge Michael O'Grady described Strachan's crimes as the "stuff of nightmares".

Strachan admitted raping the girl and charges of serious assault against two male victims in December last year.

The judge said he expected Strachan to be in custody or under supervision for the rest of his life.

News.title: Love Island UK crowns winners of twist-filled series
News.content:
This article contains spoilers for the Love Island final.

Julia Majchrzak and Lorenzo Alessi have been crowned the winners of Love Island UK 2026.

The pair beat runners-up Jasmine Muller and Kavan Murphy, and Angelista Gunda and Simba Kudyiwa, who came in third, to take home the Â£50,000 prize.

A shocked Julia thanked all those who had voted for them, saying: "I just didn't think coming into Casa [Amor] I'd be stood here."

When host Maya Jama asked what they would spend the money on, Julia revealed she wanted Lorenzo, who appeared too stunned to speak, to move in with her after leaving the villa.

Talking to Maya ahead of the reveal during the live final, 28-year-old Lorenzo said he had "never met someone who feels so well matched to me" when reflecting on his relationship with Julia.

Business owner Lorenzo, who entered the villa on day one, said he felt like he "manifested" meeting Julia, 26, in Casa Amor, the alternate villa where relationships are tested by new arrivals.

Julia said she felt an "instant spark" when meeting Lorenzo and described their relationship as "seriously unserious".

News.title: Fourth heatwave grips parts of UK with 35C forecast
News.content:
A fourth heatwave of the year is now under way for parts of the UK, with temperatures expected to climb into the mid-30s Celsius later this week.

This latest spell of heatwave threshold-level temperatures is expected to peak on Wednesday in the south-east and east of England.

The UK Health Security Agency (UKHSA) has warned the rising temperatures could increase health risks, particularly for vulnerable groups.

It has issued amber heat health alerts, external for much of eastern England that come into force on Wednesday.

News.title: Hundreds of thousands of women get morning-after pill via free pharmacy service
News.content:
The morning-after pill, known as emergency contraception, external, is medication designed to prevent unwanted pregnancies. It usually has to be taken within three to five days of having unprotected sex. The sooner it is taken, the more effective it is.

It works by delaying or preventing the release of an egg, but will only prevent pregnancy if ovulation has not already happened.

Alternatively, women can visit a doctor or nurse to have a coil or intrauterine device (IUD) fitted to prevent pregnancy at any time during their menstrual cycle. To be effective, it needs to be fitted within 120 hours or five days of unprotected sex.

The government said making the morning-after pill available free from pharmacies would end the "unfair" barriers and postcode lottery some women faced - with access varying dramatically depending on where they live.

Under the scheme, women can visit their local pharmacy and have a confidential consultation with a pharmacist or trained pharmacy technician, before receiving the medication on the same day.

Prior to this, women had to book an appointment with their GP, sexual health clinic or pharmacy to get the morning-after pill. Women could also access it privately, as they still can now.

In 2024/25, there were around 150,000 NHS prescriptions for the morning-after pill - far fewer than under the new service.

Dr Sue Mann, NHS National Clinical Director for Women's Health, said the pharmacy service was a "major step forward for women's health", with "no appointment, no waiting and no judgement".

"This service is already making a real impact, particularly for women living in more deprived communities, by making contraception easier to access closer to home," she added.

Women can check online, external to find their nearest participating pharmacy. All pharmacists and pharmacy technicians delivering the service have received specialist training to provide emergency contraception and wider contraceptive care.

News.title: Badenoch calls for emergency legislation to stop early release scheme
News.content:
Conservative leader Kemi Badenoch has called for Prime Minister Andy Burnham to bring in emergency legislation in order to stop the early release of hundreds of prisoners.

Burnham announced last week that he was pausing the scheme, which would have seen about 700 prisoners freed in the first phase in September, following a backlash from survivors and victims.

But the Conservatives say the government's review will not stop offenders being released.

The scheme was part of a bid to stop unprecedented overcrowding, which Labour says was caused by Conservative governments failing to build new prisons.

A Labour spokesperson said: "It's this government that is fixing the Tories' mess."

Early release was first used by the Conservative government, external in 2023 because of prison overcrowding, first for 18 and then 70 days, and 10,000 prisoners had been released early by June 2024 - before Labour came to power.

When Sir Keir Starmer entered Downing Street in July 2024, there were fewer than 100 spare prison places across the adult male estate, which is what prompted the Sentencing Act to release another 6,000 prisoners early from September.

While the act already excludes the most serious and dangerous offenders, such as murderers serving life sentences or those on extended sentences, the eligibility for early release is based on the length of sentence, external, rather than the type of offence.

Badenoch is calling on Burnham to fast-track legislation to keep serious offenders behind bars.

"It's all well and good cutting bills and bus fares, but that pales into insignificance when paedophiles and rapists are about to be let out on our streets," she is expected to say at a press conference with victims on Tuesday.

"Burnham needs to show us he's ready to take the tough decisions."

Without emergency legislation, Badenoch says dangerous offenders will start to be released the day after MPs return to Parliament after the summer recess on Tuesday 1 September.

She is calling on Burnham to revoke legislation coming into effect on 2 September and if necessary recall Parliament to ensure the worst violent and sexual offenders are exempted from early release.

Conservative shadow justice secretary Nick Timothy said: "Victims should not have to live in fear all summer waiting for a review.

"The clock is ticking. Thousands of rapists, paedophiles, and other serious criminals are set to be released in September.

"Labour must act now and stop the mass release of dangerous criminals."

Earlier this month, the Conservative front bench sought to put pressure on the government to rethink the earlier release plans, saying that it would mean some rapists would leave prison sooner than expected.

The government stood by the plan, saying it was a political choice to manage offenders on strict conditions in the community, rather than see the collapse of the system, leaving sex offenders and others to act with impunity.

Burnham's decision to pause the scheme came after criticism from the family of Thames Valley Police officer Andrew Harper, who was killed in Berkshire in 2019 when he was dragged by a car down a country road by three teenagers.

Two of the killers of PC Harper, who were both sentenced to 13 years in prison, would have benefited from the scheme from June 2027, when the longest fixed sentences would have been added.

PC Harper's widow Lissie called the plans "deplorable" and said politicians were "making decisions from behind a desk that will have real and lasting consequences" for the families of victims.

Defending the review of the Sentencing Act that has been announced by Burnham, a Labour Party spokesperson said: "The Conservatives have some nerve.

"During their 14 years in office, they shut 23 prisons, created just 482 jail places, and granted early release to 10,000 prisoners - leaving the criminal justice system teetering on verge of collapse.

"It's this government that is fixing the Tories' mess. We have already delivered over 3,000 prison places and we're investing billions to deliver thousands more."

Liberal Democrat justice spokesperson Jess Brown-Fuller MP said: "The reality is that in a properly functioning justice system, no victim or loved ones should ever be told that their perpetrator is being released earlier than expected.

"Unfortunately, the Conservatives left our prisons on the brink of collapse, creating a capacity crisis that required emergency action to keep the system functioning and the public safe.

"Now that the government claims to have increased prison capacity, there is a clear opportunity for Burnham to correct some of the mistakes made by his predecessors with this scheme."

Reform UK's Home Affairs spokesperson Zia Yusuf said the "disastrous" policy had been introduced by the Tories, and Badenoch had in 2024 supported efforts to expand it.

"It's clear that only one party has consistently opposed early release and proposed strong law and order reforms to ensure hardened criminals are locked up for the full duration of their sentences," Yusuf said in a statement.

"Only Reform UK will fix lawless Britain," the party's Home Affairs spokesperson added.

News.title: Funeral director who left people unburied breached families' trust 'on industrial scale', court hears
News.content:
A funeral director who failed to bury people and gave out wrong ashes has breached the trust of bereaved families "on an almost industrial scale", a court has heard.

Some 35 bodies and more than 100 sets of ashes were found by police raiding Legacy Independent Funeral Directors in Hull in March 2024.

Owner Robert Bush previously admitted 67 offences, including 30 counts of preventing a lawful and decent burial, and theft from 12 charities.

At the start of his five-day sentencing hearing on Monday, family members watching proceedings at Hull Crown Court gasped and were in tears as details of the "horror scene" at the parlour were described by prosecutors.

This story contains details some might find distressing.

Chris Paxton KC told the packed court bodies had been discovered "on the racks" of a cold storage area and one was found on a stretcher on the floor.

The vast majority were "uncovered and in varying states of decomposition", including one of a stillborn baby.

Bush, 48, was "entrusted by hundreds of bereaved families" but had "breached that trust on an almost industrial scale in a myriad of ways", Paxton said.

News.title: Very strong tide led to West Mersea drownings, relative says
News.content:
A mother and daughter who drowned off the Essex coast were swept out to sea by a "very strong" tide, a relative has said.

Shahin Ahmed said six members of his family were paddling at West Mersea beach when they were knocked off their feet on Wednesday afternoon.

Shelina Rahman, 41, and 15-year-old Sameeha, died in the tragedy, while Ahmed's seven-year-old son Musa was airlifted to hospital in a critical condition.

Ahmed said his son, who is from east London, remained on a life support machine at a hospital in London.

Three others were also taken to another hospital by ambulance after the incident. Ahmed said 12 of them were visiting West Mersea that day.

"This was 20 minutes before we were going to go home. The whole day, alhamdulillah (praise be to God), was really nice," Ahmed told Bangladeshi newspaper Surma News.

News.title: Zelensky visit sends clear message of support for Ukraine, Burnham says
News.content:
Andy Burnham has said the UK is "with Ukraine 100%" as Volodymyr Zelensky became the prime minister's first international visitor since entering No 10.

Burnham said the visit of the Ukrainian president was designed to "send a very clear message" about the UK's continued support.

"To put it simply, Volodymyr, I want you to know that we've got your back, you can count on me and you can count on us. You can count on the UK for as long as it takes," he said at a naval base in Portsmouth on Monday.

Zelensky, meanwhile, said Ukraine's relationship with the UK was "stronger than ever".

Addressing Zelensky, Burnham said: "I am personally with you 100%, Mr President, and I will honour every commitment this country has made to Ukraine in full."

Burnham added that he intended to visit Ukraine "soon" following the "very warm meeting" between the pair.

The PM also announced the sharing of the intellectual property behind the UK's new "Stone Cloak" electronic warfare system, enabling Ukraine to produce the technology at scale.

Burnham said: "It will help them to hit their targets and help save Ukrainian lives."

The Stone Cloak jammers are the size of a tablet computer and are designed to block the detection of any drones they are fitted to.

The Ministry of Defence has already given thousands of the devices to Ukrainian forces to bolster their drone operations.

Downing Street said that following its deployment in Ukraine, the technology will be built into the UK's next generation of long-range weapons.

It said this would include Project Brakestop, a government programme to develop low-cost cruise missiles - self-propelled guided weapons that fly like normal aircraft for much of their flight.

During Monday's visit, the two leaders also met more than 200 Ukrainian military personnel who have spent the last three weeks taking part in a maritime exercise in the UK.

Exercise Sea Breeze is aimed at strengthening warfighting capabilities and counter-mine measures in the Black Sea.

Burnham also said the UK would support Ukraine to get a "full and unconditional ceasefire".

"We will keep up the pressure, pushing for a ceasefire and a resumption of negotiations which must have Ukraine at the table and include a strong voice for Europe too."

News.title: TV presenter and comedian Bill Oddie dies at 85
News.content:
TV presenter and comedian Bill Oddie has died at the age of 85, his agent has said.

Oddie became a household name in the 1970s as part of zany TV comedy trio The Goodies, before concentrating on his love of wildlife, as one of the original hosts of BBC TV's Springwatch and other shows about birdwatching.

In a statement, David Foster said: "It is with deep sadness that I announce the passing of Bill Oddie, the country's best-loved birder.

"Bill was a multi-talented celebrity â wildlife presenter, broadcaster, comedian, writer, songwriter, musician and conservationist. Yet it was never fame that he valued. Instead he encouraged us to respect and protect the environment."

News.title: 'Antisemitism felt relentless' - Jewish students on life at UK universities
News.content:
Like many campuses across the UK, Cardiff University has seen pro-Palestine protests in recent years and Oliver said he believed some behaviour he witnessed crossed the line from criticism of Israel into antisemitism.

Holding Jewish people responsible for the actions of the Israeli government is a form of antisemitism, according to the International Holocaust Remembrance Alliance.

"That first year was absolutely terrifying," he said.

"You go home and think, 'do I carry on? Do I try to go to the next day?'"

Oliver said he stopped speaking Hebrew outside his home, and hid his Star of David pendant when on campus.

Over the following three years, Oliver said the antisemitic abuse he experienced at university became "relentless".

"I've been in clubs [or] just wandering around the uni and you hear these conversations and you see pamphlets being handed around where it's literally saying that your belief and your history is fake," he said.

"I've been at house parties where, when someone's found out I'm Jewish they started calling me Netanyahu behind my back.

"Like you found out my religion and you've decided I'm a bad person."

Oliver said when he had reported antisemitic incidents that had happened to him and others, he had felt they had been often "swept under the rug" by the university.

Although he said some positive action had been taken, he feels more needs to be done.

Cardiff University said it was sorry that "any student felt unsafe" on campus and that it adopts a "zero-tolerance approach to harassment and discrimination of all kinds".

It said there was no place for antisemitism or hatred at the university and there were "robust procedures" in place for investigating allegations of antisemitism. Where it is found, the university said appropriate action would be taken.

It said it had reached out to the university's Jewish Society and reminded students to report incidents to them.

News.title: Teen denies endangering lives of 165 people on migrant boat crossing
News.content:
A teenager accused of endangering the lives of 165 migrants by allegedly piloting a record-breaking dinghy crossing of the English Channel is to stand trial.

Chan Mathok Atak, 19, originally of Sudan, appeared at Margate Magistrates Court earlier, where he denied endangering lives at sea during the attempt which set off from France last Thursday.

He appeared with the aid of an Arabic interpreter and when asked how he wished to plea, denied having piloted the dinghy.

Atak was then remanded into custody and will next appear at Canterbury Crown Court on 24 August.

Prosecutor Lucie Fish told the court that, on Thursday, a rigid hulled inflatable boat departed the French coast headed towards Dover carrying the migrants.

The vessel was intercepted by Border Force and Atak is alleged to be one of two people controlling its speed and travel.

The boat was poor quality, overcrowded and "appeared to be deflating upon interception", the prosecutor added.

Pictures of Border Security Command towing the dinghy into Dover showed to be about the same size as a standard bus, at 13m (42ft) long.

During the hearing, the court heard that the French authorities had recovered the body of a man who had suffered head injuries - but there was no indication in court whether his death was related to the record-breaking dinghy.

A spokesman for the National Crime Agency told BBC News: "We are aware of an incident on Thursday 23 July in which an individual died in French waters. French partners are leading the investigation into the circumstances".

Endangerment at sea is a new offence that was created by the government under Sir Keir Starmer to target those alleged to have steered small boats over the English Channel.

In June, two men were the first to be jailed for the crime, each receiving sentences of more than two years.

The previous record arrival in a single vessel was 128 people.

Home Office figures show that while the overall number of arrivals this year is down by about 45% on 2025, the number of migrants per boat has gone up.

News.title: Ex political advisor admits fraud over expense claims
News.content:
A former advisor to a Labour MP has admitted claiming fraudulent expenses on the Parliamentary travel booking system.

Matthew Torbitt worked for Bury South MP Christian Wakeford when, between August 2022 and September 2024, he claimed rail tickets that were "not for Parliamentary purposes", Thames Magistrates' Court heard.

He also admitted making a false claim for travel and accommodation expenses on 2 October 2024.

Torbitt, 35, has most recently worked as a political commentator and regularly appears on programmes including GB News, LBC, Sky News, BBC Newsnight, and Times Radio.

Prosecutor Maisha Mannan told the court the claims totalled more than Â£6,000, according to an early estimate by the Crown Prosecution Service (CPS), but the exact sum will be calculated at a later date.

Torbitt, who appeared in court dressed in a navy blue suit, pleaded guilty to two counts of fraud by false representation.

District Judge Navneet Sher sent the case to Snaresbrook Crown Court for sentence at a later date, which has yet to be fixed.

"It's unlikely to be before four weeks, in any event," she told the defendant.

Torbitt worked in various advisory roles for Labour frontbenchers between 2018 and 2024.

An investigation was launched after police received a report that a member of staff working for an MP had allegedly made unauthorised purchases through a travel booking system, the Metropolitan Police previously said.

He was charged by postal requisition on 9 June.

Torbitt is engaged to women's rights activist and 2021 Love Island contestant Sharon Gaffka.

The couple welcomed a baby boy earlier this month, according to Torbitt's Instagram page.

News.title: UK's iconic Jodrell Bank telescope faces axe in science cuts
News.content:
The Jodrell Bank Observatory, which has housed the UK's largest telescope for nearly 70 years, has lost its funding and could now close, the BBC understands.

The observatory and its network of telescopes have been pivotal to the country's study of distant galaxies and training future astronomers. Scientists have described the decision as "heartbreaking" and "scientifically misguided".

All scientific observations at Jodrell are expected to cease on the 1 April 2028 unless alternative funding can be found.

The funding body, the UK Research and Innovation (UKRI) agency, said it had to focus investment on projects that deliver "the greatest long-term impact".

Prof Brian Cox, professor of particle physics at the University of Manchester - which hosts Jodrell Bank Observatory - described the cuts as "hasty and ill-considered".

"The damage to the UK's science base has already been substantial. I am astonished that UKRI are still ploughing ahead and not working with the Burnham government to find a solution," he said.

In response, Jonathan Reynolds, who is the new Secretary of State in the expanded business department that now has responsibility for science, told BBC News that the UK's world class research was "absolutely central to creating a better future for the UK".

"I am committed to working with UKRI to ensure the UK remains able not only to sustain its world-leading research capabilities, but also to invest in the next generation of scientific facilities and infrastructure that will underpin discovery, innovation and growth in the years ahead."

The Jodrell Bank site was first established in 1945 and pioneered radio astronomy and the study of galaxies beyond our own.

It was also pivotal during the Cold War, when it was used to monitor Soviet missiles during the height of nuclear tensions between the USSR and Nato powers.

Its contribution to global scientific efforts earned it Unesco World Heritage status in 2019.

But the UKRI, which has an annual budget of just under Â£10bn, says it has had to cut the observatory's annual Â£2.8m budget because planned research costs for physics and the running of its labs had escalated.

The announcement is part of broader cuts to astronomy, nuclear and particle physics research over the next four years which will also impact on other projects.

The UK will no longer participate in research at the James Clark Maxwell Telescope in Hawaii, which scientists are using to image supermassive black holes at the centre of galaxies.

UKRI has also cut funding for the UK's involvement in two instruments on the Extremely Large Telescope which is being built in Chile to search for signs of life on other Earth-like worlds.

And a number of upgrades to improve experiments at the Large Hadron Collider will not be paid for by the agency.

News.title: Seattle mass shooting victims identified, including 19-year-old suspect, as police search for third
News.content:
The latest headlines from our reporters across the US sent straight to your inbox each weekday Your briefing on the latest headlines from across the US Your briefing on the latest headlines from across the US Email * SIGN UP I would like to be emailed about offers, events and updates from The Independent. Read our Privacy notice

The three people who died in Sunday’s mass shooting at a Seattle food festival have been identified by officials, including a 19-year-old police believe engaged in the gunfight.

There were at least three suspects involved and a 15-year-old was detained in connection with the shooting near Seattle’s iconic Space Needle Sunday evening. Police are still searching for at least one other unknown suspect.

Carlos Israel Sanchez Villalba, 44, and 56-year-old Ashley Whitehead died in the shooting, the King County Medical Examiner said, along with 19-year-old Junior Cee Niko Semo.

Four others were injured, including a toddler, and the three adults have since been discharged from the hospital. The two-year-old boy was said to be in a satisfactory condition as of Monday evening.

The 15-year-old is being held in juvenile detention for investigation of firearms violations and first-degree assault.

open image in gallery Law enforcement believes the mass shooting at the Bite of Seattle food festival occurred because two suspects were shooting at each other ( Getty )

Shots rang out at the annual Bite of Seattle event, a street food and live music event for families held at the Seattle Center, a 74-acre entertainment and cultural complex downtown.

The attack is the latest of at least 271 mass shootings that have been recorded in the U.S. this year, according to the Gun Violence Archive.

What happened?

The festival was winding down at around 6. p.m. when the suspects started firing at one another, Seattle Assistant Police Chief Tyrone Davis said. Dozens of officers were providing security at the event and witnessed the shooting.

A large number of police and emergency crews responded and began evacuating the area around the sprawling Seattle Center campus as festival-goers took cover.

Faith Adia Hunter said she and her friends had just bought crepes from a vendor when the shooting started nearby, prompting her group to seek shelter in the nearby Seattle Children’s Museum.

open image in gallery Shortly after the mass shooting, police led a potential suspect away ( Reuters )

open image in gallery The entrance to the site at the Seattle Center, cordoned off with police tape following Sunday’s outbreak of gun violence ( Getty )

“We were right next to him when it started, so we took off running,” she said. “So we took off running too into the building with the crowd.”

Amid the chaos, many vendors bolted toward the exits, abandoning their stalls. Hours afterward, some gathered around the police tape, wondering when they would be allowed to return to collect their tents, food and cooking equipment.

One of the vendors, Roberto Ramirez, said he heard what sounded like firecrackers before people began yelling “shooter” and running frantically.

“Suddenly everything was empty,” he said. “People were freaked out.”

open image in gallery Seattle Police have said that the two people responsible may have been shooting at each other, not aiming for visitors to the food festival ( AP )

After the initial panic, new visitors continued to arrive, unaware of what had happened, and were instructed to leave by police, he said.

Estan Wakonabo said he and his girlfriend were waiting in line for a photo booth when he was shoved from behind and turned to see a rush of people fleeing.

“People were hiding, were pushing, people were falling on the ground, baby strollers were falling,” Wakonabo said.

“Once I heard a ‘pop, pop, pop,’ that’s when I knew it was a shooter,” he added, reporting that he later saw multiple victims on the ground.

The victims

Two victims, 44-year-old Carlos Israel Sanchez Villalba and a 56-year-old Ashley Whitehead, were killed in the gunfire, The Seattle Times reported, citing the King County Medical Examiner.

Sanchez Villalba died at the scene. Whitehead succumbed to her injuries after being transported to a hospital. FOX 13 Seattle reported that Sanchez Villalba died from a gunshot wound to the torso and Whitehead was shot multiple times in the pelvis.

At least four others were taken to hospital for treatment. Their identities have yet to be revealed.

As of Monday morning, three adults had been discharged and the two-year-old boy was in satisfactory condition but still under observation, a spokesperson for Harborview Medical Center told the Associated Press. The three who were discharged included a 23-year-old man, a 27-year-old man and a 39-year-old woman.

open image in gallery Seattle Assistant Police Chief Tyrone Davis have said his officers are ‘still trying to figure out’ precisely what happened ( Reuters )

A fifth person was treated at the scene for a minor injury.

Harborview said it had gone into “partial lockdown” following guidance from the Seattle Police Department.

The suspects

Police believe there were at least three suspects, according to court documents. Authorities only identified the teenager taken into custody as a 15-year-old.

One of the suspects was killed in the shooting, according to court documents. He was identified as 19-year-old Junior Cee Niko Semo of Seattle by the King County Medical Examiner Monday, per KING 5 News. He reportedly died of multiple gunshot wounds.

“Based on the evidence at the scene, investigators believe” the 15-year-old “and one of the deceased engaged in a gunfight with at least one other unknown suspect,” the document obtained by the Associated Press said.

Davis said officers do not yet have a description of the third suspect who fled, saying: “We’re still trying to figure this out.”

There is believed to be no further threat to the public.

The aftermath

open image in gallery Seattle Mayor Katie Wilson denounced the ‘act of horrific violence’ after the shooting devastating the community Sunday ( Reuters )

Seattle Mayor Katie Wilson called the shooting an “act of horrific violence.”

“Impacted families are living through the worst moment of their lives, and an entire community is trying to understand how a gathering built around culture, connection, and joy ended in gunfire,” she said at a press conference.

Washington Gov. Bob Ferguson wrote on X: “My prayers are with the families of the victims, and the responders as they work to keep people safe.”

Washington Democratic Rep. Pramila Jayapal said in a statement that she was “absolutely horrified” by the violence, calling it “senseless” and likewise expressing her condolences to the families of the victims.

The gun control advocacy group March for Our Lives said: “Our hearts are with everyone who was there tonight, and with a city that didn’t ask for this. We will not accept this as normal.”

Ariana Baio and Rachel Dobkin contributed to this report

News.title: Andy Burnham appoints equalities minister Bridget Phillipson as Labour party chair
News.content:

Equalities minister Bridget Phillipson has been appointed Labour Party chairwoman by Andy Burnham, who has tasked her with driving a "culture change" within the party.

Mr Burnham emphasised that Ms Phillipson would ensure Labour remains focused on "delivering for working people".

Her remit includes preparing the party for the next general election, modernising its digital campaigning and establishing the organisation, infrastructure and policy platform vital for electoral success.

Announcing her appointment, Mr Burnham said: "Bridget Phillipson, as party chair, will help drive the culture change our party needs, working alongside Lucy Powell and me to ensure Labour remains focused on delivering for working people.

Ms Phillipson served as Education Secretary under Sir Keir Starmer’s premiership ( UK Parliament )

“She will play a vital role in ensuring the Labour Party is match fit for the next election.

“I am delighted Bridget has accepted this role and I look forward to working closely with her on this vital task.”

Ms Phillipson, who served as Education Secretary under Sir Keir Starmer’s premiership, said: “I am honoured to take on the role of Labour Party chair, working alongside our Prime Minister to put our Labour values and the voices of our movement at the heart of government.

“By uniting together, we will bring hope back to communities and strengthen British society against those working to divide us.

“With the change Labour in government is delivering and will deliver, we have the chance to write a new chapter for our country, one which brings justice, opportunity and fairness for working people, one which brings back hope that tomorrow can be better than today.”

During her time as education secretary, Phillipson oversaw initiatives including the expansion of free breakfast clubs, changes to school inspections and efforts to tackle rising absenteeism. The Sunderland MP has kept her position as equalities minister while handing the education brief to Lucy Powell.

Deputy Labour leader Lucy Powell said: “I look forward to working with Bridget as we build on the culture change in the party that Andy has made a priority.

“Working together, we will ensure the party continues to lead the way in campaigning, with the strongest ground operation in British politics as we prepare for the next general election.”

The Trump administration is preparing to ramp up funding by hundreds of millions of dollars for programs designed to counter China’s growing influence around the world, after it had put a halt to many of those initiatives last year during a flurry of budget and personnel cuts.

The administration notified Congress late last week that it intends to spend $175.8 million to replace outdated and aging undersea telecommunications cables in the Caribbean and Central America to prevent China from moving in. The Associated Press obtained a copy of the notification on Monday.

The administration has expressed deep concern about China's activities in the Americas, pushing back on Chinese ownership of ports at either end of the Panama Canal, infrastructure projects funded by China's Belt and Road initiative in the region, and Chinese investment in the telecommunications sector.

A State Department official said China’s economic activities in the Western Hemisphere pose risks to U.S. national security and prosperity. The official, who was not authorized to speak publicly to the subject and spoke on condition of anonymity, said China's offerings may seem cheaper but in the end wind up being more expensive due to cost overruns, hidden maintenance fees and poor performance.

The underseas cable funding appears to be part of a broader push to restore support for initiatives aimed at blunting Chinese influence globally that would cost many hundreds of millions of dollars more. That is even as President Donald Trump and Chinese leader Xi Jinping put on a show of cooperation and Xi prepares to visit the U.S. this fall.

US weighs wider spending to counter China globally

The State Department is considering spending nearly half a billion dollars more on programs aimed at China throughout the Western Hemisphere, Africa and Asia, according to an internal State Department document obtained by AP.

“The United States must respond to the CCP’s growing economic, technological, and diplomatic leverage around the world which undermines our national interests,” the document says, using the acronym for the Chinese Communist Party.

Many of those proposed programs are designed to “reclaim diplomatic leverage” through investments in areas where the U.S. had previously been spending money but stopped as the Elon Musk-led Department of Government Efficiency, or DOGE, carried out deep government budget and personnel cuts last year.

Those cuts, which dismantled the U.S. Agency for International Development and eliminated several hundred diplomatic posts worldwide, also affected previously approved projects, including some aimed at countering China.

A senior U.S. official, who spoke on condition of anonymity to discuss future administration plans, confirmed the Trump administration’s intent to boost funding on countering China but could not speak to specifics. The official acknowledged discussions of large-scale projects but said many were still in the discussion phase.

Congress told about undersea cable project to keep China away

The program described to Congress on Friday is called the “Countering CCP Control of Caribbean and Central America Undersea Cables project.”

It will “fund the installation of strategically-selected undersea cable infrastructure” and support foreign governments in partnering with private sector undersea cable installers, according to the notification. The money will “support replacement of outdated undersea telecommunications cables in the Caribbean and Central America region with secure, U.S. and trusted alternatives,” it said.

Even as it pursues the war with Iran and peace efforts in Gaza and Lebanon, the Trump administration has put a focus on the Western Hemisphere, capturing Venezuelan leader Nicolás Maduro earlier this year, ramping up pressure on Cuba’s socialist government in the months since and imposing severe sanctions on the government in Nicaragua.

Under the new program, funding is anticipated to be given to or in support of undersea cable projects benefiting El Salvador, Guatemala, Honduras, Nicaragua and Haiti, the document said. The U.S. has tenuous ties with Nicaragua and would not be working with the government there.

China's embassy in Washington did not immediately respond to requests for comment.

Other anti-China efforts could focus on cyber and critical minerals

At the same time, the administration has drawn up plans to spend more than $340 million for over 50 specific anti-China projects around the world, including many in the Western Hemisphere, according to the internal State Department document outlining various proposals.

The administration notified Congress in May that it had spent several hundred million dollars in counter-China funding from the 2024 budget that was approved by the Biden administration. However, many other projects funded for 2024 and 2025 had been put on hold.

Among the plans to be resurrected are the creation of security operations centers in Argentina and Belize to monitor Chinese threats to critical infrastructure and cyber platforms throughout the region. Also coming back would be initiatives to protect Ecuador, Jamaica, Mexico, Paraguay, Peru and Uruguay from alleged Chinese attempts to infiltrate port operations and illegally exploit offshore fishing and critical minerals extraction.

More broadly, the proposal, which is still under consideration, would work against Chinese influence in the selection of a successor to the Dalai Lama “by developing proprietary technology to ensure secure communications and information collection.” It also would go after international support for China’s space program and push back against Chinese firms seeking to export surveillance and censorship technology.

The document did not describe the initiatives in detail.

Trump is expected to meet with Xi in September around the time of the annual U.N. General Assembly gathering of world leaders in New York. To prepare for that meeting, Secretary of State Marco Rubio met with Chinese Foreign Minister Wang Yi last week at a regional security conference in the Philippines.

Trump has oscillated between anger and elation with Xi, whom the U.S. leader has sought to cultivate as an ally even while China pursues goals antithetical to many of his administration's. The ultimate impact of the proposed new programs won't be known for many months or years.
