World.title: INLAND WATERWAYS AND JUDICIAL CLARITY
World.content:
The definition of responsibilities is healthy for governance and investment

For years, the governance of Nigeria’s inland waterways has been clouded by uncertainty. Disputes over regulatory powers between the federal government and the authorities in the 36 states have repeatedly complicated the development of a sector that should play a far greater role in the national transportation network. Rather than expanding infrastructure, attracting investment and improving safety, stakeholders were often preoccupied with jurisdictional disagreements. But the recent Supreme Court’s ruling, which invalidated aspects of the old National Inland Waterways Authority (NIWA) Act, has provided the much-needed judicial clarity.

By aligning the law with the judgment, the National Assembly has done more than correct a legal anomaly, they have created an opportunity to reposition inland water transportation as a strategic driver of economic growth, investment and national integration. The swift amendment of the law also demonstrates respect for constitutional governance and reinforces the principle that legislation must conform to judicial interpretation. It is healthy for the institutional cooperation that strengthens the rule of law and reassures citizens and investors that Nigeria’s democratic institutions are functioning as they should. But beyond its constitutional significance, the amended law has real potential to reshape the inland water transport industry.

Nigeria possesses thousands of kilometres of rivers, creeks and navigable waterways that remain grossly underutilised despite their enormous economic value. An efficient inland water transport system could reduce dependence on overcrowded highways, lower the cost of moving goods, ease traffic congestion in major cities, and stimulate commercial activity across several sectors. Realising this potential, however, requires a regulatory environment that is stable, transparent and predictable. Investors are naturally reluctant to commit resources where legal responsibilities are unclear or multiple authorities claim overlapping powers.

By clearly defining NIWA’s jurisdiction in line with constitutional provisions, the new law removes a major obstacle that has long discouraged private investment in the sector. This development should therefore encourage greater participation in ferry operations, cargo transportation, inland ports, logistics, and tourism. Such investment would expand transportation options while creating jobs and stimulating economic activity in riverine communities that have historically been neglected in national development planning. Equally important is the law’s recognition of state governments’ constitutional responsibilities. Waterways are not merely transportation corridor but economic assets that directly affect local communities, and states are often better placed to understand their developmental priorities. A framework that promotes cooperation rather than competition between federal and state authorities is more likely to deliver results than one defined by persistent jurisdictional disputes.

Nigeria continues to witness tragic boat accidents that claim hundreds of lives almost every year, a recurring reminder of weak enforcement, inadequate vessel inspection, poor passenger compliance with safety requirements and insufficient emergency response capacity. The National Assembly’s emphasis on navigation safety is timely, but statutory provisions alone will not suffice. Regulatory agencies must consistently enforce operational standards, ensure commercial vessels meet safety requirements, and prosecute violators.

Life jackets should be made compulsory on every commercial boat operator and emergency responders should receive continuous training, and investment in navigational infrastructure, rescue equipment and real-time monitoring systems is essential. Environmental sustainability must also be central to implementation. Nigeria’s waterways face growing threats from pollution, illegal sand mining, indiscriminate waste disposal and environmental degradation.

A clearer allocation of constitutional responsibilities should let both federal and state institutions focus on governance rather than rivalry, and it aligns with Nigeria’s growing commitment to developing the blue economy, an area where the country’s natural advantages remain far below their true potential. But it would be premature to celebrate legislative success without insisting on measurable outcomes. Citizens will judge this reform not by the number of clauses in the Act, but by safer waterways, better transport services, increased investment, stronger environmental protection and improved economic opportunities for riverine communities.

World.title: PROTECT MUHEEBAH DANKAKA’S MANDATE
World.content:
I write this open letter with deep appreciation for your enduring commitment to democracy, justice, and inclusive governance. Mr. President, throughout your political journey, you have consistently projected yourself as a leader who believes that democracy derives its strength not merely from elections but from the sanctity of the people’s mandate. It is this conviction that gives many Nigerians confidence in your leadership and inspires this humble appeal.

The recently concluded All Progressives Congress (APC) Senatorial Primary Election for Kwara South has produced a clear outcome. Party members exercised their democratic right, votes were cast, and Dr. Muheebah Dankaka emerged victorious. By every democratic standard, that victory represents the collective will of APC members in Kwara South, and it deserves to be respected and affirmed.

Mr. President, this is not simply about one candidate or one senatorial district. It is about the credibility of internal party democracy and the confidence that party members place in the electoral process. Every primary election is a solemn covenant between a political party and its members—a promise that their votes will count and that the candidate they freely choose will be recognised. Whenever that confidence is weakened, democracy itself is diminished.

This moment carries even greater significance because Dankaka’s victory represents a rare milestone for women’s political participation in Northern Nigeria. If, indeed, she is the only woman to have won an APC senatorial primary across the 19 Northern states in this election cycle, then her emergence is more than a personal achievement. It is a symbol of progress, hope and inclusion.

For decades, women in the North have remained significantly underrepresented in elective offices despite their remarkable contributions to national development. They have excelled as administrators, entrepreneurs, academics, professionals and community leaders, yet political representation has remained disproportionately low. Many capable women have been discouraged by cultural barriers, financial limitations and political structures that make elective office difficult to attain.

When one woman overcomes these obstacles through the democratic process and earns the confidence of party members, that victory should be celebrated and protected—not because she is a woman, but because she won fairly.

Your Excellency, your administration’s Renewed Hope Agenda places considerable emphasis on inclusion, equal opportunity and expanding participation in governance. Those principles have inspired millions of Nigerians to believe that leadership should be accessible to every qualified citizen regardless of gender, ethnicity or background.

This presents an opportunity to demonstrate that those ideals are not merely campaign promises but enduring principles that guide the APC.

Affirming Dankaka’s mandate would send a powerful message that the APC remains a party where merit prevails, democratic choices are respected and internal democracy is protected. It would reassure women across Northern Nigeria that politics is not a closed space but a platform where competence, perseverance and public trust can still triumph.

More importantly, it would reinforce the confidence of party members who participated in the primary election believing that their votes would determine the outcome. Democracy flourishes only when citizens believe that the ballot remains stronger than influence and that victory earned through due process cannot be arbitrarily displaced.

Mr. President, throughout your distinguished political career, you have earned widespread recognition for identifying capable leaders and giving them opportunities to serve. Many prominent public office holders today trace their political growth to your belief in talent, competence and hard work rather than narrow considerations. That legacy has become one of the defining characteristics of your leadership.

Protecting the mandate of Dankaka would reinforce that legacy. It would demonstrate that your commitment to fairness extends beyond rhetoric and that democratic victories secured through transparent processes deserve protection.

This appeal is not a request for special treatment. It is not an argument that women should be favoured over men. Rather, it is a principled call for equal treatment under the rules that govern our party. Where a candidate has competed fairly, won legitimately and secured the confidence of party members, that mandate should be respected irrespective of gender.

At the same time, affirming her victory would carry a broader national significance. It would encourage more women to participate in politics, inspire young girls across Northern Nigeria to aspire to leadership, and strengthen Nigeria’s democratic credentials by demonstrating that inclusion and merit can coexist.

Political parties are judged not only by the elections they win but also by the integrity of the processes through which they choose their candidates. The APC has built a reputation as a progressive party committed to democratic ideals. Preserving that reputation requires unwavering respect for the decisions freely made by its members.

Hajiya Zainab Ibrahim Salisu,

National President, Northern Women for Democracy and Inclusive Leadership (NWDIL)

P1

AFRICA AND INCONVENIENT ELECTIONS

The future of government of the people, for the people, and by the people is increasingly endangered, writes CHIDI ANSELM ODINKALU

José Eduardo Van-Dúnem dos Santos was 37 when the ruling Popular Movement for the Liberation of Angola, (better known by its Portuguese acronym, MPLA) chose him to succeed its founding president, Augustinho Neto, in September 1979. By 2010, dos Santos had been in power for 31 years. But the shy and retreating dos Santos was neither an enthusiastic glad-hander nor a wildly popular figure.

For a long time, dos Santos laboured in search of a cure for both ailments. In 2010, he finally found one. Under Angola’s 1992 constitution, the president was the only leader with national standing. The citizens elected him directly on a national ticket. In December 2006, the country issued a three-year notice of presidential election to be conducted in 2009. When the time came, however, President dos Santos could not be bothered with one.

Instead, on 21 January 2010, the parliament controlled entirely by the MPLA approved a new constitution. On 5 February, dos Santos formally assented to the new constitution. It abolished the right of the people to elect their president and extended the unelected tenure of dos Santos as president until a new vote in 2012.

Under the terms of the new constitution, the president was to be elected no longer by the people. Instead, the leader of the majority party in the National Assembly would automatically assume power as the president. The parliament controlled by dos Santos and his MPLA had accomplished an extraordinary power-grab at the expense of the people and without even a pretense of giving them a say or look-in.

In neighbouring Democratic Republic of the Congo, President Joseph Kabila took notice. It took every tool in the DRC’s complex political economy to foil him. Elected to a second five-year term in 2011, “Kabila employed various strategies to prolong his stay in power” and “to manipulate the system to his advantage.” After running out of tenure tarmac in December 2016, Kabila contrived to grant himself an unelected two-year extension. In the end, the country forced him to yield up power in 2019 and bring an end to his 18-year rule.

In Togo, Faure Gnassingbe has presided over two republics over 21 years as successor to his father, General Gnassingbe Eyadema. As president, Faure has never faced a term limit that he could not lift. In May 2024, faced with a term limit that seemed insuperable, Faure, president of Togo since the death of his own father in 2005, abolished the executive presidency and the right of Togo’s citizens to elect their own president in order that he could continue in power.

Under a new constitution to usher in Togo’s 5th Republic in 2024, Parliament doubled the number of presidents in Togo from one to two. The office of the state president became largely ceremonial. Beside him, the constitution created the new and all-powerful office of President of the Council of Ministers in which it reposed all executive powers. In one swoop, Faure Gnassingbe ended all speculations about term limits and presidential elections.

Under the new constitution, the President of the Council of Ministers can hold office indefinitely as long as his party is in power. Indeed, Faure “could…. remain in power for life as president of the council as long as his party remained in the majority.” In a close reprise of the script by Angola’s MPLA, the amendment in Togo was authored entirely by the ruling party and with no opportunity for the people to participate. The political opposition in Togo called it a “constitutional coup”. Elsewhere in Africa, others have called it “a blueprint for dictators.”

One dictator who took close notice was Zimbabwe’s Emmerson Mnangagwa. When he overthrew the long-serving regime of President Robert Mugabe in November 2017, Mnangagwa – who goes by the nickname “the Crocodile” in homage to his political ruthlessness and cunning – was already 75. Many regarded him as no more than a stop-gap figure in what they hoped would be an assured transition to more open and democratic Zimbabwe. Instead, he began a methodical process of consolidating power in a scheme that appears clearly designed to guarantee him a life presidency (which he denied his predecessor).

When the tenure of the Chief Justice, Luke Malaba, fell due upon his turning 70 in May 2021, President Mnangagwa contrived to grant Malaba an unprecedented five-year extension and eventually got a compliant court system to fall in line. To manage suspected judicial un-ease ahead of presidential elections in August 2023, he awarded all judges a non-repayable housing loan of $400,000 US dollars.

In the period since Mnangagwa’s rise to power, over 25 leading military generals, including four of the six who propelled him to power, have died, most of them mysteriously.

Under Zimbabwe’s 2013 constitution, the president is elected to a five-year tenure, which can be renewed once. Elected to his first presidential term in 2018, Mnangagwa was liable to become term-limited in 2028. However, in October 2025, the ruling ZANU-PF Party decided to seek an extension of his tenure for the sake of continuity and national stability.

On 7 July, 2026, President Mnangagwa assented to a constitutional amendment “extending the presidential term from five to seven years and abolishing the popular election of the president in favour of selection by parliament, a change that will keep him in office two years beyond the limit previously set by the constitution.” Again, it was an entirely parliamentary affair.

So, in 2028 when he is due to turn 86 and become term-limited, President Mnangagwa will instead be presented to the people of Zimbabwe for the formality of continuing his rule until he is at least 93. If his tenure is renewed at the end of that, Mnangagwa will be eligible to rule until he is a centenarian, and the people of Zimbabwe will have no say in this.

Nearly three years ago, in November 2023, Nigeria’s former President, Olusegun Obasanjo, who himself tried – and failed – to grant himself an extended tour of duty in the presidency beyond the eight years permitted by the constitution under which he took office in May 1999, complained that Western-style democracy was forced on Africa and was not good for the continent. He was short of clarity on a model that could replace it.

Perhaps inspired by Obasanjo’s complaint, his disciples in power across different political traditions on the continent now offer experiments in how to attain his goal. The emerging elements are clear.

First, the people are inconvenient. Increasingly, the question of who sits at the top of the pecking order of power is to be decided by folks entirely beholden to the ruler and not by a perennially obstreperous citizenry.

Second, parliament and judges are dependable enablers of dictatorship. It is a lot cheaper to pay them off and much easier to eliminate or isolate hold-outs among them with no complaints.

Third, popular elections are an unaffordable luxury. It is more efficient to carve up the country into small, manageable constituencies in the service of pretend democracy.

Fourth, periodic renewal of mandate is an anachronism. It pays to keep things predictable and simple. A life presidency does it.

Around the continent, many wannabe life presidents are limbering up. Wherever you look, the future of government of the people, for the people, and by the people in Africa increasingly looks beleaguered, if not indeed bleak.

A lawyer and a teacher, Odinkalu can be reached at chidi.odinkalu@tufts.edu

World.title: Gencos: Over 2,500MW Generated Power Wasted Due to Grid Unreliability
World.content:
Peter Uzoho

Approximately 85 million Nigerians currently live without electricity access, with over 2,500 megawatts of available generation wasted daily because the grid cannot evacuate it, the Association of Power Generation Companies (APGC) has said.

Chief Executive Officer of APGC, Dr. Joy Ogaji, told THISDAY that the numbers paint a damning picture of a sector producing power that never reaches homes and businesses.

“Nigeria’s stranded power crisis is a transmission failure, not a generation failure,” Ogaji said. “The country has an installed capacity of over 15,500MW, yet the grid can only wheel around 4,500MW. That gap is where the crisis lives,” she added.

According to the APGC, stranded or unutilised generation capacity runs between 2,500 MW and 4,000 MW, with declared stranded capacity averaging 150 MW to 400 MW daily. This is power that has been generated or is ready to be generated but cannot be delivered because transmission infrastructure is either absent or has broken down.

As of December 2025, THISDAY’s checks showed that 2,275.67 MW of available generation sat wasted and undelivered, the highest level in five years and equivalent to 33.6 percent of available generation going nowhere.

The trend has been consistent as data shows 2,248 MW was stranded in 2021, 1,816 MW in 2022, 2,227 MW in 2023, 2,180 MW in 2024, and 2,275 MW in 2025.

The human cost is immediate when viewed from the prism of hospitals having to run on generators, students studying by candlelight, and small businesses bleeding cash on fuel.

Between 2000 and 2022 alone, Nigeria’s national grid collapsed 564 times, according to APGC records, more than twice a month for over two decades.

In January 2026, the country suffered three nationwide blackouts in 30 days. On January 27, 2026, grid output fell from 3,825 MW at 10am to 39 MW by 11am. At that time, within one hour, 99 per cent of Nigeria’s electricity vanished as every distribution zone fell to zero simultaneously.

It is estimated that Nigerian businesses and households spend an estimated $23 billion annually on diesel and petrol to self-generate power across about 22 million generators. The World Bank puts the broader economic loss from unreliable electricity at $26 billion to $29 billion per year.

Similarly, the African Development Bank’s (AfDB) African Economic Outlook 2026 estimates outages cost firms 3 per cent of annual sales, with 70.7 per cent of Nigerian businesses forced to own or share generators.

“A small tailor earning N4,000 a day can spend N3,000 of it on generator fuel,” Ogaji said. “Banks report diesel at 20 to 30 percent of operating expenses. Every megawatt stranded is a business struggling or failing to survive.”

On the revenue side, the electricity market itself is hemorrhaging. The Nigerian Independent System Operator (NISO) estimated that transmission inefficiencies cost the sector approximately N5 billion daily. Distribution Companies (Discos) recorded combined losses of N2.349 trillion over the past two years from billing and collection inefficiencies, rising from N1.015 trillion in 2024 to N1.334 trillion in 2025.

For Gencos, the pain is acute as they lost an estimated N2.28 trillion in capacity payments in 2025 alone due to grid constraints that prevented evacuation.

That figure excludes energy charge losses. Sector debt to Gencos has now exceeded N6.8 trillion and is projected to rise another 33 per cent by end-2026.

Ogaji said: “Gencos are effectively maintaining and operating assets for a market that cannot pay them. These losses cascade. Gencos cannot pay gas suppliers. Transmission Company of Nigeria (TCN) loses wheeling revenue. Discos cannot fund network upgrades. Nigeria Bulk Electricity Trader (NBET)’s payment gaps widen. The entire value chain is caught in the same spiral.”

She insisted that Gencos were not the problem arguing that gas supply to thermal plants has fallen to under 43 per cent of daily requirement. She added that pipeline vandalism destroyed 128 transmission towers in 2024 alone while unpaid gas invoices have also left plants unable to run at capacity.

Among stakeholders, the transmission bottleneck remains the biggest chokepoint, as they argue that installed capacity of 15,500 MW far exceeds the 4,500 MW the grid can wheel. They say technical losses alone run at 1,200 MW to 1,300 MW daily, enough to power Lagos. According to APGC, liquidity is equally dire, saying starved of payment, Gencos cannot fund maintenance or buy parts. At distribution level, billing gaps, metering failures and energy theft mean that Discos lose billions before revenue reaches the market. The utility firms’ Aggregate Technical, Commercial and Collection (ATC&C) losses run at about 50 percent, against a global best practice of 15 percent.

Ogaji said the solutions were known but require urgency as APGC is calling for the privatisation or commercialisation of the TCN to inject private capital, similar to Egypt’s addition of 14,000 MW in six years.

World.title: Nigeria’s Petrol Consumption Drops 15.7% to 4.2bn Litres as Fuel Prices Rise
World.content:
Emmanuel Addeh in Abuja

Nigeria’s total petrol consumption dropped from 5.07 billion litres in Q1 to 4.27 billion litres in Q2 2026, representing a 15.7 per cent fall, amid rising pump prices induced by the US-Iran war, a THISDAY analysis of data from the Nigerian Midstream and Downstream Petroleum Regulatory Authority (NMDPRA) has revealed.

The official downstream performance statistics reflected the steady contraction in daily distribution volumes throughout the period, with 2026 beginning with a robust daily consumption average of 60.2 million litres in January.

However, the figures released by the NMDPRA indicated that consumption declined to 56.9 million litres in February and fell further to 47.3 million litres in March.

The downward trajectory persisted straight into the second quarter as average daily truck-outs recorded 51.1 million litres in April, 46.3 million litres in May, but rose slightly to 47.4 million litres in June. In total, the nation consumed roughly 797.6 million fewer litres of petrol in Q2 compared to Q1 as the global oil market crisis ramped up, the data showed.

The US-Iran conflict has led to major blockades along the critical Strait of Hormuz shipping route, through which a fifth of global oil supplies transit. With global crude benchmarks surging past $100 per barrel, the landed cost of refined petroleum products in Nigeria has also skyrocketed.

Consequently, retail pump prices across major Nigerian cities leapt from N800 per litre prior to the conflict to as high as N1,400 per litre currently. This has forced households, commercial transporters, and industrial operators across the country to cut back drastically on fuel usage.

However, in sharp contrast to declining domestic demand, petrol import volumes expanded significantly over the same timeframe. Total petrol imports jumped from an estimated 266.9 million litres in Q1 to 836.9 million litres in Q2, representing an increase of over 213 per cent quarter-on-quarter

The heavy reliance on foreign supply was particularly pronounced in June, when daily import receipts spiked to 18.1 million litres as marketers moved to bridge domestic refining variances and maintain baseline national stock sufficiency during the peak of global market instability as well as, according to them, provide a viable competition to the Dangote Refinery.

Besides, the economic pressure of elevated fuel costs extended well beyond petrol, causing visible demand contractions across other essential refined products monitored by the regulator. Diesel saw consumption fall from 1.67 billion litres in Q1 to 1.47 billion litres in Q2. Daily diesel averages dropped from 20.3 million litres in February to 16.0 million litres in May and June.

In the same vein, cooking gas consumption slid from a daily peak of 5.2 kilotonnes in February to 4.1 kilotonnes by June, amid skyrocketing prices, which rose as high as N2,000 per kilogramme. During the same period under consideration, kerosene also experienced minor fluctuations before closing Q2 at 2.9 million litres per day.

In all, during the period, the dual pressure of international market volatility and domestic cost adjustments fundamentally reshaped consumer behaviour across the country as vehicle owners, especially in Abuja, now increasingly resort to carpooling while reducing non-essential trips.

At the same time, small businesses that rely on petrol-powered generators have been forced to alter operational hours or pass rising overhead costs directly to consumers, with no end in sight to the global oil market crisis.

Also, the NMDPRA’s tracking data indicated that stock sufficiency levels for petrol remained within operational thresholds throughout the period, averaging between 16 and 33 days.

World.title: AEDC Promotes 1,126 Employees to Boost Career Growth
World.content:
The Abuja Electricity Distribution Plc (AEDC) has announced the promotion of 547 employees and the approval of 579 step increments following the successful conclusion of its 2025 performance appraisal exercise, reaffirming the company’s commitment to recognising excellence, rewarding performance and building one of Africa’s most admired workplaces.

The milestone, it said in a statement, reflects AEDC’s deliberate investment in its people as the company accelerates its transformation into a customer-centric, high-performing electricity distribution company with global standards and pan-African aspirations.

Speaking on the development, the AEDC Managing Director/Chief Executive Officer, Chijioke Okwuokenye, described the announcement as another significant milestone in the company’s people transformation journey.

“Our people remain our greatest asset and the foundation upon which AEDC’s future will be built. Today’s announcement is more than a reward for performance; it is a reaffirmation of our belief that excellence should always be recognised, talent should be nurtured and hard work should create opportunities for growth.

World.title: How MUCH is Wednesday Lotto and Lotto Plus worth?
World.content:
All you need to know about Wednesday Lotto and Lotto Plus. Image: File

How much is Wednesday Lotto and Lotto Plus worth on 29 July 2026? Well, it breaks down like so. Straight Lotto is worth R4 million, Lotto Plus 1 sits at R3.5 million and for Lotto Plus Max 5 you can tag on another R1.5 million.



All tallied up that put’s the total worth of the Wednesday game at R9 million, a R2.5-million increase over Saturday’s game past …

Crucial to your success for Wednesday Lotto and Lotto Plus is knowing how recently one of the three lottos has paid out. A bit like the old days playing slot machines in the casino, the longer it goes, the bigger the payout becomes.

Looking at the above figures, we can see that almost all have paid a small amount recently. This has been one of the criticisms of new game mechanics – that payouts, while more frequent, rarely allow winnings to climb to big numbers anymore.

WEDNESDAY LOTTO AND LOTTO PLUS

As such, Wednesday Lotto and Lotto Plus has always been the National Lottery’s kind of bread-and-butter game. Cheaper than PowerBall and PowerBall XTRA, easier to win, but less dramatic when it comes to jackpots. Nevertheless, Sizekhaya’s 1 June 2026 takeover reshaped it further. The core mechanics require players to choose six numbers from a pool of 1 to 52, which is reduced from 1 to 58 previously.

As ever, numbers can be chosen manually or auto generated through the popular Quick Pick. Pricing sits lower than PowerBall’s controversial increase. A standard Lotto board costs R5, with Lotto Plus 1 adding R2.50 and Lotto 5 Max adding a further R2.50 on top. Therefore, playing all three together costs R10 per board.

What players are still wrapping their head around is the new MultiPlay (MP) option. It lets players add a seventh number to their existing six in each of the three games. And it gets proportionally more expensive as you go. The total combination if you add MP1 across all boards is R70 – that’s R35 + R17.50 + R17.50. However, your odds are massively improved if you do go down this rabbit hole.



HOW TO HANDLE MULTIPLAY

Lotto Plus 1 had a small payout this weekend, keeping the winnings for Wednesday muted. Image: File

If you add MP1 to Wednesday Lotto and Lotto Plus across all three games, your total ticket will cost R70.00. Plus, if you’re using your banking app, be sure to lookout for digital banking fee of roughly R2.95 added to the transaction. So, the question remains, is it worth spending the extra money?

Jackpot odds have already improved substantially under the new number matrix. The chances of matching all six numbers now sits at 1 in 20 million. That’s twice as likely as the old 1 in 40 million under ITHUBA. However, dabble with the MP1 and all of a sudden, you’re playing with seven numbers instead of six. This means your odds now become just 1 in 2.9 million, which represents a straight sevenfold improvement. And don’t forget that’s across all three games since they share the board.

DRAW TIMES AND CLAIMING POWERBALL WINNINGS

Remember, if you’re someone like a playing Wednesday Lotto and Lotto Plus, decide on a budget before buying lotto tickets, and don’t chase a bad week by spending more. The National Responsible Gambling Programme runs a toll-free counselling line on 0800 006 008 for anyone who is struggling.

Lotto and Lotto Plus draw every Wednesday and Wednesday at 21:00. Sizekhaya brought back live televised draws using physical draw machines. Ticket sales cut off half an hour before the draw typically at 20:30. All lottery prizes must be claimed within 365 days of the draw date. Anyone who misses that window forfeits their prize and the money is transferred to the National Lottery Distribution Trust for charitable causes.

How and where to claim Wednesday Lotto and Lotto Plus winnings depends on the amount won:

Small prizes (up to R4 999 ) get paid out directly at licensed retailers.

) get paid out directly at licensed retailers. Mid-tier prizes ( R5 000 to R49 999 ) can be claimed at selected partner banks.

) can be claimed at selected partner banks. Anything above R50 000 requires an in-person visit to a Sizekhaya regional office, with the original ticket and a valid South African ID.

The new lottery operator took over on 1 June 2026. Image: File

Anyone unsure where to start can call the Sizekhaya helpline on 0861 026 000. Or you can visit one of the eight regional offices nationally:

And one final note, around R257 million in lottery prizes currently sits unclaimed across South Africa from the previous operator. Therefore, checking old ticket numbers against those drawn (up to one year ago) costs you nothing and might just turn up forgotten money. You can do so by clicking past results HERE.

World.title: ‘Jobs need to be created’: Debate grows over SASSA Children’s Grants
World.content:
While some demand that grants be scrapped, others reacting to the SASSA Children’s Grants amendments say the government is treating the symptom, not the cause.



Mapontsho Pearl pushed back against the idea that people have children purely for grant money, pointing out that R580 a month can’t even support a child on its own. She argued the real issues are a lack of jobs paying a liveable monthly salary and the R370 SRD grant, which she believes should be scrapped in favour of employment. She also called for child support laws to be amended so fathers face real consequences, rather than mothers having to chase absent parents for money.

‘You should only have what you can afford’

Heather Ann Beykirch took a different angle, arguing that pensioners have earned their support through a lifetime of work, and warning that unchecked population growth is unsustainable. Her view: people should only have as many children as they can genuinely afford to raise and educate.

Despite different starting points, both commenters land on a similar theme: responsibility, whether from absent fathers or from parents themselves, should carry more weight in the debate than the size of the grant itself.

Take part in our survey and stand a chance to win R2 000. Your responses help us tell the stories that matter.

World.title: ‘Time fathers paid maintenance’: Backlash over SASSA Children’s Grants
World.content:
Not everyone reacting to the SASSA Children’s Grants amendments wants stricter limits; some want the system to look harder at who actually needs help and who should be paying instead.

Commenter Sandi Rogers said she understood the need for a grant in cases where a father cannot find work or has passed away, but suggested that food parcels, medical assistance and free schooling support might be more effective than a blanket cash grant.

Coreen Isabella Kruger echoed the call for closer scrutiny, arguing that SASSA should check household income and individual circumstances before making decisions, pointing out that some fathers who do work still can’t cope with low wages, while some mothers have lost jobs or husbands and are genuinely struggling.



Fathers in the spotlight

Virginia Olieslager February took a more direct line, saying it’s time fathers of these children start paying maintenance, placing responsibility back on absent parents rather than the state.

Meanwhile, Bee Fuze summed up growing frustration with a blunt question: where do people sign to stop the grants system, “with immediate effect.

Together, the comments reflect a public that isn’t simply anti-Children’s Grants but increasingly wants a system that properly verifies need and holds absent parents accountable, rather than one that relies purely on monthly cash payments.

World.title: Derick Hougaard relationships: Love, loss and scandals
World.content:
Derick Hougaard’s cry for help has touched the hearts of many South Africans. The former Springbok – who was once married to a popular Afrikaans singer and dated another – has appeared to have hit rock bottom after several public scandals.

DERICK HOUGAARD RELATIONSHIPS: KARLIEN TO NADINE

Here’s a look back at Derick Hougaard’s high-profile relationships…

The rugby star and singer, and actress Karlien van Jaarsveld were married from 2013 to 2015 and share twin boys, Eliah and Daniel.



In 2018, Derick made headlines when his ex-wife claimed their twin boys had gone “missing” while in his custody. She also claimed that Derick was “drunk” during a day out with their kids.

However, the incident turned out to be a misunderstanding, and the children were found safely in Derick’s care.

Derick Hougaard en Karlien van Jaarsveld skei, kraai me a riverhttp://t.co/7dbfQjm89t pic.twitter.com/meE8heoeTp — Stix Gevaaalik (@gevaaalikdotcom) September 2, 2015

In a Facebook post shortly after, Karlien claimed that a court had granted Derick supervised visits to his “pill and alcohol addiction”

She shared: “He has been in and out of rehabilitation centres several times. I was terrified of concern because I feared for the safety of my children”.

Karlien added that Derick had also not paid child support, and she had been financing her children.



That same year, Derick Hougaard began dating another Afrikaans singer, Nadine Hoffeldt.

The couple would make their first red carpet appearance together at the Miss South Africa pageant. Derick and Nadine would also make regular features on each other’s social media accounts. “She’s a piece of gold. There aren’t many or any more girls like that left”, he said of his partner.

Just a few months later, a publication published pictures of Derick Hougaard seemingly in bed with another woman.

Nadine confirmed with the media that she had discovered Derick in bed with a mystery blonde woman in a hotel room. She also revealed that she was “beyond broken.” Derick also spoke to the publication but denied cheating on Nadine. Instead, he claimed he was “heavily under the influence” and could not remember much from the night.

The couple “patched things up” and continued to date over the next few years.

In 2022, Nadine hinted at ending her roller-coaster relationship with Derick Hougaard.

She posted on social media: “Four years. Six months. 20 days. It’s over. Final.” The post was deleted hours later. Derick responded to the break-up rumours saying: “I don’t know, I suppose, I don’t know. I can’t talk right now…”

Derick later hinted at the hotel room saga, posting on Facebook: “I was framed for doing something I did not do”.

In 2023, Nadine found Derick unconscious at his Pretoria home. She would continue to support him through his health battles, which saw him land in a medically induced coma in the ICU.

A year later, Nadine and Derick split for good.

ANOTHER WOMAN IN THE PICTURE?

According to reports, Derick Hougaard was snapped at the bar and later in bed with a young blonde woman.

However, the woman, identified as a marketing assistant, claimed that she had been merely helping an intoxicated Derick into bed.

Since his split from Nadine in 2024, Derick has kept a low public profile.

World.title: Banyana Banyana begin WAFCON with shock defeat
World.content:
Desiree Ellis’ Banyana Banyana dominated possession for long periods. They also celebrated Linda Motlhalo’s 100th appearance for the national team. However, they failed to turn their control into goals. Tanzania defended bravely before striking twice to claim a famous victory.



LINDA MOTLHALO REACHES MILESTONE

Banyana Banyana started brightly and controlled the tempo. They pinned Tanzania deep inside their own half. Despite the return of Thembi Kgatlana, the South Africans struggled to create clear-cut chances.

Against the run of play, Tanzania took the lead in the 37th minute. Diana Msewa beat her marker with a brilliant run. Her shot took a deflection and wrong-footed Andile Dlamini before finding the back of the net.

Also read: Orlando Pirates dominate PSL awards

South Africa responded well before the break. Najat Idrisa failed to deal with a corner in stoppage time. The ball fell kindly for Bambanani Mbane, who headed home from close range to make it 1-1.

BANYANA BANYANA LEFT WITH WORK TO DO

The second half was evenly contested. Both teams searched for a winning goal. Ellis introduced Nthabiseng Majiya at half-time to add fresh energy in attack.

At the other end, Dlamini produced a fine save to deny Hasnath Ubamba from a dangerous free-kick. The match looked destined for a draw as the clock ticked down.



However, South Africa failed to clear their lines in the closing minutes. Tanzania punished the mistake on the counter-attack. Ubamba scored in the 87th minute to hand the Twiga Stars a famous 2-1 victory.

The result gives Tanzania a perfect start to their WAFCON campaign. Banyana Banyana return to action against Côte d’Ivoire on Friday, 31 July.

The final Group B game will be against Burkina Faso on Tuesday, 4 August. Both matches will take place at Moulay Rachid Stadium in Casablanca. Only the top two teams will advance to the next round.

World.title: Orlando Pirates dominate PSL awards
World.content:
Relebohile Mofokeng and Oswin Appollis play for Orlando Pirates in the 2025/26 Betway Premiership season. Image: Orlando Pirates media

Orlando Pirates dominated the ceremony, with Relebohile Mofokeng leading the way after claiming three of the night’s most prestigious awards.

The PSL named the young star the PSL Footballer of the Season, Betway Premiership Players’ Player of the Season, and Betway Premiership Young Player of the Season.

RELEBOHILE MOFOKENG LEADS THE WAY

The 20-year-old’s remarkable campaign was recognised with a clean sweep of the league’s biggest individual accolades. His performances throughout the season established him as one of South African football’s brightest talents.



Orlando Pirates also celebrated several other winners. Abdeslam Ouaddou was named Betway Premiership Coach of the Season, while Sipho Chaine collected the Goalkeeper of the Season award.

Lebone Seema claimed the Betway Premiership Defender of the Season award, while Oswin Appollis won the Midfielder of the Season accolade.

Also read: Orlando Pirates coach to be paid R12 million

The club’s dominance extended to the knockout competitions. Tshepang Moremi won the MTN8 Last Man Standing award, while Mbekezeli Mbokazi was named Carling Knockout Player of the Tournament.

BETWAY PREMIERSHIP AWARDS COMPLETE LIST

Outside of Orlando Pirates, Durban City goalkeeper Darren Keet claimed the Nedbank Cup Player of the Tournament award.

TS Galaxy youngster Seluleko Mahlambi was recognised as the Nedbank Cup Most Promising Player of the Tournament.



In the Motsepe Foundation Championship, Cape Town City enjoyed a successful evening. Emile Witbooi won the Players’ Player of the Season award, Gabriel Amato was named Young Player of the Season, and Mickey Van Der Hart collected the Goalkeeper of the Season prize.

Mamelodi Sundowns prospect Bennet Mokoena was crowned the DStv Diski Challenge Player of the Season.

The PSL named Euguene Mdluli Referee of the Year, while Nandipha Menze won the Assistant Referee of the Season award.

World.title: Kaizer Chiefs unveil stylish new supporters’ range for 2026/27 season
World.content:
Kaizer Chiefs have unveiled their official 2026/27 supporters' range, giving Amakhosi fans a fresh look to wear as excitement builds ahead of the new Betway Premiership campaign. Image: Kaizer Chiefs website

Kaizer Chiefs have unveiled their official 2026/27 supporters’ range, giving Amakhosi fans a fresh look to wear as excitement builds ahead of the new Betway Premiership campaign.

Something for every supporter

“Fully geared for the entire Amakhosi family, from women’s and kids’ ranges to training wear, supporter leisurewear and on-field-inspired training gear,” the club said in a statement.

“What a collection. What a season. What a kingdom. The Kingdom Rises.”

The launch ensures supporters can head to stadiums in style while backing Kaizer Chiefs throughout the 2026/27 campaign.

Confidence high after Toyota Cup success

The new merchandise arrives just days after Kaizer Chiefs claimed the Toyota Cup with a 1-0 victory over Zimbabwean champions Scottland FC at the Royal Bafokeng Stadium.

World.title: Inside the money trail: How SIU probe linked Lucky Montana to PRASA tender
World.content:
JOHANNESBURG - The Special Investigating Unit (SIU) says years' worth of tedious investigation allowed for the tracing of the flow of money from a multibillion-rand PRASA contract to luxury properties linked to former Group CEO Lucky Montana.

According to SIU spokesperson Selby Makgotho, the investigations, which focused on the controversial R5.6 billion Interpreted Security Access Management System contract, started around 2014.

This was when the SIU came in with a proclamation.

The contract in question was awarded to Siyangena Technologies.

The two properties linked to Montana are in Hurlingham, Johannesburg, and Waterkloof, Pretoria. Combined, they are worth nearly R16 million.

READ | Former PRASA CEO unlucky as SIU targets assets

Makgotho said investigators worked through years of money trails from PRASA around 2009 to 2015 while also analysing available evidence.

“We are confident that we have done this investigation, considered all the available evidence, subpoenaed all the required documentation, but also followed the money trail,” he said.

Part of the investigations also saw bank records being analysed with “due diligence”, as well as Montana’s income and spending patterns being analysed.

That was when they realised something was amiss.

“Those incomes do not tally,” he said

According to Makgotho, there was a property of R13.5 million that was purchased and immediately thereafter demolished.

“I think there were modifications that they needed to do, and again, the funds to subsidise all those things, in our view, do not tally. “They raised a very questionable relationship between the income that was received versus what was actually spent," Makgotho he said.

The SIU has secured a preservation order freezing two luxury properties linked to the former PRASA CEO.

In a lengthy statement on X, formerly known as Twitter, Montana responded to the SIU, saying they have “become desperate”.

He said the SIU did not obtain any order to freeze his assets.

READ | Discussion | Scopa grills Prasa over rands and cents

“The SIU approached the Tribunal which is equivalent to a court, not seek a provisional order, pending my filing of a notice to oppose, within 10 days. I was served with papers on or about 9 July 2026 and filed my notice to oppose last Thursday.

He damned the manner in which the matter transpired, even going to the extent of questioning the day on which the order was obtained.

“What surprises me is the SIU choosing Sunday, a holy day for many Christians in the land, to lie to citizens that it had obtained a preservation order against two of my properties. It is a blue lie. It obtained a provisional order to start the legal process. They chose Sunday to tell this lie, hoping this would have the biggest impact and present me as a criminal.”

He vowed that the SIU will not defeat him.

“The SIU and other Organs of State continue to dream of the day they will feed on the carcass of Lucky Montana. But this will not happen, not in this lifetime,” he said.

SIU confirmed that the preservation order is an interim order which seeks to invite Mondana on 11 August to show why this interim order should not be made final.

READ | PRASA Train Scandal | R7.5bn spent as trains remain unused

But he said their work does not end there.

“In a month, we are looking at instituting civil recovery proceedings so that we move with the speed that is required, but not only with the speed but also having gone through the witness statements and having done a thorough and meticulous investigation.

“We are convinced that we have a case that will be presented before the Special Tribunal in our favour," Makgotho said.

World.title: Code name 'wigs': Court hears Mapisa-Nqakula threated to clear tender funds
World.content:
PRETORIA - The High Court in Pretoria has heard that former Defence Minister Nosiviwe Mapisa-Nqakula allegedly threatened to clear funds from a defence tender account if her demands for money continued to be ignored.

State witness Nombasa Ntsondwa-Ndhlovu detailed fresh allegations of bribery against her.

She accused the former Defence Minister of soliciting bribes worth R4.5-million from her between 2016 and 2019.

Ntsondwa-Ndhlovu said after repeatedly ignoring calls and messages from Mapisa-Nqakula, the request for 'wig' funds linked to a R104-million contract was cleared from the project's account as punishment.

READ | Witness alleges Mapisa-Nqakula demanded R2m bribe

Ntsondwa-Ndlovu says the word wig is code for money.

She claims the money had been transferred to an Air Force account on the instruction of a deputy chief financial officer, identified only as Nangamso, who she claims is the former minister's relative.

But the defence objected, arguing that the evidence is hearsay.

The court also heard Ntsondwa-Ndhlovu paid the former minister an additional R500 000 in two separate payments later that year.

The State has concluded its evidence-in-chief.

Cross-examination is set to begin on Tuesday.

World.title: Ramaphosa calls for African action on migration
World.content:
JOHANNESBURG - President Cyril Ramaphosa called on Monday for African countries to work together to manage migration, as his government faces mounting pressure over attacks on foreign nationals.

Ramaphosa's appeal to the Pan-African Parliament follows weeks of protests against undocumented migrants in South Africa, where protestors have blamed undocumented migrants from elsewhere in Africa for crime, unemployment and strain on public services.

He warned that unmanaged cross-border movement could undermine security and social order, and said no country could address the challenge alone.

"As African countries, we have to acknowledge and address the conditions that drive migration in the first place," Ramaphosa told a session of the parliament, which is the legislative body of the African Union.

"We need to work together to address issues like conflict, instability, governance failures, poverty and social discord."

Demonstrations that began last year over undocumented migrants' access to public health facilities intensified this year as protestors demanded that they leave the country by June 30.

More than 160,000 foreign nationals have departed South Africa over the past two months, according to an AFP tally based on figures from repatriating governments, in one of the country's largest recent migrant exoduses.

At least four migrants have been killed in the violence.

'Sad and abhorrent '

The attacks were "sad and abhorrent", Ramaphosa said, adding that "we in South Africa deeply regret and mourn" the lives lost.

"We've taken a firm stand against hatred for people from other countries, xenophobia or Afrophobia," Ramaphosa said.

Ghana has called an African Union debate on the violence.

Two of its citizens have also petitioned the International Criminal Court to investigate "repeated xenophobic attacks", a move Pretoria has dismissed as "opportunistic".

South Africa, the continent's wealthiest nation, has long been a magnet for migrants from elsewhere on the continent.

World.title: 'Cat' Matlala Trial |Defence accuses security officer of tailoring evidence
World.content:
PRETORIA - Alleged hitman Musa Kekana claims he wasn't the driver of the Hyundai i20 police were looking for in connection with the murder of Vereeniging engineer Armand Swart.



The firearms found during his arrest in April 2024 link Kekana to the botched assassination attempts the state says alleged criminal kingpin Vusimuzi 'Cat' Matlala ordered.



A trial within a trial is now underway to determine the admissibility of evidence retrieved during Kekana's arrest.



Captain Phimi Sekgobela, who's the state's third witness, is now detailing how Kekana's subsequent arrest took place and what was retrieved.



The trial within a trial resumes on Tuesday with the state leading Sekgobela in his evidence in chief.



eNCA senior reporter Silindelo Sebata has the latest from the trial in the video above.

World.title: Overflowing bins: Pikitup promise falls flat as rubbish piles up
World.content:
JOHANNESBURG - Weeks after Pikitup promised to clear Johannesburg’s refuse collection backlog, many communities say little has changed.

Residents in parts of Sandton and Randburg are still living with overflowing bins, foul smells and growing health concerns.

They're questioning why they’re still paying for a service they say they are not receiving.

eNCA reached out to Pikitup for an update on the outstanding backlogs and when affected communities can expect normal refuse collection to resume.

The entity is yet to provide answers.

eNCA’s Nabeelah Shaikh reports in the video above.

World.title: Resignation won't erase accountability or prosecution - Expert on Andrea Johnson
World.content:
JOHANNESBURG - Independent Directorate Against Corruption (IDAC) head Andrea Johnson's resignation does not shield her from accountability.

This is the view of legal expert Zola Majavu, who said that the Madlanga Commission of Inquiry can still make adverse findings against her.

Additionally, there could be considerations for possible criminal charges that she may be subjected to.

In a 17-point application to vacate office addressed to Ramaphosa and National Director of Public Prosecutions Andy Mothibi, Johnson wrote that “the recent five months or so have been challenging and the attacks on both my person and official capacity have been unprecedented.

READ | Resignation fails to shield Andrea Johnson from tough Madlanga questions

But despite this resignation, she still returned to the Madlanga Commission for the third day of her testimony

"Accountability does not stop on a mere resignation or the acceptance thereof. If that were the case, she would not have continued with her testimony. She remains in the hot seat until excused formally by the commission. "At the end of the day in the fullness of time the commission is not precluded from reaching and pronouncing whatever findings they may make or arrive at in relation to advocate Johnson regardless of whether or not at that particular point in time she would no longer be in the employ of the NPA or heading IDAC," Majavu said.

Majavu's comments also extended to questions about whether the resignation could be viewed as an attempt to protect the institution.

He, however, argued the other side, saying any reputational damage to IDAC had already been done and that concerns of such a nature are 'too late'.

READ | Ramaphosa accepts Andrea Johnson's resignation

Majavu said while he notes that the decision to resign could have very well been Johnson's personal decision, it does not shape or minimise accountability or the damage that IDAC has already suffered under her watch.

"If there were to be any reputational damage at the instance of the institution, that has already happened, and it's an ongoing thing. It may well be that the most sensible thing to do under these circumstances was to go the route that advocate Johnson elected," he said.

On the role of the NPA now has against Johnson, Majavu said her resignation ends the employer's ability to institute disciplinary proceedings against her.

World.title: Vodacom lifts targets after Safricom deal
World.content:
JOHANNESBURG - Vodacom is expecting to grow faster now that Safaricom is in its fold.

It now has a controlling stake in Safaricom, which leads the mobile market in Kenya and had more than 62 million customers in December.

Safaricom also owns the fintech M-Pesa which facilitates more than 100 million transactions every day.

READ | Vodacom boosts Safaricom stake to 55%

Vodacom raised its target as it reported a 6.3% rise in first quarter revenue driven by strong growth in Egypt and other parts of Africa.

The telecoms group has cut its dividend payout target to at least 65% of headline earnings.

Vodacom says retaining more capital will help fund expansion in fast-growing markets while continuing to support dividend growth.

The company has also raised its 2030 revenue target to R300 billion.

World.title: NDPP orders withdrawal of Dumisani Khumalo's charges
World.content:
JOHANNESBURG - National Director of Public Prosecutions (NDPP) Andy Mothibi has ordered the withdrawal of charges against Crime Intelligence head, Lieutenant-General Dumisani Khumalo and six others.

The decision follows representations made by the group and an Investigating Directorate Against Corruption memorandum.

Mothibi says the investigation is yet to be finalised.

The matter may not be re-enrolled without his express written approval.

That's over the appointment of Brigadier Dineo Mokwele.
