World.title: France continues to fight devastating wildfires, while progress is made in Spain
World.content:
France continues to fight devastating wildfires, while progress is made in Spain

toggle caption Oscar del Pozo/AFP via Getty Images

SEVILLE, Spain — French President Emmanuel Macron called a crisis meeting Monday to coordinate efforts to fight the wildfires in southern France that have forced the evacuation of more than 250,000 people.

The emergency session came as the active fire in the Gironde region of southwest France slowed down overnight into Monday, offering a first sign of relief after the flames burned more than 100,000 acres.

The prefecture of Gironde said the situation overnight had remained stable, a welcome change after the wildfire came close to the wine region of Bordeaux over the weekend.

No new evacuations were ordered on Monday. Over 220,000 residents were evacuated in the region alone. But authorities took some precautionary steps, banning holiday camps for children, as Gironde is a popular tourist destination.

On the ground, firefighters worked tirelessly to make progress in a race against time before a forecast surge in temperatures this week could complicate efforts to put out the fires.

Sponsor Message

In a weekend social media post, Macron pledged long-term support for communities hit by the fires, saying: "We will rebuild, we will repair, and we will be present for as long as necessary."

toggle caption Julien de Rosa/AFP via Getty Images

In Spain, a fire in the region of Madrid that has burned over 60,000 acres was still active on Monday. Firefighting crews were making progress in keeping the blaze under control, but strong wind gusts were complicating those efforts.

That fire came close to another large blaze, in the region of Ávila‎, over the weekend. That fire has burned over 100,000 acres.

Authorities said on Sunday that the two large fires had been brought under control, after a difficult day on Saturday when authorities had openly said the two large fires were uncontained.

A third major fire in eastern Spain, in the region of Castellón, has affected about 75,000 people, with some of them evacuated and others asked to remain at their properties. That wildfire is still active, although it has slowed down, and authorities hope it will be under control by Tuesday.

On Monday, Aemet, Spain's national meteorology agency, forecast the fourth heat wave so far this summer, starting Wednesday. That leaves authorities with 24 hours to contain the wildfires before conditions worsen considerably. This summer is on track to be the hottest on record in Spain, according to Aemet.

toggle caption Oscar del Pozo/AFP via Getty Images

The devastating wildfires in Spain and France have forced more than 300,000 people to evacuate their homes.

Sponsor Message

More than 242,000 acres have been burned in France this year — a historic record — French Interior Minister Laurent Nuñez said Saturday.

Fires have burned over 300,000 acres already this year in Spain, up from an annual average of 250,000 acres over the past decade, Spanish Prime Minister Pedro Sánchez said on Saturday, placing the focus on the impact of climate change.

The fires also affected the Tour de France, the country's annual cycling race, which ended Sunday. The route for the race's final stage was shortened because security and police for the event were reassigned to assist with the fires, organizers said.



NPR's Chandelis Duster contributed to this report.

World.title: Kalshi attacks a Wisconsin law banning election bets as 'voter suppression'
World.content:
Kalshi attacks a Wisconsin law banning election bets as 'voter suppression'

toggle caption Scott Olson/Getty Images

Ann Jacobs is a commissioner with the Wisconsin Elections Commission, a quiet, low-profile state agency that oversees elections. Recently, though, her day was anything but quiet.

"I was sitting at my desk, and all of a sudden Twitter was showing a lot of alerts," said Jacobs, who watched a flood of posts inundate her screen from employees, lawyers and other boosters of the prediction market company Kalshi.

"My reaction was, boy howdy are they mad," Jacobs said.

Sponsor Message

The outrage took Jacobs aback because of what set off the attacks: a commission advisory informing voters that they cannot place a bet in an election in which they cast a ballot.

Wagering on such a race could disqualify a ballot, or even result in a referral to state prosecutors, according to the commission's statement.

This is not a new policy. The advisory was simply stating the basics of a Wisconsin election law originally passed in 1849, Jacobs said.

"You can't be a felon on active supervision and vote. If you're 17, you can't vote, and betting on an election where you vote, it's the same thing, it's not allowed," she said.

Jump ahead to 2026, and Kalshi, the company leading the prediction market craze, is criticizing the law, calling it "bananas," "illegal" and a type of "voter suppression."

Watching employees of the multibillion-dollar company whip up a social media frenzy against an antebellum Wisconsin law left Jacobs puzzled.

To her, pointing out election law months before an election was "simply responsible work by a government entity."

The commission was spurred to issue the warning as prediction markets have become increasingly mainstream and a more prominent part of political discussions.

"We want people voting for the person they think will do the best job at the position they are being elected to. We don't want people voting for someone who isn't the best person for the job simply because it is going to line a voter's pocket," Jacobs said.

Election expert: Betting raises election integrity concerns

Billions of dollars are traded every week on prediction market sites Kalshi and Polymarket.

Sponsor Message

Nearly half the states, including Wisconsin, are locked in legal battles with Kalshi over who should regulate prediction markets. States insist the companies are no different than gambling operators and should be subject to state gaming laws, whereas Kalshi and the Trump administration say the federal government should oversee prediction markets as a financial product known as "a swap."

As the legal fights bang on, the bets keep pouring in.

Big sporting events, like the NBA Finals and the World Cup, saw tens of billions of dollars wagered. The companies expect the midterm elections to be another massive event.

Yet that vision conflicts with another reality: Election betting is illegal in some or all circumstances in 32 states, according to the National Conference of State Legislatures.

"There should be absolutely no money involved in the outcome of our democracy. We should be voting on candidates for their positions and policies to represent us, not because we can make a buck," said Matt Barreto, director of the UCLA Voting Rights Project.

Election betting presents numerous possible election integrity issues, he said.

Foreign actors or partisan interests could use prediction markets to make a candidate appear more popular than they are in an effort to influence turnout.

Then there's the potential for insider trading, something that has dogged the prediction market industry, where everyone from President Trump's teleprompter operator to a special forces soldier has been accused of trading with confidential information. Kalshi has said it blocked "dozens" of political campaign staffers who have tried to bet on their own candidates since May.

Imagine, Barreto said, how this could play out during the midterms.

Say a poll worker places a bet on one candidate, and in order to make money, the person slows down the vote count or does an intentional undercount to change the real election result.

Sponsor Message

"If we found people who were somehow connected to either political campaigns or to the administration of elections, in the secretary of state's office or county elections office, were somehow involved in this, in the same way that Pete Rose tarnished the sanctity of baseball," said Barreto, referring to the baseball legend who was banned from the sport in 1989 in a betting scandal.

Charles Stewart, who runs MIT's Election Data and Science Lab, said most states have vote-counting checks that would prevent such manipulation from happening, but it is a hypothetical that could become part of already heated political discourse.

"If you are looking for a reason to be skeptical about election results, election officials trying to manipulate them for financial gain becomes another straw to grasp at," Stewart said. "However, these people don't need prediction markets to concoct some conspiracy theory to explain away why their candidate lost."

Kalshi declined to comment.

The company has argued that election betting will engage people who might not have cared otherwise about politics. The company argues that states like Wisconsin trying to prevent election betting are engaged in "voter suppression," because some voters who place wagers on a race might also be motivated to vote in the election — when they otherwise might not go to the polls.

Barreto does not buy that argument.

"If they sincerely cared about voter suppression, they would use some of their profits to set up a charity to mobilize the vote," he said.

Kalshi is not backing turn-out-the-vote efforts.

The company did recently launch something else: a midterm election dashboard to allow traders to monitor and place money on dozens of races at once.

World.title: Baltimore will turn 911 into more than just an emergency number
World.content:
Baltimore will turn 911 into more than just an emergency number

toggle caption Matt Gush/Getty Images

In March in a McDonald's parking lot off a busy Baltimore street, mental health clinician Michala Williams met a 38-year-old woman in a car.

"So, you called the police for help?" Williams asked the woman, who was sobbing uncontrollably and said she sometimes thinks about harming herself.

This story was produced in partnership with KFF Health News.

She told Williams she has children ranging from age 2 to 22, she was dealing with health issues, and that her fiancé had recently been jailed. She felt so overwhelmed she couldn't eat.

The woman, who asked not to be named so that she could freely discuss her mental health, explained she'd tried to get help the previous month by driving to the hospital but got pulled over on the way because her car registration had expired.

"I don't care if I get pulled over," she said. "But I was saying, 'I don't know what to do. I just want to go to the hospital.'"

Sponsor Message

The officer arrested her for acting erratically, so instead of going to the hospital she went to jail.

"I had to sit inside of a cold cell. I couldn't use the bathroom or anything," the woman said.

On the day she met Williams, she'd decided to call 911. The dispatcher recognized the woman didn't need a police response but instead needed one of Baltimore's mobile crisis teams, which send a clinician and a peer counselor to meet people in mental health distress.

By the end of an hourlong conversation, Williams set the woman up with referrals to a psychiatrist, a therapist, legal help and a case manager to determine if her child with autism was eligible for government services.

toggle caption Scott Maucione/WYPR

"She's been through a lot of trauma, and no one is going to deny that," Williams said. "But I now have to take all of that and decide, 'OK, here's steps 1, 2, and 3,' because we got to find a little bit of sliver of something to give her some hope that there's help out here."

Problem solving 24/7, without badges, guns or handcuffs

For years, the mobile crisis teams, which are overseen by Behavioral Health System Baltimore, a nonprofit that acts as the city's mental health department, have diverted calls from police to mental health professionals. However, the units have a limited scope, focused on people in mental health crises.

Sponsor Message

Now Baltimore is tapping into some of the roughly $400 million it has received from opioid-related legal settlements to build out a broader service to operate around the clock and respond to other kinds of crises when police aren't needed.

Baltimore logged 1.68 million calls to 911 in 2024, but tens of thousands of them didn't require traditional emergency services, like police, firefighters, or EMTs, according to Tahir Duckett, an expert in community safety at Georgetown Law.

Instead, the calls were about, for example, a homeless person who fell asleep in a store, a person who seemed confused in a public park, and someone who was yelling at passersby on the street.

Such calls "don't require a badge, a gun, and handcuffs to resolve," Duckett said.

Often those people end up in jail instead of getting the help they need, he said.

A study recently found that when a non-law enforcement team responded to 911 calls in Durham, N.C., it resulted in fewer arrests than when police responded — especially for callers who were Black, men, or ages 25-39.

Police responses can also lead to trauma for that person or a less satisfactory outcome than another community service response would produce, Duckett said.

The idea behind the Baltimore mobile crisis teams — and the new service — is to find out what people in crisis may need and how to connect them to those resources instead of arresting them.

How a legal windfall will pay for expanded 911

From 2021 to 2025, Baltimore's homicide rate decreased by 60%, setting records for the drop in violence. But at the same time, drug overdoses made national records, as about 1,000 people here died of an overdose each year from 2020 to 2023.

In 2018, Baltimore opted out of a global settlement that other jurisdictions made with opioid makers and distributors and instead sued them independently.

As these opioid-related lawsuits settled, city officials decided that the settlement awards it receives must be spent on drug-related harms — or on services that help prevent addiction such as housing support, healthcare, and education.

Sponsor Message

One new program seeks to directly address overdoses by placing boxes of the overdose reversal drug naloxone at every subway stop.

Expanding 911 services is part of a larger strategy to beef up city services, with $15 million in settlement funds allocated so far, according to Sara Whaley, Baltimore's director of overdose response.

Whaley hopes the expansion will help the city think differently about how it responds to residents in crisis — regardless of why they're calling 911.

She views the calls as an opportunity to help solve a problem rather than be punitive. "What are the wraparound services and support that can help prevent them from being involved in this, in that emergency system?" she said.

For example, the person falling asleep in a store may need connection to community housing. The goal is to reduce violence, get people proper resources, and avoid the cycle of incarcerating people dealing with poverty, addiction, and mental health.

"The right response at the right time"

Rebecca Neusteter, executive director of the Health Lab at the University of Chicago, studies the impacts of services like these. She said they offer peace of mind for callers that "they're going to be met with the right response at the right time."

"We also see responders themselves feeling like they have a better toolbox in their ability to pursue actual resolution to these calls," she said.

To expand its system, Baltimore looked to cities — including Durham — that have adopted similar models to reroute callers who don't need emergency responders.

Durham's diversion program is called the Holistic Empathetic Assistance Response Team, or HEART. The program estimates it has diverted more than 12,000 calls in four years. It said police backup was needed for only 0.02% of those calls and that response times have improved for all types of 911 calls.

Durham has collected descriptions of the HEART calls, showing that nonpolice responders in Durham have helped with everything from finding housing for a woman fleeing domestic violence to setting up medical appointments for a homeless veteran.

Sponsor Message

In one case, a hotel manager called 911 asking for help finding a blind man housing for the night, since the hotel didn't have accessible rooms available. The HEART responders booked him a room and the next day provided a ride to meet with an organization that could help secure housing.

This story comes from NPR's health reporting partnership with WYPR and KFF Health News.

World.title: Philanthropist behind Canadian human rights museum says family pausing funding over Palestinian exhibit
World.content:
The audio version of this article is generated by AI-based technology. Mispronunciations can occur. We are working with our partners to continually review and improve the results.

A Winnipeg philanthropist who played a critical role in bringing the Canadian Museum for Human Rights to the city says her family is pausing any financial support for the institution over concerns around an exhibit on the displacement of Palestinians.

Gail Asper said she found elements of the exhibit — titled Palestine Uprooted: Nakba Past and Present — compelling, from interviews with displaced Palestinians to artifacts including people's property deeds and keys for their former homes.

But she feels the way the museum describes the related history on panels in the exhibit is missing context.

The collection explores the Nakba — Arabic for "catastrophe," and the term Palestinians use to describe Israel's declaration of independence in 1948, which led to the displacement of approximately 750,000 Palestinians.

A pair of keys to a home Winnipegger Rana Abdulla's family was expelled from, in what is now Israel, is featured in the exhibit. (Tyson Koschik/CBC)

The exhibit drew criticism even before it opened at the national museum last month, including from some Jewish Canadian organizations who said there was a lack of consultation during its development, and that it fails to acknowledge the estimated 850,000 Jews who were expelled from Arab countries in the wake of Israel's creation.

In a recent interview with CBC, Asper echoed that concern and raised others about details she said were missing from the relatively small exhibit — like that Canada has listed militant group Hamas as a terrorist entity , and that Arab leaders rejected a 1947 United Nations resolution for Palestine, then under control of the British government, to be divided into Arab and Jewish states.

While the displacement of Jews in the wake of Israel's creation and the Arab rejection of the UN resolution are acknowledged elsewhere in the museum, Asper said she fears not having that context included in the Nakba exhibit could fuel antisemitism.

But her biggest concern, she said, is that "all the work that we put into this is going to be for naught, if people don't trust this museum anymore."

The exhibit "to me, brings the curatorship into disrepute," Asper said.

"If it's so small that you can't include the truth, then you need to either not do it or you need to expand it. That's a museum decision to make it so small — the museum's got lots of room. I think they have room for the truth."

A multimedia gallery on the museum's second floor that introduces visitors to a timeline of human rights acknowledges 'hundreds of thousands of people became refugees' in the 1948 Arab-Israeli war, including Palestinian Arabs and Jews from surrounding Arab countries. (Tyson Koschik/CBC)

Asper — who took over the campaign to bring the human rights museum into existence after the 2003 death of her father, philanthropist and CanWest Global Communications founder Israel Asper — said the fallout from the Nakba exhibit has felt both surreal and embarrassing.

Her family's foundation donated over $23 million toward the museum's construction, while she personally gave another $1.4 million. That's in addition to more recent contributions to the museum's fundraising efforts and exhibit development, Asper said in an email following her interview.

While the Asper Foundation stopped funding the museum's annual gala after 2023 "because of concerns about its programming," it was about to make a $50,000 donation to support a Holocaust exhibit, but has now paused that donation, she said.

Museum stands behind curation

Asper said she hopes to see an immediate review of the exhibit and the museum's policies on how it decides what to present. But she still encourages people to see the Nakba collection themselves — and look at it with a "critical eye."

And though she hopes to see changes made at the museum, in the meantime, the financial support her family would normally give will likely go toward a recent request to increase security measures at spaces like places of worship and schools in the Jewish community, she said.

"I just know that this is a disappointment for an organization that's supposed to bring people together," Asper said in her interview. "I'm always hopeful that things can be remedied, and with dialogue and understanding, we can get back on track."

A spokesperson for Marc Miller, the federal minister of Canadian identity and culture, said in an emailed statement Monday that it's "not the role of the federal government to dictate programming at Canada’s national museums." The spokesperson directed any questions about the operation of the museum and its exhibits to its chief executive officer or board of trustees.

People gathered outside the Canadian Museum for Human Rights on June 26 to protest the Nakba exhibit. (Rudi Pawlychyn/CBC)

Museum spokesperson Amanda Gaudes said the small Nakba exhibit focuses on "the impact forced displacement continues to have on the Palestinian community here in Canada, and their ongoing struggle for human rights."

In an emailed statement, Gaudes said the museum decided on that focus because Palestinian Canadian stories were underrepresented in its galleries, and "they are important to understand the landscape of human rights today."

Building an understanding of those stories and experiences "is squarely within our mandate," and focusing on them in one exhibit "does not detract or minimize experiences of Jewish people who were displaced and who have also faced human rights violations, which our galleries also share stories about," Gaudes's statement said.

The statement said telling stories of one community "in no way negates the experiences of another," and the museum stands behind its curatorial process "and our reputation as a trusted source of human rights information."

World.title: Ottawa vows to 'get to the bottom' of spying allegations against Canadian NATO intern
World.content:
The audio version of this article is generated by AI-based technology. Mispronunciations can occur. We are working with our partners to continually review and improve the results.

As a Canadian woman who was an intern at NATO's military headquarters in Belgium is facing 'quite serious' spying charges, Public Safety Minister Gary Anandasangaree said that Canada would investigate its security screening processes and 'get to the bottom of what happened.'

Minister commits to 'get to the bottom' of Canadian NATO intern spying allegations

Public Safety Minister Gary Anandasangaree is committing to "get to the bottom" of the arrest of a Canadian in Europe on spying charges.

The Belgian Federal Prosecutor's Office said Saturday that "a Canadian national of Chinese origin" had been arrested on charges of espionage and participation in a criminal organization.

The suspect, who was not named in the office's statement, worked as an intern at NATO's Supreme Headquarters Allied Powers Europe (SHAPE) in Mons, Belgium.

The prosecutor's office said she came to the attention of SHAPE's security services, who reported the matter to Belgium's military intelligence agency.

Speaking at an event today in New Westminster, B.C., Anandasangaree said he didn't want to speculate on the case.

He did say, however, that the allegations are quite serious and that officials will look into whether the suspect has done any work for agencies in Canada.

He said Canada needs to get to the bottom of the matter and ensure that such incidents do not happen in the future.

World.title: Toronto mayor files urgent motion demanding province 'return our waterfront' after feds reject airport plans
World.content:
The audio version of this article is generated by AI-based technology. Mispronunciations can occur. We are working with our partners to continually review and improve the results.

The federal government says it won't support Premier Doug Ford's plans to expand Billy Bishop Airport to accommodate jets. As CBC’s Shawn Jeffords explains, the City of Toronto has now filed an urgent motion to get its land back, including Little Norway Park.

Toronto's mayor filed urgent motion Monday to demand the province give back waterfront land after the federal government rejected a proposal for a jet expansion at Billy Bishop Airport.

In a post on social media platform X, Mayor Olivia Chow said she wants Little Norway Park and the Toronto Islands back in the control of the municipality.

"Council has formally opposed the unacceptable overreach. We still do," she said. "Return our waterfront to us."

CBC Toronto has reached out to the Transportation Ministry for comment.

Chow’s motion, seconded by Deputy Mayor Ausma Malik, comes after federal Transport Minister Steven MacKinnon announced Friday the government would be "exclusively" focused on approved safety upgrades already underway at Billy Bishop, rather than on building the airport out to allow jets to land.

The conclusion was based on public consultations that garnered more than 87,000 responses with nearly 87 per cent of respondents opposed to changes, a spokesperson for MacKinnon said. But the minister left the door open for a potential change of course in future years, framing the decision as "at this stage," instead of a final one.

Ford's proposal to extend the airport's runway 600 metres west — on top of the 150-metre runway end safety zones already in the offing — drew criticism from environmental and community advocates over concerns around the project's effect on noise, traffic and pollution levels, as well as affordable housing and the Toronto waterfront itself. (Patrick Morrell/CBC News)

Ontario Premier Doug Ford's proposal to extend the airport's runway 600 metres west — on top of the 150-metre runway end safety zones already in the offing — drew concern from environmental and community advocates over noise, traffic and pollution levels, as well as affordable housing and the Toronto waterfront itself.

More than 6,000 lawn signs were distributed across Toronto by advocacy groups NoJetsTO and Environmental Defence, with thousands of residents sending letters to their local Member of Parliament. On Sunday, the two groups hosted a celebration to commemorate the power of community.

Liberal MP Chi Nguyen (Spadina—Harbourfront) told CBC Radio's Metro Morning her office heard from nearly 7500 residents, with almost 3,000 of them partaking in the public consultation process.

"We are all thinking about what happens in Ontario and Toronto in terms of being ready and resilient in terms of our economy, but we have to do this [by] thinking about what's right for Toronto," she added. "Toronto's waterfront has to grow with our community and not at its expense."

Province will continue 'to work to advance the expansion'

Ontario Transportation Minister Prabmeet Sarkaria said in a post on X Friday night that the provincial government still has plans for the airport and looks forward to "continuing to work to advance the expansion."

He said the plan would ensure the project addresses potential noise and environmental impacts, expands Little Norway Park, protects public spaces and supports new housing opportunities in the area.

On Saturday, Ford’s office sent CBC Toronto a statement that replicated Sarkaria's statement verbatim. Asked for comment on Chow's motion Monday, Ford's office directed CBC Toronto to its Saturday statement.

On Sunday, advocacy groups NoJetsTO and Environmental Defence hosted a celebration to commemorate the power of community. (Mercedes Gaztambide/CBC)

Sarkaria is set to host a news conference in St. Thomas, Ont., Tuesday morning.

John Gradek, a faculty lecturer in aviation management and supply networks at McGill University, said he wasn’t surprised by the federal government’s decision.

"We've had enough opposition in the marketplace, whether it's local citizens or whether it's local MP's and the media," he told CBC Radio’s Metro Morning Monday. "There really wasn't any data that was really available to us."

In her post to social media, Chow said the city has been demanding to see the plans for the airport, but the Toronto Port Authority has actively tried to hide them. She added the city has researched the impacts on housing, congestion and the environment and found the project would most benefit Wall Street bankers at JP Morgan.

According to Gradek, Toronto’s Pearson International Airport is more than satisfactory for the city.

"There is no [dire] need to create more capacity," he said, noting Billy Bishop plays a more niche role in serving the local market.

Despite this, the need might grow in the next generation, which may be why the federal government didn’t entirely close the door on the opportunity, Gradek said.

"But extending the runway by 2,000 meters and going into it and putting landfill into the lake is not the answer."

World.title: Firefighters from Yukon, Alberta coming to B.C. to aid in wildfire fight this week
World.content:
The audio version of this article is generated by AI-based technology. Mispronunciations can occur. We are working with our partners to continually review and improve the results.

Local firefighting crews will get a bit of a reprieve soon as help from other parts of North America are set to start arriving in British Columbia today.

As of Monday afternoon, there are more than 130 wildfires burning across B.C., covering tens of thousands of hectares of land. Hundreds of people are out of their homes as a result of evacuation orders, while hundreds more have been told to be ready to leave at a moment's notice.

Forests Minister Ravi Parmar said local crews are working flat out to try to stop the fires from spreading.

"We are maximizing all of our resources within British Columbia," he told CBC News Monday.

A total of 25 firefighters from Yukon will arrive in B.C. on Monday, and on Tuesday 66 Albertan firefighting personnel will be on deck to help out their neighbours.

Next week, on Aug. 3, 114 personnel from Mexico are expected to join wildland firefighting efforts in British Columbia.

"Wildfire response is a shared effort, and these partnerships ensure additional support is available when conditions are most challenging," the B.C. Wildfire Service said in a provincial situation report Monday.

Parmar said those out-of-province crews help local firefighters get some time off.

"This is us now planning ahead for what very well could be a challenging end to our wildfire season into August, into September," he said.

Several large fires, including the Brunswick fire complex near Boston Bar, are burning out of control in B.C. (B.C. Wildfire Service)

Sebastian Kallos with the B.C. General Employees' Union, which represents about 2,000 wildland firefighters, said outside support is a must for local crews.

"Firefighters need to take a break from time to time, they can't work in perpetuity," he said.

He said wildland firefighters in B.C. work 19 days on — 14 on the fire line and other days around the office — and two days off. And while B.C. has no trouble recruiting firefighting personnel, he said, they do struggle to retain folks who work in challenging conditions for such long periods.

"No shift workers do that kind of shift rotation," Kallos said.

B.C. has long called on other provinces, territories and countries to help fight wildfires. In 2023, about 1,750 personnel came from outside the province to assist with what is considered the most destructive wildfire season on record.

In return, the province often sends personnel to help others when they need support — something Democratic Sen. Patty Murray recognized in statements made in the U.S. Senate last week in response to President Donald Trump's criticism of Canada's wildfire management.

Two weeks ago, in fact, 56-year-old Nicholas Dale of Sooke, B.C., died in a helicopter crash while helping fight wildfires in Colorado.

Parmar said the province has reached out to jurisdictions in the U.S., but because they're dealing with their own challenges with regards to wildfires, they aren't able to help out.

Kallos said those outside resources are becoming less available in general.

"You look at the national situation, Ontario, you know, big wildfire situation and B.C. has had a bit of a season, and so when all those agencies peak at the same time, the availability of resources becomes less," he said.

World.title: Calgary hiker dies falling from Mount Temple in Banff National Park
World.content:
The audio version of this article is generated by AI-based technology. Mispronunciations can occur. We are working with our partners to continually review and improve the results.

A 65-year-old Calgary man died at Mount Temple in Banff National Park after slipping and falling on the trail, according to Parks Canada.

The federal agency’s Lake Louise, Yoho and Kootenay field unit said the incident took place at about 8 p.m. on Saturday.

Justin Brisbane, a public relations and communications officer, said Parks Canada rescuers responded to the area.

“The man was hiking with a group at the time of the incident, who were able to call for help,” said Brisbane in an email.

“Visitor safety specialists responded via helicopter, located the individual and deployed a heli-sling to airlift him to a staging area, where he was pronounced dead.”

CBC News reached out to RCMP for additional information, but they were unavailable before this story was published.

Mount Temple is one of the most difficult hikes in Banff National Park. In July 2022, a man died when he lost his footing climbing the mountain. A 70-year-old hiker died in September 2019 on the steep mountain.

And a Saskatchewan man was killed in January 2024 on the north face of Mount Temple during a backcountry skiing trip.

Parks Canada warns people to only hike Mount Temple in the summer. It’s about a 16-kilometre round trip hike, and the summit is 3,543 metres.

World.title: Gordie Howe’s family are the 1st to cross Canada-U.S. bridge
World.content:
The audio version of this article is generated by AI-based technology. Mispronunciations can occur. We are working with our partners to continually review and improve the results.

The Gordie Howe bridge officially opened to commercial trucks and personal vehicles on Monday. The bridge between Windsor, Ont., and Detroit is named after the legendary hockey player, and officials invited Howe's family to take the first passenger car across it.

Gordie Howe's family were in the first passenger vehicle to go across the new international border span on Monday, says the Windsor Detroit Bridge Authority (WDBA).

Howe's grandson, also named Gordie, was in the Dodge Charger that made its way across.

"It just feels surreal to be the people who were chosen to do that," he told reporters.

"We got a call yesterday about that ... it just makes me think about all of the people who have worked on this bridge and all the people we've talked to today, just how happy everyone must be that this the bridge is come to fruition. It's just, it's an honour to have been the first to cross. "

Gordie Howe family members were the first to cross the Gordie Howe International Bridge Monday morning, July 27, 2026. (Susan Goodspeed/CBC)

Howe said it's been strange to observe all of the politics around the structure from afar.

"I know it's been frustrating for a lot of people. And so I think that makes today all the more amazing that it has actually opened today and a lot of people are very happy."

U.S. Ambassador to Canada Pete Hoekstra said in a Monday statement America welcomes the opening.

“Adding new capacity to one of the busiest and most economically significant border crossings between the United States and Canada,” he said.

“President Trump made the opening possible and has consistently prioritized a safer, more secure, and more prosperous North America.”

Michigan Gov. Gretchen Whitmer drove across the bridge in a Ford Mustang, built in Michigan, to mark the opening.

"I fought to open this bridge to strengthen the economy and connect Michiganders to opportunities on both sides of the Detroit River," she said in a social media statement.

The first truck to cross the Gordie Howe International Bridge on July 27, 2026 was from Onfreight Logistics from Tecumseh, Ont. (Susan Goodspeed/CBC)

Tecumseh trucking company Onfreight Logistics is poised to be the first commercial vehicle to cross.

Bridge officials say the standard passenger vehicle toll will be $8 ($5.75 US) to cross and $12 ($8.75) per axle for commercial trucks, oversized vehicles and larger passenger vehicles.

The span provides a highway-to-highway connection between Ontario’s Highway 401 and Michigan’s Interstate-75 — with six traffic lanes, 16 toll lanes and 60 Canada and U.S. inspection lanes.

An aerial view of the Gordie Howe International Bridge the day before it opened to traffic in 2026. (Patrick Morrell/CBC)

Walkers and bike riders will be allowed to go over the Detroit River on the span starting Aug. 5.

The one-lane path will accommodate two-way pedestrian traffic. The path is 2.5 kilometres long and 3.6 metres wide and connects into existing local trail networks on either side of the border.

Heavy traffic anticipated

U.S. Customs and Border Protection is reminding travellers planning trips across the bridge to be prepared and to anticipate heavy traffic.

“Being prepared will help minimize delays at the port of entry,” the CBP said in a statement.

They say to have applicable travel documents readily available, and for crossers to accurately declare all goods, alcohol, and agriculture items. And that while legal in some states, marijuana remains illegal under U.S. federal law.

Customs booths at the Gordie Howe International Bridge the day before it was set to open to passenger and commercial vehicles, July 26, 2026. (Patrick Morrell/CBC)

Border mayors chime in on The Current

Windsor Mayor Drew Dilkens says he’s weighing the long-term benefits of the span versus current tensions on either side of the Detroit River.

“I just look at this and say it's taken us 25 years to build this bridge, and it will stand for more than a hundred,” he told CBC Radio's The Current.

"The disruptions that we're feeling today, it's easy to get wrapped up in the ... tweet of the day. Let's play the long game here and recognize that what we've created together will stand to the benefit of families on both sides of the border, businesses on both sides of the borders for many generations to come.”

The Current 19:23 Will the Gordie Howe bridge deliver on its promise? A multi-billion dollar bridge between Canada and the U.S. was supposed to strengthen North American supply chains and ease bottlenecks on the nearby Ambassador Bridge and Detroit-Windsor tunnel. We hear from mayors on both sides of the Detroit River about whether tariffs are putting that investment at risk.

Bryan Barnett is the Mayor of Rochester Hills, Mich., in the Detroit metro area. He also spoke with CBC Radio's The Current.

He doesn’t think the political and economic climate overshadows Monday’s opening of the bridge to traffic.

“I don't think it diminishes it because I think people understand, as Mayor Dilkens said, the long game here is what's important, and I think that's true in the trade discussions as well. I mean, Michigan is so dependent on trade with Ontario and particularly trade with Canada as well, that it just, it's too important.”

A bridge service vehicle crosses the Gordie Howe bridge July 26, 2026. (Patrick Morrell/CBC)

Barnett says he’s not a fan of tariffs and doesn’t think they’ve worked well in curbing economic behaviour.

“I hope that we use the next few weeks, both the president and the prime minister and the leaders on both sides to negotiate quickly to something that doesn't end up looking like it has in the past.”

According to Dilkens, the Gordie Howe span is not a bridge over "troubled waters."

“There is no light of day between Bryan Barnett and Drew Dilkens and between most people in the United States and Canada at this point," he said.

"We are good friends, we love our friends in the United States and I don't want to let Donald Trump overshadow what is a momentous day for us here."

World.title: Calgary police end ground search for missing 11-year-old Parker
World.content:
The audio version of this article is generated by AI-based technology. Mispronunciations can occur. We are working with our partners to continually review and improve the results. Calgary police officials give an update on the search for Parker, a missing 11-year-old boy. Calgary police say they are "refocusing" physical search efforts for 11-year old Parker, the autistic boy who went missing more than a week ago. Police search efforts will now be focused on specific information, such as tips, rather than the extensive ground searches that have been conducted since his disappearance. "Physical search efforts in his last known whereabouts and in the Nose Hill Park, including nearby waterways, have been completed," Chief Katie McLellan told reporters Monday. "However, we are not giving up." Police have carried out an extensive search to find Parker since he went missing July 16 from his day home in the 0 to 100 block of Connaught Drive N.W. Upwards of 650 people, including officers and trained volunteers, have searched day and night, with help from police dogs, bike and horse patrols, aircraft and underwater camera deployments. McLellan said police have also been in contact with rideshare and taxi companies, delivery truck businesses, truck rental agencies and railways to ensure vehicles have been searched. "Despite these exhaustive efforts, sadly, Parker has not been located," McLellan said. "The reality that Parker remains missing is difficult for all of us, especially for his family, who continues to face unimaginable uncertainty. "Parker in many ways has become one of us, and we won't stop looking to bring him home," she said. "We have a responsibility to Parker and his family to follow the evidence and make decisions based on the information available to us." An undated photo of Parker shared by the Calgary Police Service. (Calgary Police Service) Police say they've reviewed more than 600 tips and 100,000 individual CCTV clips from over 650 cameras. "As more information comes back to us, and if we have to stand up another 600 members to go and search a particular area, that's exactly what we'll be doing," McLellan said. "But for now, those specific areas where we put those hundreds of resources in, we've been through those areas multiple times now. It's about refocusing strategies." Last known whereabouts Parker was last seen in the Thorncliffe neighbourhood on July 16 between 12:30 and 1 p.m., acting staff Sgt. Scott Guterson said. Before that, he had been at his day home, last spotted there somewhere between 11:08 and 11:41 a.m. Clothing that’s believed to belong to Parker was found at noon that same day in the 0 to 100 block of Northmount Drive N.W., police said. Police released CCTV footage of the boy they say was captured July 16 at 12:34 p.m. from a business adjacent to McKnight Boulevard and Centre Street N.W. WATCH | Police release CCTV footage of Parker taken the day he went missing: Police release new CCTV footage of missing 11-year-old Calgary boy | Duration 2:26 On the fifth day searching for Parker, police released a video of the boy recorded Thursday at a business in the area of Centre Street N.W. and McKnight Boulevard. Investigators also gave an update on the scope of the search. Police also released CCTV footage of the boy taken at 12:52 p.m. on July 16 in the 5500 block of Travis Crescent N.E. WATCH | More CCTV footage of Parker: CCTV footage of Parker, missing in Calgary | Duration 0:27 Footage released by the Calgary Police Service on July 19, shows missing 11-year-old, Parker, walking past a home on Travis Crescent N.E. on Thursday, July 16, 2026. Police have produced a map of what they believe was Parker's route the day he went missing. The map outlines his known and believed locations based on CCTV footage. Calgary police have released a map of Parker's route on July 16, the day the 11-year-old boy went missing. The map outlines his known and believed locations based on CCTV footage. (Calgary Police Service) Parker was last seen shirtless, wearing grey shorts, black Skechers shoes and black noise-cancelling headphones. He’s four feet 11 inches tall and weighs approximately 90 pounds, with brown hair and brown eyes. Police are asking anyone with information about Parker's location, or who may have CCTV or dashcam footage, to call 403-266-1234 or use the police evidence submission portal. 'We continue to ask the public for help' Guterson said the Calgary Police Service handles about 5,000 missing persons reports every year, about 250 of which are children under the age of 12. "Ninety-nine per cent of those people are found safe and well," he said. "I want to stress how deeply concerning and deeply unusual Parker's disappearance is, which is why we're going back to the public." On July 27, Guterson encouraged people to continue sharing information and searching for Parker. "It is our sincerest hope that Parker is still alive, but realistically, every day that goes by makes that hope less likely," he said. Guterson said Parker is autistic and functions at a two- or three-year-old level. He advised the public that if they come across Parker, they should not engage him, but instead call police. He said the boy is non-verbal, and gets agitated when strangers approach him. Guterson asked the public to continue checking their yards, garages, open vehicles, RVs, sheds, pools or anywhere else a child would go. He said Parker tends to lock doors behind him, meaning people searching their properties should take the time to check behind doors even if they're locked. 🚨 How to search for Parker on your property 🚨

Many people have asked what we mean when we ask residents to "check their property." In this video, Sergeant Chris Martin demonstrates how to properly search areas where Parker may seek shelter.

What might not make sense to you… pic.twitter.com/tMpqZl7rwy —CalgaryPolice Police officers have entered and searched homes in certain locations. Calgary police are encouraging anyone aware of vacant properties on Travis Street, Travis Crescent, Trelle Drive, Taylor Crescent, Travis Place and Thomas Street — all in the city's northeast — to contact police. Guterson said if Parker were in an abandoned or vacant home, police believe he would be able to survive on his own there. "It's our understanding that he would be able to use the tap to get water and he would know to use the fridge to get food, which is one of the reasons why we're asking those vacant homes or those homes where the occupants are on vacation to be checked and double checked," Guterson said. Police vehicles and horses at a search command post for Parker at Nose Hill Park on Saturday, July 25. (Chelsey Mutter/CBC) "To any volunteer searcher out there who is trying to help, I would say don't give up," Guterson said. "Don't give up hope. We're certainly not going to." Police warn of interfering with investigation, fake online posts Police ask that any Calgarians choosing to search on their own do not interfere with police operations. Police say they've also become aware of members of the public trespassing on private property, confronting others and encouraging people to investigate criminal tips on their own. "This behaviour is unacceptable and is putting community members at risk," said a CPS statement. "Everyone wants to find Parker, and we understand the emotions involved. But showing up at private homes, confronting residents or organizing your own investigations can hinder our efforts and draws police resources away from the search and investigation." CPS also said it is aware of AI-generated, altered and unverified images of Parker or his whereabouts circulating online, and cautioned the public against viewing or sharing the content. "Unverified images, videos and claims can create confusion, spread misinformation and divert investigative resources away from credible leads that may assist in locating Parker," CPS said in a social media post on July 18. Police also encouraged people to be mindful of GoFundMe campaigns claiming to be for Parker, as the family says there are no online fundraisers associated with him. Family issues statement In a statement on July 18, Parker's family said they have been living "every parent's worst nightmare" since he went missing. "Every hour that passes without knowing where he is or whether he is safe has been incredibly difficult for us," the family said in the statement, sent out by CPS on their behalf. The family implored people to continue searching their properties for Parker. "Parker experiences the world in his own way. He may not respond when his name is called, and he can become frightened when approached by people he does not know," the family said. "Parker is deeply loved, and he is missed immensely. We just want our son home." Alert for vulnerable children There was no Amber Alert following Parker's disappearance, as that alert is used for children believed to have been abducted. Police have said they are exploring every possibility, but do not have reason to believe Parker was abducted. On July 18, an emergency alert was broadcast for Parker after the provincial government made an exemption following a police request. WATCH | Why there are calls to expand Amber Alerts as police search for autistic Calgary boy: Stephanie Karas, a Calgary mother of two children with autism, told CBC News that the alert came too late. "We've gotten alerts for tornadoes that have not touched down. We've gotten alerts for less, so I don't know why there wasn't [one]," Karas said. Karas added that she's lobbying the municipal and provincial governments to create an emergency alert protocol specifically for situations like this. Alberta Premier Danielle Smith told reporters Monday that the province would work to make that happen. She said Public Safety Minister Mike Ellis had approved the emergency alert "immediately when we were asked," but said law enforcement ought to be able to make that call themselves. "They shouldn't have to go through an extra step of asking the minister of public safety and Emergency Services if, in their opinion, it would help in ... the search," she said.

World.title: Emily Wilson's translation of The Odyssey helped inspire the film. She just panned it in a new review
World.content:
The audio version of this article is generated by AI-based technology. Mispronunciations can occur. We are working with our partners to continually review and improve the results.

British American classicist Emily Wilson's translation of Homer's The Odyssey made waves when it was released in 2017, marking the first time a woman translated the ancient Greek epic to English.

It also served as an inspiration for British American director Christopher Nolan. In early publicity for his recently released The Odyssey, Nolan cited Wilson's controversial opening line — "Tell me about a complicated man" — as a reference point for main character Odysseus.

But Wilson's feelings about Nolan's take, which has so far made more than $600 million US since its release just over a week ago, appear more mixed, according to a new essay published online Monday in the London Review of Books (notably titled "An Uncomplicated Man").

"I was humbled to learn that Nolan has read at least the first line of my translation," she wrote. "But I would be ashamed to have written any part of this script."

WATCH | The Odyssey trailer:

Nolan film lacks depth, narrative: Wilson

The essay took issue with nearly every aspect of The Odyssey aside from its entertainment value, which is credited to the source material — "impossible to mess up entirely," wrote Wilson, who is also a classical studies professor at the University of Pennsylvania.

But the film's narrative and emotional depth is at about the same level as "an elaborate Fourth of July fireworks display," she wrote.

The movie doesn't have a through line pulling together the multitude of ideas it presents, she argued, nor does she believe it develops its characters enough to deliver a clear message.

WATCH | Wilson previously spoke with The Sunday Magazine: What surprises translator Emily Wilson about Nolan’s The Odyssey | Duration 2:10 Emily Wilson, who translated The Odyssey into English, breaks down Christopher Nolan's blockbuster version that has everyone talking about Homer this summer. Wilson spoke with Megan Williams, guest host of CBC Radio's The Sunday Magazine. CORRECTION (July 27, 2026): A previous title of this video suggested the word "slave" was not used in Christopher Nolan's The Odyssey. In fact, the term is referenced in the film.

"Nolan's Odyssey lacks many of the elements that make the poem great," the essay reads. The main couple, Odysseus and Penelope (Matt Damon and Anne Hathaway, respectively), have neither chemistry nor a deep connection, she wrote, while Tom Holland does well playing their son, Telemachus, as a man aged "20 going on 12."

Of the leading performers, meanwhile, Damon's Odysseus is "lummoxy," "neither a master storyteller nor a flirt," while Hathaway's Penelope "looks beautiful and mysterious" but is given little to do but yearn for Odysseus "for reasons unknown."

Chief among her objections was that she didn't feel the film had a clear message. When Odysseus defies the gods, for example, the act is portrayed as noble and brave, but when his second-in-command Eurylochus does the same, it is "stupid and greedy," she wrote.

On a larger scale, the Trojan War, which Odysseus helps start, is portrayed as being horrifying, with innocent civilians subjected to violence and terror. But at the same time, the final scene, where Odysseus massacres Penelope's suitors, is presented as a series of "action-movie sequences in which the reluctant warrior finally gets his hands on his bow and the blood starts flowing."

She also challenged Nolan's decision to film part of the movie in the Moroccan-occupied territory of Western Sahara, which she said "[normalized] the ongoing violence against the indigenous Sahrawi people."

Wokeness allegations

Both Nolan's and Wilson's takes on The Odyssey have received similar criticism from some right-wing users , who charge them with diverting from the source material for political means. Wilson, in particular, has received so much backlash that she has included a separate contact form on her website for "misogynistic trolling."

The war against her translation focused on her "complicated man" opening line. "Complicated" was her interpretation of the ancient Greek word polytropos, an unusual term that has in other versions been translated to "skilled in all ways," or "man of twists and turns."

For her part, Wilson defended the choice on her Substack , saying that other phrases didn't fit her meter- and pacing-related constraints, nor did she feel they were as evocative. But online critics fought back, calling it " vandalism ," "condescending" and even an " assault on a foundation of Western culture " with a " clear feminist woke agenda ."

From left, Charlize Theron, Samantha Morton, John Leguizamo, Tom Holland, Matt Damon, Anne Hathaway, Lupita Nyong'o and Zendaya attend the premiere of The Odyssey on July 14 in New York City. (Mike Coppola/Getty Images for Universal Pictures)

The Odyssey the film also garnered its own share of racist and transphobic backlash even before its release, due to its casting of Lupita Nyong'o, who is of Kenyan descent, as Helen of Troy, and Elliot Page, who is trans.

In her review, Wilson didn't take issue with the race-neutral casting itself but said there was "nothing progressive about" it, noting that most of the non-white actors' roles resembled the "Black best friend," referring to the trope of Black characters being reduced to supporting roles for (often) white leads, with no lives of their own.

Even still, she concluded that the film's release was "an event to celebrate," bringing audiences back to theatres and potentially sparking new interest in ancient Greek and the humanities.

She acknowledged that it helped propel sales of her own book and that Nolan was doing his best to "get the general public reading again." Besides, her teenagers had a good time.

World.title: Colombia’s “Shield of the Americas” to operate from Medellin: De la Espriella
World.content:
Medellin will be the home of the US-led “Shield of the Americas” security program, according to Colombia’s President-elect Abelardo de la Espriella and Mayor Federico Gutierrez.

At a meeting with authorities from the Antioquia province, De la Espriella and Gutierrez agreed that Colombia’s second largest city is the “head of the snake of drug trafficking and organized crime.”

From Medellin, the metropolitan area, most orders are sent out to the rest of the country. So we’re going to focus our efforts on Medellin to fight crime. Abelardo de la Espriella

The announcement followed alleged calls between De la Espriella, US President Donald Trump and US Secretary of State Marco Rubio, and meetings between incoming Defense Minister Jorge Mora and the US’ Deputy Assistant Secretary of War for the Americas, Joseph Humire.

Following the meeting, Mora and Humire announced “Plan Patriota 2.0” and the creation of a “Regional Training Center against Drug Trafficking and Transnational Threats,” which would be “aimed at improving interoperability, operational readiness, and cooperation with allied countries” from the Americas.

During these meetings, the parties explored the joint development of a new bilateral program for cooperation and strategic assistance with a regional scope, known as Plan Patriota 2.0. This initiative is conceived as part of Colombia’s accession to the American Coalition Against the Cartels and is based on the design of the new Policy on Defense, Security, and Civic Coexistence, as well as on the strategy for military and police campaigns in priority areas for the restoration and stabilization of security. Jorge Mora

Plan Patriota was a US-backed military strategy that was implemented by former President Alvaro Uribe between 2003 and 2006.

The plan sought to dismantle the military organization of the now-defunct FARC guerrilla group, which it largely did while also killing thousands and forcibly displacing hundreds of thousands civilians.

De la Espriella has said that he seeks to restart Plan Colombia and seek to militarily destroy groups that were formed during and after peace processes with the FARC and the now-defunct paramilitary organization AUC.

World.title: “Water will run out:” Colombia declares emergency over upcoming El Niño
World.content:
Colombia’s government agreed to declare a national emergency over the consequences of El Niño, a climate phenomenon that is expected to bring extreme drought in December.

According to the government’s environmental institute, IDEAM, this year’s Niño could become the worst since the 1950’s and will peak between November 2026 an March 2027.

During a minister’s council, President Gustavo Petro said that excessive heat and water shortages could lead to energy shortages in regions that rely on hydroelectric dams for their electricity.

Petro asked Finance Minister German Avila to transfer COP4 trillion ($1.2 billion) to disaster management agency UNGRD to double the purchase of solar panels to lessen the demand on these hydroelectric dams.

In December last year, the UNGRD already signed a COP4.2 trillion deal with electricity firm Gecelca to buy solar panels.

In order to maintain food production, the president ordered the purchase of desalination plants for the Caribbean region.

Water is what’s going to run out—we don’t know to what extent, but hopefully Bogotá won’t have to suffer through this again. So, any drinking water supply project that’s already been designed but lacks funding must be funded. Drinking water—all the desalination plants we can bring in, because we don’t build them in Colombia — in all the towns in the northern Caribbean. President Gustavo Petro

Last but not least, Petro urged the Justice Ministry to secure “the accelerated surrender of lands, 500 thousand hectares, that have not been awarded” to landless farmers.

“Provide more land and more water to grow food, grow more food in Colombia, because the sun is going to scorch a lot of food and burn crops. And so it’s likely that we’ll be able to make up for the loss in food supply over these six months with new food supplies,” said the president.

Petro urged his ministers to be careful of corruption, which sank the UNGRD in a crisis in early 2024 and resulted in the detentions of multiple government officials.

World.title: De la Espriella denied aspired control over Colombia’s Congress
World.content:
Colombia’s Congress denied control over the legislative agenda to President-elect Abelardo de la Espriella and voted for a president loyal to former President Alvaro Uribe.

De la Espriella proposed his friend, Senator Alfredo Deluque of the U Party, to assume the leadership of the Senate, which would have given the government control over the congressional agenda.

Ahead of the vote, eight parties expressed their support for Deluque’s candidacy, which would have given him a 55-vote majority in the anonymous vote.

Former President Alvaro Uribe, whose Democratic Center party would be granted the presidency, accused “Abelardo’s circle” of trying to “get rid of this party” and vowed to “defend ourselves.”

Uribe had put up Democratic Center Senator Honorio Henriquez for the job and ordered his 17 senators to stick to their original vote.

If the Tiger roars to destroy the Democratic Center, we’ll have to become hardworking bees and defend ourselves, just like bees do when they’re attacked… I’m frightened by the idea circulating among De La Espriella’s inner circle of destroying that party. Former President Alvaro Uribe

The former president got the support of President Gustavo Petro, arguably Abelardo’s biggest political enemy.

At a rally that was held ahead of the vote, Petro warned senators of his leftist Historic Pact party “not to vote for fascism.”

Under the leadership of Senate bench leader Ivan Cepeda, who lost the presidential election to De la Espriella last month, all 26 of the pact’s senators voted for Henriquez.

Enjoying the secrecy of their vote, dissidents from the parties who were ordered to vote Deluque also turned on the president-elect and delivered Henrique 56 votes. Deluque ended up with only 45.

Less than three weeks before taking office, De la Espriella lost the loyalty of its largest coalition partner in Congress and will have to negotiate his agenda with them.

World.title: Petro calls for “peaceful resistance” against Colombia’s incoming “viceroyalty”
World.content:
President Gustavo Petro called on the people to “prepare peaceful resistance” to the “viceroyalty” that “has been imposed as the president of Colombia.”

During an Independence Day speech in the poor south of Bogota, Petro told thousands of supporters that “the next president of Colombia will be a servant to the rulers of the United States who helped him ‘get elected’.”

“We move from the status of a republic to the status of a viceroyalty again, just like 216 years ago,” said Petro, who on Sunday accepted to become the political leader of the leftist opposition.

It is time to give the second cry of independence… Shout freedom and resistance! Gustavo Petro

Rather than a repetition of the 1810 revolution, the outgoing president proposed to “prepare for peaceful resistance” in defense of communities who benefited from the government’s reforms.

How do you repeal the decree on hourly work that ends the labor reform that created stability, a vital wage, and better working conditions? How? Well, with a permanent general strike of millions of working men and women in Colombia! It is not just by shouting, it is not just by raising flags, they are already used to that… No, it is with a production strike, which is permitted by the National Constitution of Colombia, it is a universal right! And that indeed is civil disobedience! If they are going to strike down the stabilities, the working conditions achieved in this government, a general and indefinite strike in Colombia! Gustavo Petro

Petro threatened to “surround the centers of illegitimate power in Colombia until legitimacy exists once again, which can only be achieved through free popular decision without algorithms, and without foreign money.”

To protect the people, the president suggested the creation of unarmed “liberatory guards” that work in a network, “because they want to kill.”

Wherever they touch a neighborhood, wherever they touch a peasant estate, the network must summon solidarity, it must become a demonstration of all adjacent neighborhoods, of all adjacent villages, of the whole country if necessary. Gustavo Petro

“The only way to stop fascism,” said Petro, “is in peace. It is with joy, but it is with millions and millions of Colombian men and women.”

World.title: Petro to assume political leadership of Colombia’s leading leftist party
World.content:
President Gustavo Petro said Sunday that he would become the leader of Colombia’s largest political party on the left, the Historic Pact.

In a tweet, Petro responded to Senator Ivan Cepeda, who proposed him as party president at a political rally in the city of Tunja on Saturday.

Petro said he would “accept the proposal of my party after surrendering power to the far-right President-elect Abelardo de la Espriella.

The president said he would first go “on a vacation I deserve and didn’t have during four years of governance.”

We will work toward peace and social justice and for a national agreement that prevents violent confrontation among Colombians, and we will seek to contribute to the democratic stability of the countries that Simon Bolívar liberated. President Gustavo Petro

The Historic Pact party was formed in March from a coalition of multiple parties that have long supported the political careers of Petro and Cepeda.

Following a significant electoral victory, the party became the largest of Colombia and will assume 25 of 103 seats in the Senate.

Petro’s former party, Colombia Humana, contributed 12 senators to the collective.

The president started his political career while being a member of the M-19 guerrilla group, which demobilized in 1990.

Petro was elected to the House of Representatives in 1998 an became a senator in 2006.

Between 2012 and 2015, the president was mayor of the capital Bogota.

Petro has been the most popular and powerful leftist politician since the violent death of Liberal Party leader Jorge Eliecer Gaitan in 1948, and was sanctioned by the US Government amid his opposition to the genocide in Gaza.

The president has insisted that his successor won the June elections through fraud and has refused to recognize De la Espriella as his successor.

World.title: Colombia’s peace and human rights offices to close: De la Espriella
World.content:
Colombia’s President-elect Abelardo de la Espriella announced on Monday that he will close the Peace Commissioner’s Office, which was in charge of negotiating peace and implementing peace deals with illegal armed groups.

“The Office of the Peace Commissioner is coming to an end, because there will be no more sham peace processes during my administration,” said De la Espriella in his weekly address to the nation that was broadcast on his social media platforms.

According to the far-right president-elect, who will take office on August 7, other presidential commissioners that will disappear are those of National Reconciliation. and the Office of Human Rights and International Humanitarian Law.

The functions of these offices will be taken over by the Interior, Foreign and Defense ministries that, according to De la Espriella, have been doubling the work of the presidential commissioners.

“These are functions that, by law, are already carried out by other ministries,” so the government can “avoid duplication and extra costs,” said the president-elect.

De la Espriella seems keen to abruptly end the peace policy of his predecessor, President Gustavo Petro, for being too lenient to illegal armed groups.

The president-elect also promised to close war crimes tribunal JEP, which has been trying thousands of former guerrillas and former members of the military.

De la Espriella could only do this through legislation that would change the constitution and the international treaties that protect the victims of an armed conflict between the State and the now-defunct guerrilla organization FARC.

World.title: Petro to seek court order to annul election of De la Espriella
World.content:
Colombia’s President Gustavo Petro said Tuesday that he will seek a court order to annul the election of President-elect Abelardo de la Espriella.

In a post on social media platform X, Petro said he had gather enough evidence to prove that his successor “was elected from abroad, with nonexistent votes.”

“Today we are presenting the body of evidence we have gathered to the representatives elected by the people, and we will file a lawsuit with the courts to annul the elections, as is our duty,” said the outgoing president.

We are not making things up when we say that Abelardo’s government was elected from abroad, with nonexistent votes included in the percentage automatically adjusted by algorithms created by private Israeli companies with the endorsement of their genocidal government. President Gustavo Petro

“We are facing not only the imminent rise of fascism in Colombia but also what may be the greatest threat to global democracy since Hitler’s time,” said Petro.

In a response that was broadcast on his social media channels, De la Espriella reiterated that Petro was a “tyrant” who was trying to perpetuate power through a coup d’etat with the help of the leftist runner-up in the election, Senator Ivan Cepeda.

Even before becoming a candidate, I warned you: Petro is a tyrant in the making who seeks to perpetuate himself in power by any means necessary. And today, as the president-elect of all of you, I ratify what I have said for so many years. This is no longer an analysis or an opinion; it is a palpable reality. From the moment nearly 13 million Colombians stood by me to defeat him and his political frontman, Petro and Cepeda began their Plan B to stay in power, no matter what it takes. And they want to do so through a coup d’état. President-elect Abelardo de la Espriella

The president-elect asked the armed forces “to protect the Constitution and democracy, and to disobey any order that Petro may be giving to the contrary.”

Resistance, dear compatriots. We cannot allow them to snatch away what we achieved at the ballot box in an epic democratic battle this past June 21. Let us resist, for August 7 is near. God, the vote, and democracy have spoken; we are going to defend the Constitution and the rule of law as we must. President-elect Abelardo de la Espriella

De la Espriella has long claimed that he will extradite his predecessor to the United States.

World.title: Chile’s Municipalities, Senapred Meet Ahead of Storm Forecast
World.content:
SANTIAGO, Chile â As Chile prepares for an approaching winter storm system, the Association of Municipalities of Chile (Amuch) held a high-level coordination meeting with the National Disaster Prevention and Response Service (Senapred) to strengthen municipal emergency response measures.

The discussions focused on improving collaboration among municipalities, national agencies, and private service providers to better protect residents during severe weather events.

Power Companies Face Pressure Over Response Times

A central topic in the meeting was the performance of electric utilities during past emergencies. JosÃ© Manuel Palacios, mayor of La Reina, expressed concern over delayed responses from power companies in recent years.

âWe are exploring ways, together with Senapred and other institutions, to develop more efficient actions and hold the companies accountable to meet the response times our residents need,â Palacios said.

Rural Water Supply Risks Tied to Electricity

For rural municipalities, electrical outages pose a dual threat, as potable water systems often rely on electric power. Paula GÃ¡rate, mayor of Melipilla, emphasized the heightened vulnerability of rural areas during storms.

âLosing electricity also means losing access to potable water. Many rural water systems depend on electricity, and that remains our greatest concern,â GÃ¡rate noted.

Coordinated Municipal Efforts to Mitigate Risks

Senapred Director Alicia CebriÃ¡n highlighted the essential role of municipal governments in both preparation and response phases.

âMunicipalities play a crucial role in coordination, information gathering, and implementing mitigation works to reduce the impact of winter threats on residents,â CebriÃ¡n stated.

She underscored that emergency prevention and mitigation is a shared responsibility across public agencies and institutions. âPublic authorities who are directly involved in disaster management bear this responsibility, and we are committed to fulfilling it,â she added.

Winter System Expected to Test Emergency Readiness

The coordination meeting comes as Chileâs central regions brace for a frontal system expected to bring heavy rain and strong winds. Authorities emphasized that ongoing preparation and inter-agency cooperation will be key to minimizing disruption and protecting vulnerable communities.

World.title: Brian Wilson, Legendary Beach Boys Co-Founder, Dies at 82
World.content:
LOS ANGELES â Brian Wilson, the legendary musician, songwriter and co-founder of The Beach Boys, has died at the age of 82, his family announced.

“We are heartbroken to announce that our beloved father Brian Wilson has passed away,” the family said in a statement. “We are at a loss for words right now. Please respect our privacy at this time as our family is grieving. We realize that we are sharing our grief with the world.”

Born in 1942 in Hawthorne, California, Wilson formed The Beach Boys in 1961 with his younger brothers Carl and Dennis, cousin Mike Love, and friend Al Jardine. The band became one of the most influential and commercially successful acts in music history, selling over 100 million records worldwide.

Wilson was the creative force behind the groupâs distinctive harmonies and groundbreaking studio sound. His 1966 album Pet Sounds is regarded as a masterpiece that reshaped the boundaries of pop music production.

Among The Beach Boys’ many hits, Wilson co-wrote and produced I Get Around, Help Me, Rhonda, and Good Vibrations. Rolling Stone ranked The Beach Boys 12th on its list of the “100 Greatest Artists of All Time.”

Tributes poured in following news of his death. Nancy Sinatra shared a photo with Wilson on Instagram, writing, âHis cherished music will live forever as he travels through the Universe and beyond. God bless you, sweet Brian.â

View this post on Instagram A post shared by ð½ðððð¢ ððððððð (@nancysinatra)

Sean Ono Lennon called Wilson the “American Mozart” and a “one of a kind genius from another world,” adding: âAnyone who really knows me knows how heartbroken I am about Brian Wilson passing. Not many people influenced me as much as he did. I feel very lucky that I was able to meet him and spend some time with him. He was always very kind and generous.”

Throughout his life, Wilson faced significant personal struggles. Diagnosed with paranoid schizophrenia in 1984, his condition was linked by doctors to earlier psychedelic drug use. In early 2024, his family revealed he had developed dementia.

Wilson’s wife, Melinda, with whom he shared 24 years of marriage and five adopted children, died earlier in 2024. He also had two daughters, Carnie and Wendy, from his first marriage.

Despite his health battles, Wilsonâs legacy remains unparalleled. His influence on songwriting, vocal harmony, and studio innovation continues to inspire generations of musicians.

World.title: Chile and Norway Deepen Antarctic Cooperation with New Agreement
World.content:
Chile and Norway signed a memorandum of understanding on Antarctic cooperation Monday, reinforcing their shared commitment to peace, science, and environmental protection in the region.

The agreement, signed by Chilean Foreign Minister Alberto van Klaveren and Norwegian Minister of International Development Ã smund GrÃ¸ver, aims to strengthen bilateral coordination under the Antarctic Treaty System. It outlines enhanced collaboration on scientific research, climate monitoring, and the preservation of marine ecosystems through frameworks such as the Antarctic Treaty Consultative Meetings and the Commission for the Conservation of Antarctic Marine Living Resources (CCAMLR).

The accord includes provisions for regular dialogue between scientific and governmental institutions in both countries and seeks to optimize joint efforts in Antarctic and sub-Antarctic research. Both nations also pledged support for the Polar Codeâs implementation, aiming to improve safety and environmental standards for ships operating in polar waters.

Operational and logistical cooperation between Chileâs and Norwayâs national Antarctic programs will also be explored, particularly in alignment with CCAMLRâs conservation objectives.

This renewed alliance builds on the long-standing historical ties between the two nations and reaffirms their role as active stewards of one of the worldâs most fragile and strategically vital environments.

World.title: Full Moon in June 2025: Date, Meaning, and What’s Ahead in the Night Sky
World.content:
The full moon in June 2025 will occur on Wednesday, June 11, and will be visible in most regions depending on local moonrise and moonset times. Known as the Strawberry Moon, this lunar event is tied to Native American traditions marking the ripening of wild strawberries and the approach of summer in the Northern Hemisphere.

In Argentina, for example, the moon will rise around 5:52 p.m. and set at 9:19 a.m. on June 12. This full moon, like others throughout the year, has long held cultural, astrological, and even emotional significance. While there is no scientific consensus on its effects, itâs commonly associated with heightened emotions, sleep disturbances, and symbolic transitions.

World.title: Japan Tops Global Waste Index 2025; U.S., Israel, and Chile Rank as Worst Polluters
World.content:
