She staked her leadership on housing affordability and residential development, declaring she wanted to be the premier that got millennials into homes.

But she was criticised internally for failing to differentiate her leadership from that of Andrews, who had led the state for more than nine years including the COVID-19 era.

Allan raised in Labor

Allan lives with her husband Yorick and their two children on a rural property south of Bendigo, the regional city she grew up in, having hailed from a prominent local Labor family.

Her grandfather Bill was president of the Bendigo Trades Hall.

In May, she told Labor faithful how her father Peter was made redundant in the early 90s when the State Electricity Commission (SEC) was privatised under Kennett.

Jacinta Allan and her father Peter at their Bendigo house in the early 1990s. (Supplied: Victorian Premier's office)

She joined the party when she was 19, studied arts at La Trobe University's Bendigo campus and, in 1997, led a campaign to stop a lap dancing bar from opening.

Otherwise, she worked for Labor MPs.

Then she entered parliament herself.

Jacinta Allan (centre) became the youngest female MP in Victorian history after being elected to the seat of Bendigo East in 1999. (ABC News)

In her inaugural speech to parliament in 1999, Ms Allan wore two brooches.

One was a poppet head — a logo for her hometown — which served as a totem of her dedication to the people of Bendigo.

The other was an Emily's List brooch, the Labor women support network that was established by Joan Kirner, Victoria's only other female premier.

On the day she became premier, Allan was emotional as she described the late Kirner as a mentor, and reflected on following in her footsteps.

"I hope ... it says to young women, older women, women from across different backgrounds of all parts of the state that leadership takes on different shapes and sizes," she said at the time.

Like Kirner, the outgoing premier has served in the role, but has missed her chance to win an election in her own right.

World.title: Breaking: Jacinta Allan steps aside as Victorian premier
World.content:
Victorian Premier Jacinta Allan will resign from the top job, paving the way for her deputy Ben Carroll to become the state's next leader.

Ms Allan made the announcement this morning, ahead of an expected spill motion she was tipped to lose.

The meeting came after a whirlwind 24 hours, which saw Ms Allan write to Labor's state secretary to confirm she would contest any leadership ballot, and Mr Carroll say he had been approached to launch a challenge.

Speaking at parliament this morning, the outgoing premier said she would give her unqualified support to Mr Carroll should he put his hand up.

"I am making this decision because it is the right thing by the Labor Party and the Victorian people," she said.

"I was prepared to put my record and my plan to a ballot of members as our rules allow.

"I believe I would have won. But doing so this close to an election takes up valuable resources, including the most precious … one, time.

" At the end of the day, I am and always have been a team player. "

Ms Allan has led Victoria since she replaced Daniel Andrews in 2023.

Her term has been overshadowed by scandals that have followed her from the Andrews era, most notably allegations of corruption in the state's Big Build construction program.

Ms Allan was the state's youngest-ever female MP when she was elected on the eve of her 26th birthday in 1999, and only the second woman to hold the top job.

Speaking this morning, she encouraged more women to enter politics.

"Please don't look at what I have experienced this week and think, 'Stuff that. I don't want to be involved,'" she said.

"Look at the support I've experienced over my career, and think, 'I can make a difference here too.'"

World.title: Quick hits: Davies makes history, Diamonds clap back in uni debate
World.content:
Rose Davies runs a "race of a lifetime" to make Australian history, and the Diamonds remain in the spotlight even off the court.

Here are the quick hits from day four of the Commonwealth Games.

1. Davies makes history on the track

Rose Davies celebrated Australia's first athletics gold of the Games. (Getty Images: Michael Steele)

The eagerly anticipated athletics program finally got underway on the fourth day of competition in Glasgow, and it wasn't long before Australia claimed its first gold on the track.

Rose Davies sat back for much of the women's 10,000m but timed her move to perfection, waiting until less than a kilometre remained before galloping ahead of Kenya's Diana Wanza.

And Davies eventually won in a canter, crossing the finish line almost 11 seconds before silver medallist Wanza.

Australian commentary great Bruce McAvaney called it "the race of a lifetime" during the Network Seven broadcast.

Davies became the first Australian woman to win the 10,000m at a Commonwealth Games.

"These moments come once in a lifetime, and I'm so happy I got to achieve this," Davies told the Seven Network.

2. From a cancer diagnosis to a Games final

Scotland's Archie Goodburn did not win a medal, but he has won the respect of everyone as he competes in Glasgow while dealing with three brain tumours. (Getty Images: SNS Group/Ross MacDonald)

When people say the phrase "there are more important things in life than sport," they're probably speaking about Scotland's Archie Goodburn.

The 25-year-old breaststroke specialist had a chance to compete at the Paris Olympics when he was diagnosed with three inoperable brain tumours in 2024.

But speaking after his race in the final, where he finished seventh, his interview put everything in perspective and made it very hard not to get emotional watching him.

"My dream was to make the final, but outside the pool I dream, like, of a future where brain cancer isn't the biggest killer of those under 40," he said.

"Where the UK government establish a national brain cancer lead to make that change, and I'd much prefer that that change was made and that dream is completed than any of my personal goals in the pool.

"Because what families and young people are going through out there is really beyond the comprehension of many people out here and certainly far harder than anything I've ever had to do as a world-class sportsman."

3. Welsh sisters twinning in bronze

Abigail Roper won bronze first, but sister Emily got her own an hour or so later. (Getty Images: Naomi Baker)

Wales has not been flush with supreme gymnasts at the Commonwealth Games.

But, given their national colour, perhaps it's no surprise that at these Scottish Games, two have come along at once, like lithe, smiling versions of red London buses.

Both Abi Roper and Emily Roper were in action in the vault, with Abi claiming a bronze medal with a score of 13.433, just a fraction ahead of her sister, who scored 13.283 after being penalised 0.3 for her landing on her second vault.

Then, an hour or so later, Emily put her disappointment behind her to deliver a display worthy of a medal, also winning bronze behind Australian gold medal winner Katie McDonald.

In a heartening display of sisterly love, Abi could be seen roaring her support from the stands, her own bronze medal dangling around her neck, as her sister delivered the performance of her life to win Wales its first-ever medal on that apparatus at a Commonwealth Games.

"Sometimes we bicker because we are competitive, so we are constantly fighting to see who is better," Emily told a BBC interviewer in 2025.

Who knows how much bickering there would have been had Emily come away from Glasgow empty-handed.

4. Diamonds can't help being icons, even on a day off

After winning their first two matches, our netball world champions had day four off in Glasgow, but everyone's still talking about the Diamonds: just not for the broadcast-related reason you might expect.

Diamonds disappointed first two games only live on streaming service Diamonds fans are disappointed to discover Australia's dominant netball team's Glasgow matches are only being aired live on Seven's online streaming service.

Folks online have been debating Australia's netball uniform, which rides up during play and often ends up looking more like a singlet.

Some are worried the poor design is distracting our goal shooters, who have to take their shots before readjusting the awkward uniform (lest they be penalised for a held ball!).

Currently competing in her third Commonwealth Games, Courtney Bruce has worn a few iterations of the kit over the years, and she says the team isn't too worried about the 2026 uniform.

"It is what it is, there's literally nothing we can do about it, [so] we don't think about it," she told the ABC.

In a video posted on social media, Commonwealth Games debutant Sophie Garbin poked fun at what she described as "the most talked about" aspect of the Glasgow event.

Loading...

All it takes is one look at the comment section to see people on either side of the heated debate: from supporters saying shorter dresses are easier to play in, to those who reckon the Diamonds look "silly".

Responding to haters, Bruce says it's a "good thing we're strong … fit, and we train hard".

I mean, it's not like they aren't wearing shorts under the dress... (Getty Images: Lintao Zhang)

5. Mollie O'Callaghan pulls out of the backstroke

Mollie O'Callaghan has withdrawn from the 50m backstroke. (Getty Images: Adam Pretty)

Coming into this Commonwealth Games, Mollie O'Callaghan revealed she was managing a back injury, and it cost her a chance in her backup event, the 50m backstroke.

The 22-year-old was worried that she might not even be able to compete in Glasgow after scans revealed stress fractures and bone bruising on her lumbar spine.

She was, however, cleared by a specialist to compete.

"Things might look a little different for me at the Commonwealth Games and Pan Pacs, but I'll give everything I have and do my absolute best every time I race," O'Callaghan said in an Instagram post before the Games.

Some things remained the same though, the Queenslander claiming yet another gold medal for her burgeoning collection in the 200m freestyle and 4x100m freestyle relay.

However, she withdrew from the mixed 4x100m freestyle relay and did not line up in the 50m backstroke heats on Monday morning to focus on the 100m freestyle final that evening.

World.title: Singer D4vd to stand trial for allegedly killing and dismembering 14yo girl
World.content:
Content warning: this story involves the death of a minor, allegations of sexual abuse of a child and graphic violent details.

Singer D4vd will stand trial for the alleged killing and dismemberment of 14-year-old Celeste Rivas Hernandez, who authorities say had threatened to expose their sexual relationship.

Los Angeles Judge Charlaine Olmedo decided that the evidence that prosecutors presented at a five-day preliminary hearing provided probable cause for a trial on charges of murder, continuous sexual abuse of a child under the age of 14 and unlawful mutilation of human remains.

D4vd, the 21-year-old singer born David Burke whose career was steeply rising before the allegations emerged, has pleaded not guilty.

Celeste Rivas Hernandez's dismembered body was found in D4dv's car. (AP: Damian Dovarganes)

Held without bail

"The people have met their burden on all counts," Justice Olmedo said.

She ordered that Mr Burke continue to be held without bail.

US singer D4vd pleads not guilty to murdering 14yo girl found in his Tesla The 21-year-old, who rose to fame after going viral on TikTok, has pleaded not guilty to a murder charge of a 14-year-old whose dismembered body was found in his seemingly abandoned Tesla.

Justice Olmedo emphasised that the probable cause standard for a preliminary hearing like this is much lower than the threshold at trial.

However, prosecutors asserted that the evidence was overwhelming.

"Based on the mountains of evidence presented," Deputy District Attorney Beth Silverman said, "all of the allegations have been proved way beyond the standard required".

Mr Burke had no visible reaction to the decision and the defence team declined to comment outside court.

Prosecutors wrapped up their case by giving a moment-by-moment account of Ms Rivas Hernandez's last night, showing that, after a stream of text messages with Mr Burke, her phone went permanently silent when she arrived at his home.

As she neared his Hollywood home shortly after 10am on April 23, 2025, in an Uber he had sent to pick her up, she sent her final text: "girly pop i'm almost there open ur door if ur home".

Prosecutors allege Mr Burke stabbed her to death when she came through the door.

Fighting via text messages

D4vd has pleaded not guilty but is being held in custody. (AP: Bill Robles)

The night before, the two argued via text about his relationship with a woman.

Ms Rivas Hernandez sent him an angry and profane text saying she would tell her dad so many lies about him and "i will end ur career and ur life".

Los Angeles Police detective Corey Farrell, under questioning from the prosecution, read the texts that were obtained from warrants on Mr Burke's iPhone and iCloud accounts.

After the final witness on Monday, the defence argued that the evidence was insufficient and the murder charge should be dismissed.

d4vd charged with first degree murder and sexual acts against a minor d4vd was arrested in relation to the murder of Celeste Rivas Hernandez, whose body was found in his abandoned car in late 2025.

"There's no evidence that Mr Burke harboured a deliberate intent to kill Miss Hernandez," Mr Burke's attorney Marilyn Bednarski said.

She said the communications between Mr Burke and Ms Rivas Hernandez showed "no threat, no evidence of a history of violence" and that he had "the opposite of homicidal malice" toward her.

She argued that a medical examiner ruling that her death was a homicide from two puncture wounds was too vague and inconclusive to be evidence of murder.

The defence did not directly give an alternative theory on how she died and was not required to.

Mr Burke's legal team showed several other texts from Ms Rivas Hernandez threatening him about their relationship, and saying she would go to his mother, talk to his friends and "leak" information about them.

No suggestion of legal action

Under questioning from defence lawyer Blair Berk, Detective Farrell said he saw no indication that she ever threatened to go to police or pursue any legal action against him.

The defence also established that Ms Rivas Hernandez had asked seven times to come to see Mr Burke in the days before her death, and he reluctantly agreed only after she demanded it, and that she had threatened to kill him and to mutilate him.

D4vd released his first full-length album, Withered, two days after authorities say Celeste was killed. (AP: Jordan Strauss/Invision)

Mr Burke's lawyers argued that all of the malice had come from Ms Rivas Hernandez.

Ms Silverman told the judge that "the defence tried numerous times throughout these proceedings to dirty up the victim" despite her being a child.

The detective also said under questioning from Ms Berk that the parents of both Mr Burke and Ms Rivas Hernandez knew about their relationship, that he had attended church with members of her family and that her parents had given their consent for her to go to London with him for a week.

After her phone went silent, Mr Burke sent Ms Rivas Hernandez several other messages that night asking where she was and expressing concern.

Prosecutors allege that those messages were sent as cover after he had killed her.

Body found in Tesla five months after death

Prosecutors allege Mr Burke dismembered Ms Rivas Hernandez's body in his garage.

A police analyst testified earlier in the hearing that samples pulled from apparent blood stains there matched her DNA .

Her body was found in a Tesla registered to him nearly five months later.

Lawyers for D4vd argued that the prosecution had not met the threshold for murder, but the judge disagreed. (Reuters: Arafat Barbakh)

In earlier testimony, Detective Farrell recounted dozens of sexually explicit photos of Mr Burke and Ms Rivas Hernandez and years of text messages that described the same things, along with conversations that indicated she had gotten an abortion in 2024 at 13 after he got her pregnant.

Detective Farrell described the photos that could not be shown in court, material so graphic that it left Celeste's mother in tears and prompted both parents to leave the courtroom on Friday.

They were back in court on Monday.

D4vd (pronounced "David") became an online musical phenomenon as a teen with a blend of indie rock, R&B and lo-fi pop.

He had huge followings on TikTok, SoundCloud and Spotify, where his top songs, including his 2022 breakthrough Romantic Homicide, have more than a billion plays.

In 2024, he played the Coachella music festival and released his first full-length album, Withered, two days after authorities say Ms Rivas Hernandez was killed.

AP

World.title: Queens Domain land handback proposal gets Hobart council's 'strong support'
World.content:
An Aboriginal land return proposal near Hobart's CBD has passed its first hurdle after receiving "in-principle support" at a Hobart City Council meeting.

The 4.9-hectare parcel of land near the summit of Queens Domain was identified by the council last year as a possible site for an Indigenous-owned cultural centre operated by the Tasmanian Aboriginal Centre (TAC).

Lord Mayor Anna Reynolds said Monday's motion, which passed nine votes to three, had "strong support around the table".

Councillor Reynolds said those who voted against the proposal had raised procedural questions, including whether the hand back could be blocked at a later stage.

"If we had a state government who did not want this to happen, roadblocks could be put in place," Cr Reynolds said.

"But we've heard from the Minister for Aboriginal Affairs, Bridget Archer … and we know that she sees this as a good idea.

"Whether that process is smooth or takes a really long time is really incumbent on all the partners on this journey. This includes the council, but it is also the state government and all their different departments, and also the Aboriginal Land Council."

Hobart Lord Mayor Anna Reynolds says the motion passed 9 votes to 3. (ABC News: Luke Bowden)

The vote was not the final approval for the land return but will allow the council's chief executive to undertake the necessary work to progress the proposal, which includes investigating any title issues for subdivision and legal costs.

A development application and public consultation would still need to be completed, and any cultural centre would be subject to a separate future development application.

This parcel contains an area suitable for development alongside part of the lowland native grassland. (ABC News: Andrew Cunningham)

'Unique opportunity' for establishing cultural centre

If approved, the land parcel off Domain Road would be Tasmania's first Aboriginal land return in more than two decades.

Loading...

Aboriginal Land Council of Tasmania (ALCT) general manager Sarah Wilcox said the transfer would be welcomed by the community.

"This is a really unique opportunity to think about establishing a cultural centre which can serve as a keeping place," she said.

" Currently in the Aboriginal community, we have absolutely nowhere to look after our sacred cultural items. "

If it gets final approval, it would be the first Aboriginal land handback in Tasmania in more than 20 years. (ABC News: Andrew Cunningham)

'People do care': Why private owners are handing land back It has been two decades since substantial land hand-backs in Tasmania, so private owners are doing it instead.

The council was asked by the TAC last year for support to build an Aboriginal-owned and operated cultural centre in the state's capital.

The centre would host cultural items, act as a performance space and support Aboriginal food enterprises and other tourism activities.

There have been no large-scale land returns in Tasmania since 2005, when Truwana/Cape Barren Island and Lungtalanana/Clarke Island were returned to the ALCT.

World.title: Savannah Guthrie pleads with mother's kidnappers to 'help us find her'
World.content:
NBC's Today show co-host Savannah Guthrie says her family is living an unending nightmare nearly six months after her mother's disappearance, pleading with her kidnappers to "tell us where to look for her".

A video released on Monday, local time, is the latest public plea from the journalist since Nancy Guthrie, 84, disappeared from her home just outside Tucson, Arizona on February 1.

She said her family would never stop looking for her.

"The world can be a cruel and unforgiving place, and I know that you have tried to do things the right way," she said.

"So I'm asking you, begging you, to do the right thing now. Make the right choice. Help us find her. Tell us where to look for her. I truly believe it is never too late to do the right thing."

Loading Instagram content

Authorities believe Nancy Guthrie was taken against her will on February 1.

They found blood near the front doorstep of her home just outside Tucson, and the FBI later released surveillance videos showing a masked man on the porch that night.

Volunteers and search teams scoured nearby desert terrain filled with cactuses, bushes and boulders in the weeks after she vanished.

A volunteer group recently searched for her body near the Arizona-Mexico border.

It has been four months since Nancy Guthrie vanished It has been four months since Nancy Guthrie, the mother of America's Today show co-host Savannah Guthrie, was reported missing.

Three notes gained wide attention

Authorities have not said how many purported ransom demands were made after Guthrie's disappearance, though three news organisations reported receiving such notes and turned them over to investigators.

The FBI has discounted some of the ransom notes as nothing more than extortion attempts, but said it was still evaluating others that might be legitimate.

The federal agency hasn't specified which ransom notes might be genuine.

The US television personality has previously made a series of social media posts about her mother after she went missing.

In the days after the disappearance, the broadcaster and her siblings acknowledged they were aware of media reports of a supposed ransom letter and were ready to talk and listen, but wanted proof their mother was alive.

Weeks later, Savannah Guthrie said her family was offering a $US1 million ($1.45 million) reward for information leading to the recovery of her mother.

She also acknowledged for the first time that her mother might not be alive, but added that there was still hope.

AP

World.title: Regional NSW council cuts services as it weighs 42pc rate hike
World.content:
Albury councillors have voted six-two to reduce opening hours at some of the regional New South Wales city's facilities and make its Visitor Information Centre unstaffed as the council works to address a multi-million-dollar budget deficit.

The changes, approved at last night's meeting, form part of the council's Financial Sustainability Program, which aims to reduce costs.

The measures will see the Visitor Information Centre at the LibraryMuseum become unstaffed, reduced opening hours at Lavington Library and the Murray Art Museum Albury (MAMA) close on Mondays.

The changes are expected to save about $110,000 a year.

Councillors voted six-two in favour of the changes, which include reducing opening hours at the art museum. (ABC News: Gaye Pattison)

The service reductions come as councillors consider whether to apply to the NSW Independent Pricing and Regulatory Tribunal (IPART) for a Special Rate Variation (SRV), with options of a 40 per cent increase over three years, or a 42 per cent increase over two years.

Any increase would require IPART approval before taking effect.

An update on the Financial Sustainability Program before councillors last night said the council had reduced its projected General Fund deficit from more than $22 million in late 2025 to $18.9 million.

The meeting heard council had delivered about $1.6 million in ongoing savings with a potential further $3.3 million in savings through changes to services, property management and day-to-day operations.

Mayor Kevin Mack has encouraged the entire Albury community to have their say on a possible 42 per cent rate increase over two years. (ABC Goulburn Murray: Philippe Perez)

Councillor Darren Cameron, who voted against the motion, said the measures did not go far enough.

"In my view we're only dabbling with the measures that have been taken so far," he said.

"We have to reconcile ourselves to the fact that we are going to have to massively reduce services if we are going to avoid a SRV."

Cr Cameron said he believed council should consider more significant service reductions, including placing MAMA into care and maintenance until the city's financial position improved.

Councillor Stuart Baker, who supported the motion, said there was no simple solution to the council's financial challenges.

"I am having trouble seeing an easy path that Albury City can get out of it," he said.

"We can't get out of it by just cutting everything and reducing services because then Albury isn't the way we want it to be.

" People come here and live here because it is a good place to live, work and do business and bring up families. "

Albury will be one of the most expensive councils in terms of household rates in NSW if it seeks a Special Rate Variation. (ABC News: Ashlee Aldridge)

Speaking during the public forum, Albury Ratepayers Association spokesperson Susan Keighran said the group was "representing a large number of the community that are deeply concerned about the proposed SRV".

"My primary concern is that Albury City Council has shifted the financial burden primarily onto ratepayers without first exhausting internal structural reforms," she said.

"I appreciate that managing a growing city like ours involves difficult decisions and I don't underestimate that responsibility for a second."

Ms Keighran said many residents were already struggling with rising living costs.

Albury City Council is considering a rate rise of up to 42 per cent over the next two years. (ABC News: Ashlee Aldridge)

Ms Keighran said the association believed council should continue looking for savings before asking residents to pay higher rates.

"We, the community, are asking council to look within themselves, sort out your own back of house, balance incoming funds with affordable projects and trim some financial fat," she said.

"We, the ratepayers and renters that make up this wonderful community, should not be expected to be a bank for Albury City."

She said higher rates would also affect local businesses as households reduced spending on dining out, entertainment and other discretionary purchases.

Community consultation on the proposed SRV closes on July 31. Councillors are expected to consider the feedback before deciding whether to lodge an application with IPART.

World.title: Jacinta Allan leadership LIVE: Premier resigns before crucial caucus vote; Ben Carroll arrives at parliament
World.content:
Allan thanked the Victorians, and said this was the most important thing she would say today.

“It has been the honour of my life to serve you as your premier,” she said.

“I step down after 1036 days in this role. Not one of them wasted, not one of them easy. And let’s be honest, this week has been tough.

“But let’s be clear: the average working family has it tougher. They’re the ones managing interest rate rises. They’re the ones living in a housing crisis and facing economic change that no one can predict. They’re the people I always put first.

“I got into politics to fight for them, and whatever I do next, I will still be fighting for them.”

World.title: Toronto reels after shootings targeting Jewish bakeries, US consulate
World.content:
WorldNorth AmericaAntisemitism Toronto reels after shootings targeting Jewish bakeries, US consulate Michael Koziol July 28, 2026 — 10:10am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

Washington: Canada’s largest city is reeling after a string of violent acts targeting Jewish shops and – for a second time in six months – the US consulate, in what could be another example of an alleged “guns for hire” scheme involving foreign entities. The attacks have drawn parallels with the Iran-orchestrated arson attacks against Jewish businesses in Australia that led Prime Minister Anthony Albanese to cut diplomatic ties last year and expel the Iranian ambassador from Canberra. Monday morning’s gunfire at the US consulate in Toronto marked the second time the building has been targeted this year. The Canadian Press via AP Jewish groups in Canada are also increasingly worried about a major attack like last year’s massacre on Bondi Beach, which “looms large for all of us here”, said Noah Shack, chief executive of Canada’s Centre for Israel and Jewish Affairs. Two locations of the same Jewish-owned bakery chain in Toronto were targeted in attacks overnight on Saturday. One shopfront was struck by gunfire, and the other had a window smashed.



The assailants hit Kiva’s Bagel Bar, a Toronto institution that has served bagels since 1979 and a fixture of the city’s Jewish community. Prime Minister Mark Carney said he was appalled by the attacks. “Jewish Canadians should be able to live, work and worship free from fear, intimidation and hate,” he said. “Canada’s government is absolute in our commitment to combating the scourge of antisemitism.” Canadian Prime Minister Mark Carney and Ontario Premier Doug Ford both condemned the attacks. The Canadian Press via AP Then, early on Monday morning, a gunman fired a single shot at the US consulate in central Toronto, before leading police on a high-speed chase. Police ultimately broke off the pursuit. Deputy police chief Frank Barredo said an officer stationed outside the consulate heard a gunshot at 4.46am, before witnessing a white Honda Accord with no licence plate speeding away from the scene.



Toronto Mayor Olivia Chow called it a “brazen attack” and vowed to work with authorities to “remove the illegal American guns off our streets”. There were no injuries from any of the three incidents. It was the second time the US consulate in Toronto was shot at this year, after a similar incident in March. Police have said young people are being paid to carry out attacks on synagogues and other targets. Sammy Kogan/The Canadian Press via AP Last month, Toronto police said young people were being hired over encrypted messaging services to carry out targeted and connected shootings, including at Jewish schools and synagogues.



“In order to get paid, they are required to film their attacks,” Toronto police chief Myron Demkiw said at the time. “Who is paying for this? This is what we’re trying to determine.” An operation in June recovered two firearms – a 9mm handgun and a 45-calibre pistol – both from the US. Police said the 9mm was linked to at least six shootings and the 45-calibre to at least 21. Two people were arrested in that operation and an officer, Marc Pinizzotto, was killed. A third person, already in custody, faced additional charges over the matter, while a fourth person was subsequently arrested. Ruby Sahota (right) used a speech in Canada’s parliament last month to publicly state that a “foreign entity” was responsible for orchestrating the attacks. Bloomberg Canadian MP Ruby Sahota, the secretary of state for combatting crime, told parliament that the people responsible for firing shots at Toronto synagogues in early March were hired and paid by a “foreign entity”. She did not identify the country.



A late June report from Canada’s Integrated Threat Assessment Centre referred to terrorist activity by the Islamic Movement of the Companions of the Right, an Iran-linked network which claimed responsibility for attacks in Britain, and was recently designated a terrorist group by that country. The report, excerpts of which were obtained by this masthead, also said Canadian authorities had disrupted four terrorist plots inspired by Islamic State since the war between Israel and Hamas began in October 2023. Toronto Mayor Olivia Chow condemned the “brazen attack” while pledging to get American guns off her city’s streets. The Canadian Press via AP In 2024, father and son Ahmed and Mostafa Eldidi were arrested and charged with allegedly plotting an Islamic State-inspired attack in Toronto. They are due to face trial in September. On Monday, police said it was too early to say whether the latest shooting at the US consulate and the violence at the Jewish bagel shops were linked to the aforementioned guns-for-hire scheme.



Shack told this masthead that Islamist terrorism posed a serious threat to Toronto and Canada and “represents a ticking time bomb that needs to be defused”. Related Article Exclusive

Terror charges Why underworld kingpin Kaz Hamad struck a deal with Iran to attack a Melbourne synagogue The alleged criminals-for-hire scheme “follows the pattern that was uncovered in Australia of the Iranian regime hiring criminals to attack the Jewish community with a spate of arson attacks”. “This is a clear tactic that is being used in Australia, in Europe and we believe here in Canada as well,” he said. Shack said Toronto’s Jewish community was shaken by the latest attacks, which “sit squarely in a pattern that’s recognisable to us”.



But the community was also resilient and determined not to let terrorists succeed, he said. Kiva’s Bagel Bar sold out of bagels on Monday, he added. Ontario Premier Doug Ford said he was “totally disgusted” by the shootings and vandalism in Toronto over the preceding 48 hours, and expected those responsible to be punished to the fullest extent of the law. Related Article Crime Berlin Pride van attack suspect shot dead in confrontation with police It comes as authorities in Germany are questioned over their handling of Abdul Ballout, a German-born citizen with Lebanese roots, suspected of driving a van into a crowd at Berlin’s Pride festival, killing one person and injuring 29. Ballout previously sought to join Islamic State, prosecutors said, and was convicted in Berlin of preparing a serious act of violence. But a court released him pending an appeal. He was killed in a confrontation with police responding to the Pride festival attack. Get a note directly from our foreign correspondents on what’s making headlines around the world.

World.title: ASX slides lower, oil prices retreat; Trump pushes for rate cut
World.content:
Updated BusinessMarketsWorld markets ASX slides lower, oil prices retreat; Trump pushes for rate cut Damian Troise and Alex Veiga Updated July 28, 2026 — 10:05am ,first published July 28, 2026 — 5:17am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

The Australian sharemarket has slid lower at the open after a mixed session on Wall Street, while oil prices continued to fall after the US and Iran paused their attacks while work resumed on restarting negotiations to end the war. The S&P/ASX 200 was down 22.8 points, or 0.3 per cent, to 8871.2 in early trade, after jumping by 1.4 per cent on Monday. The Australian dollar was 0.1 per cent lower to US69.86¢. Wall Street has kicked off its week with a mixed session. AP Overnight, the S&P 500 fell 0.2 per cent. The index is coming off two weekly losses in a row. The Dow Jones rose 155 points, or 0.3 per cent. The Nasdaq composite fell 0.4 per cent. Oil prices reversed course from a week ago, when a sharp escalation in fighting between the US and Iran worsened worries about global oil supplies. The price of Brent crude, the international standard, dropped 8.7 per cent to close at $US88.36 a barrel for September delivery. Prices surged to over $US100 a barrel last week before easing.



The war between the US and Iran has sharply curtailed, and at times halted, traffic through the vital Strait of Hormuz. That has had a ripple effect throughout the world’s economy. Gasoline prices have surged and shipping costs for most goods are rising, with businesses typically passing those costs along to households. Related Article Opinion

Aviation Alan Joyce thinks it could’ve been worse Kishor Napier-Raman Senior Business Writer President Donald Trump called on the Federal Reserve to lower interest rates, saying the US should have the lowest interest rate in the world. “Rates should be lowered... We have other countries that are paying less interest rates,” Trump told reporters aboard Air Force One. “We should have the lowest interest rate in the world,” Trump said.



“Kevin is fantastic, but he’s got a board, and the board members are very political,” Trump said, referring to Fed chair Kevin Warsh, adding he knew what Warsh wanted to do. The Federal Reserve will announce its interest rates decision on Thursday (AEST), with markets expecting the central bank to stay on hold. Bond yields fell. The yield on the 10-year Treasury fell to 4.65 per cent from 4.69 per cent late Friday. Technology companies were behind much of the shifts on Wall Street, with gains and declines for a mix of big companies resulting in uncertain trading. Nvidia fell 5 per cent and Micron Technology slumped 2.3 per cent. At the same time, Microsoft rose 1.9 per cent and Apple rose 1.2 per cent. They are all among the most valuable companies in the world and those market values give them more influence over the direction of the broader market. The mix of gains and losses from a variety of those companies had more impact in pushing and pulling the market, even as the majority of companies in the S&P 500 gained ground.



In Asia, Chinese memory chipmaker CXMT soared in its debut in Shanghai. The company jumped to become China’s most valuable listed company with an estimated market capitalisation of 3.3 trillion yuan (nearly $US490 billion). Wall Street has a busy week ahead with several potentially mark-moving updates on the economy and company earnings. Reports are due out on consumer confidence Tuesday and inflation on Thursday. Related Article Opinion

Trade wars Trump’s America is sinking as his war on the world sputters Stephen Bartholomeusz Senior business columnist “This is a week with more than its fair share of potential surprises, good and bad,” said Chris Larkin, managing director, trading and investing, at E-Trade from Morgan Stanley. The big focus will be on the Federal Reserve, which will give an update Wednesday on its interest rate policy. The central bank has been grappling with the impact from rising inflation because of the ongoing US war with Iran. It also has to contend with a fresh round of US-imposed tariffs globally, which could further worsen inflation.



Wall Street anticipates a nearly 36 per cent chance that the Fed will raise interest rates at its meeting this week. Higher rates can help cool inflation by making borrowing more expensive and slowing economic growth. The central bank has been holding rates steady throughout the year as it monitors inflation’s direction and impact, but Wall Street expects at least one rate hike by the end of the year. Stubbornly high inflation has been squeezing households and fuel costs have hit budgets and spending particularly hard. Gasoline costs are taking a bigger chunk out of household budgets, and that could mean tighter spending on other things like clothing and travel. Investors are monitoring the latest round of corporate earnings for signs of consumer stress along with whether the yearlong jump in stock values throughout Wall Street is justified by profits and forecasts for profit growth. Investors also have a heavy round of corporate earnings to review this week. Many of those reports could provide more clues into the health of different areas of the economy. Paint and coatings maker Sherwin-Williams, aircraft maker Boeing and payments processor Visa will report their latest results on Tuesday.



Starbucks and Chipotle will report results on Wednesday. Technology companies are being especially watched because their sharp gains throughout the year have been behind the Wall Street’s record run. Microsoft will report results Wednesday. Amazon, with its growing cloud services business and AI-focus, will report results on Thursday, along with Apple. World.title: Is your dog protection out of sight and out of mind?
World.content:
Sponsored LifestyleHealth & wellnessZoetis Is your dog protection out of sight and out of mind? Sponsored by Zoetis Simon Webster July 28, 2026 — 9:18am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

A lot of people would do anything for their dog. Ask them what they’d sacrifice for their pooch’s health, and it seems there are almost no limits: 46 per cent of Australian dog owners say they would give up takeaway coffee if it meant their dog would never get a parasite, according to a recent survey conducted for animal health company, Zoetis. A consistent health routine helps protect your dog from invisible threats. Image by Alexandrena Parker And when an Australian says they’d give up coffee for someone, that’s true love. Yet our actions don’t always match our words. Many dog owners overlook basic health routines, says vet Dr Chris Ng, a veterinary operations manager at Zoetis Australia. “It is something I witnessed regularly in clinical practice,” Ng says. “Many dog owners come to us with the very best intentions, but life gets busy, and preventative health care is often the first thing to slip when routines are disrupted.”



Part of the problem is that prevention is invisible, he adds. When it works, nothing bad happens, so owners don’t always see the benefit. “There’s also an awareness gap around how frequently parasites and other threats affect dogs, even healthy-looking ones. Cost is a factor, too, but prevention is almost always far less costly – both financially and emotionally – than treating a disease.” For many dog owners, the issue is simply that they don’t have a clear, structured plan to follow. But if you want such a plan, you’ve come to the right place. Here are five simple steps to prevent many problems and catch others early. 1. Prevent parasites What: There are many options for parasite control to suit different dogs, owners and lifestyles, from spot-ons to tasty chewables – like Simparica Trio® – which protects against fleas, ticks and heartworm. “No single product covers every parasite. Your vet can help you understand what different products cover to ensure we don’t leave any gaps. The key is not which options you choose but finding a routine that works for you and doing it consistently,” Ng says.



Why: Parasites can cause harm all year round, Ng says. Fleas can cause skin disease, ticks can cause illness or paralysis and heartworm can be fatal. “Some are zoonotic, meaning humans can also catch them, posing a risk to your whole family,” he says. “Lapsed prevention leaves your dog and household vulnerable.” 2. Keep up with vaccinations What: It’s essential you keep core vaccines (parvovirus, distemper and hepatitis) up to date, plus supplementary vaccines (kennel cough and leptospirosis) where relevant, according to your vet’s advice. Why: “Some of these diseases can be fatal. Parvovirus is a common infection that has a very high mortality rate in unvaccinated dogs. Lapses in vaccination leave your dog at serious risk.” 3. Manage their food and weight



What: Feed a nutritionally complete diet in correct portions, monitor your dog’s body condition score regularly, and discuss any dietary concerns with your vet, Ng advises. Weight checks can be done at home or during vet visits. Why: “Obesity significantly increases the risk of osteoarthritis, diabetes, heart disease and cancer, and shortens life expectancy. I have seen many dogs whose quality of life improved dramatically once their weight was managed.” 4. Don’t forget dental hygiene What: Ng recommends brushing your dog’s teeth with a soft brush and a dog-specific toothpaste (not a human one) once or twice a day. You can also give them dental chews for dogs (follow your vet’s advice regarding these), and ask your vet to conduct a dental inspection when you take your dog in for a general check-up (see below). Why: “Dental disease causes pain and tooth loss, and untreated oral bacteria can damage the heart, kidneys and liver. Dogs rarely show obvious signs of dental pain.”



5. Take them for regular health checks What: Take your dog to the vet at least once a year (twice a year for older dogs), for a physical exam covering eyes, teeth, heart, joints and overall wellbeing, Ng tips. Why: “Dogs are stoic creatures and often early signs of disease are subtle. Conditions like osteoarthritis, skin conditions and dental disease are far easier to manage when caught early. Skipping health checks at the vet means problems are often only discovered once advanced and more costly to treat.” A good preventive health routine doesn’t need to be complicated. It just needs to be consistent. According to Ng, tailoring the right plan to your furry best friend’s age, breed and lifestyle is essential to saving lives and avoiding costly medical treatments before problems arise — a strategy supported by the entire veterinary community.



Ready to winter-proof your pet’s health? Fieldwork was undertaken online between March 13 and 18, 2026. The figures have been weighted and are representative of all Australian dog owners aged 18 and over.

World.title: ‘Completely unprecedented’: Europe races to fight out-of-control blazes ahead of new heatwave
World.content:
WorldEuropeBushfires ‘Completely unprecedented’: Europe races to fight out-of-control blazes ahead of new heatwave David Crowe July 28, 2026 — 8:58am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

London: Spanish Prime Minister Pedro Sanchez has warned of more devastating wildfires across Europe, with climate change making heatwaves more frequent, as emergency crews raced to contain blazes in Spain and France before temperatures soar later this week. Sanchez pledged more funding for fire shelters ahead of a meeting of national ministers that is tipped to commit to new measures on climate change during a growing debate on the country’s worst wildfires in decades. Burnt vehicles in a parking yard in Chapinería, Spain, on Monday. AP Photo/Manu Fernandez A firefighter monitors flames in La Adrada, in Spain’s Avila province. Anadolu via Getty Images The Spanish fires appeared to slow on Monday after spreading over the weekend in the Avila province west of Madrid, but a fire near Valencia in the south of the country continued to burn out of control.



In south-western France, a vast fire heading toward Bordeaux slowed as winds died down, but government officials warned of mounting risks when temperatures reach 39 degrees in the coming days. French authorities have evacuated about 220,000 people, including local residents and people on holiday, while Spanish authorities have told some 100,000 people to leave their homes or seek shelter. A charred bicycle in Lège-Cap-Ferret, outside Bordeaux, France. AP Photo/Emma Da Silva Firefighters work to suppress a blaze near Lacanau, France, on Monday. AP Photo/Baz Ratner Sanchez visited La Vall d’Uixo in Castellon province, north of Valencia, to step up his calls for a “state pact” across governments to do more to address climate change.



“What we’re experiencing isn’t a succession of isolated events,” he said. “It’s the most painful expression of a climate emergency ​that is making sixth-generation wildfires more ferocious, heatwaves more frequent, and our territory more vulnerable.” The Spanish Civil Guard released dramatic drone footage on Monday (shortly after 10pm, AEST) that showed the Avila fire spreading quickly through dense forests. The agency has deployed more than 8000 personnel to fight the fires. The State Meteorological Agency in Spain, AEMET, forecast another heatwave – the fourth of this northern summer – to begin on Wednesday and continue until at least Sunday.



“The wildfire danger level will continue to increase, reaching extreme levels and making firefighting efforts more difficult due to high temperatures, locally gusty southerly winds and widespread low humidity,” it said in a statement. Fires across Spain have scorched 150,000 hectares and killed 13 people since the start of this year, according to Sanchez. Waterbombing outside Bordeaux. AP Photo/Emma Da Silva Houses destroyed in Navas del Rey, Spain. AP Photo/Manu Fernandez The Avila blaze alone, which is now within 100 kilometres of Madrid, has burned an estimated 47,000 hectares, which would make it the country’s worst wildfire since official records began in 1968.



While the fires heightened arguments about climate change, French Prime Minister Sébastien Lecornu revealed concerns about arson in police investigations into suspected criminals. Related Article Updated

Extreme weather Fire ‘at the gates’ of Bordeaux as Europe battles blazes Lecornu said fires across France had burned 116,085 hectares since January, surpassing the record year of 2022, when 72,000 hectares burned. “Our country is going through an unprecedented fire season,” he said, noting that there had been 13,566 “fire starts” recorded since January. “The fight against wildfires begins with prevention. Nine out of 10 fires are human-caused and most arise from carelessness: a cigarette butt, a barbecue, work carried out without precaution.



“But not all these fires are accidents. Some are deliberately set. Since July 6, 162 arrests have already taken place. “Security forces are fully mobilised to identify arsonists. They will be found, arrested, and held accountable for their actions before the courts.” Loading Lecornu said deliberately lighting a fire was a crime punishable by 15 years in prison.



In a visit to Bordeaux, French President Emmanuel Macron thanked firefighters for their hard work, warning the coming weeks would remain difficult. French President Emmanuel Macron at the fire and rescue operational centre in Bordeaux on Monday. Kenzo Tribouillard/Pool AFP via AP “We must hold on. We are going ​to win this battle together. The whole nation is behind you,” he said. “We’re facing a completely unprecedented fire,” Macron added, describing the situation as the country’s worst fire-related crisis since World War II. A pyrocumulonimbus – a giant cloud created by a large bushfires – near France’s Lège-Cap-Ferret late last week. AP Photo/Caroline Blumberg



Macron said more than 200 houses had burned down and that “all those who have lost everything” would be supported by the government. Smoke emanating from the Lege-Cap-Ferret fire in southwestern France. AFP The fire in French south-west remains about 15 kilometres west of the main entry points to Bordeaux, a city of about 1.3 million people across metropolitan region. Officials said 80 firefighters had been injured tackling the blaze. Related Article Heatwave Europe’s summers are changing. The continent isn’t ready The fire was so powerful its smoke column became a thunderstorm that generated lightning that struck the ground and ignited new fires beyond the original blaze, French officials told the Associated Press.



The thundercloud also produced violent, erratic winds capable of driving the flames in new directions. The phenomenon, called a pyrocumulonimbus, is rare in Europe and more commonly documented in North America and Australia, where it occurs only over some of the most extreme fires. France’s national firefighters federation said it had never before recorded one in the country. Scientists in Australia drew attention to the pyrocumulonimbus events, also known as pyroCb firestorms, in February 2020 after some of the country’s most horrific bushfires that summer. With Reuters, AP Get a note directly from our foreign correspondents on what’s making headlines around the world.

World.title: Alan Joyce’s self-serving tell-all packs plenty of action, attitude and drama
World.content:
CultureBooksReview Alan Joyce’s self-serving tell-all packs plenty of action, attitude and drama Chris Zappone Updated July 28, 2026 — 8:58am ,first published 5:30am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

People who know poverty in their youth can grow up to be ruthless about money in their adulthood. Perhaps that explains Alan Joyce’s determination when it comes to Qantas’ finances. No one leads Qantas for 15 years without having the blend of skills Joyce was known for: both managerial discipline and a flair for marketing. But it’s when he has to make “unpopular” decisions that his readable, if somewhat self-justifying, account of his time at Qantas sharpens. Alan Joyce: Riding the Jet Stream was always going to recount Joyce’s side of the story: the response to lockdown, the “ghost flights” scandal, even the sacking of 1820 ground crew in 2021. Alan Joyce’s memoir is not short on action and attitude. Rather than presenting these as lofty, dispassionate executive decisions, Joyce frames them as real-time responses to a grim financial reality, made with imperfect knowledge of a rapidly evolving situation.



Yes, the “ghost flights” happened, yes, $1 billion in flight credits were withheld and customers were insulted for not being prepared for travel, but it all happened for reasons. Repeatedly, Joyce shows he was willing to take nearly any action to ensure that Qantas survived the pandemic. Referring to the 2001 demise of another Australian air carrier, Joyce pledges: “I’d never let an Ansett collapse happen on my watch”. The aversion to financial failure could very well be a lesson that he absorbed growing up in working-class Dublin, which he portrays with satisfying detail at the beginning of the book. Perhaps Joyce would have led Qantas through the same choices even if he were earning just a fraction of the $125 million that he pocketed in his time as CEO there. His individualised perspective brings to mind Margaret Thatcher’s claim that “there is no such thing as society” – emphasising personal responsibility to the exclusion of collective obligation (or even awareness).



In a way, this might be the legacy of Joyce, whose career rise dovetailed neatly with the triumph of the until-recently unchallenged notion that the CEO exists first and foremost to return shareholder value, an idea that came out of the 1980s in Britain and the US. Such a conception conveniently ignores the collateral effects a company’s operations can have on society, such as the vague and troubling reality of 1820 people being turfed from their jobs, or indeed thousands of customers who paid for non-existent flights. Joyce’s 15-year tenure as chief executive of Qantas ended in 2023. Rhett Wyman Joyce is a well-known champion of causes including marriage equality, LGBTQ rights and the Indigenous Voice to parliament, but the cause of basic economic fairness for staff, for customers, and for broader society? Well, those things come downstream from ... shareholder value. This perspective is sustained throughout the book. Joyce is a man on a mission. And that mission is the success of Qantas and, when the pandemic hit, the survival of the airline he ran.



For an aviation CEO’s tell-all, the book is well paced and has plenty of action, and attitude. It is, after all, Alan Joyce. Whether measuring how fast a meal service can be completed on Aer Lingus flights, setting up and leading Jetstar, or telling Simeon Boikov (the Aussie Cossack) to “feck off” on Sydney’s streets, he’s never at a loss for words. Rather than presenting these as lofty, dispassionate executive decisions, Joyce frames them as real-time responses to a grim financial reality. An unexpected highlight is Joyce’s account of how COVID-19 shut down Australia’s borders and his role in advocating for their reopening. Here, Joyce’s style of leadership is on display as he contemplates the shortcomings of the decisions on COVID-19 closure by state and territory leaders. Joyce writes: “Too often, those decisions seemed driven by a pursuit of zero risk. Borders were closed or kept closed not because the data demanded it, but because the politics of absolute safety prevailed.” He notes that if we applied “the standard of zero risk in daily life, we wouldn’t get out of bed in the morning”. Moreover, airlines “wouldn’t allow metal tubes with rockets attached to take off multiple times a day. “But we do. We minimise risk, we manage it, and we weigh it against the benefits ... That’s how life works. And that’s how leadership should work, too ... Leadership in a crisis means making decisions – sometimes unpopular ones – and standing by them.”



Editor's pick Aviation ‘I’m sorry ... but’: Apologetic Alan Joyce tells his side of the Qantas story Joyce then steers the point into an argument for COVID-era cost-cutting: “Playing it safe wasn’t an option. We took over $1 billion out of the cost base, including the difficult but necessary decision to outsource ground handling.” As CEO for 15 years, Joyce put his stamp on the company. His shadow hangs over the Chairman’s Lounge, too, due to allegations – which he rejects – that he used free access as a magic wand to influence politicians, including the prime minister. Rather, the search for status through Qantas’ masterful loyalty program is remarkable for a country whose identity was once centred on the economic fair go. It is precisely this tension between financial success and societal fairness that makes Joyce, and his account of his legacy, so deeply polarising.

World.title: Toronto reels after shootings targeting Jewish bakeries, US consulate
World.content:
WorldNorth AmericaAntisemitism Toronto reels after shootings targeting Jewish bakeries, US consulate Michael Koziol July 28, 2026 — 10:10am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

Washington: Canada’s largest city is reeling after a string of violent acts targeting Jewish shops and – for a second time in six months – the US consulate, in what could be another example of an alleged “guns for hire” scheme involving foreign entities. The attacks have drawn parallels with the Iran-orchestrated arson attacks against Jewish businesses in Australia that led Prime Minister Anthony Albanese to cut diplomatic ties last year and expel the Iranian ambassador from Canberra. Monday morning’s gunfire at the US consulate in Toronto marked the second time the building has been targeted this year. The Canadian Press via AP Jewish groups in Canada are also increasingly worried about a major attack like last year’s massacre on Bondi Beach, which “looms large for all of us here”, said Noah Shack, chief executive of Canada’s Centre for Israel and Jewish Affairs. Two locations of the same Jewish-owned bakery chain in Toronto were targeted in attacks overnight on Saturday. One shopfront was struck by gunfire, and the other had a window smashed.



The assailants hit Kiva’s Bagel Bar, a Toronto institution that has served bagels since 1979 and a fixture of the city’s Jewish community. Prime Minister Mark Carney said he was appalled by the attacks. “Jewish Canadians should be able to live, work and worship free from fear, intimidation and hate,” he said. “Canada’s government is absolute in our commitment to combating the scourge of antisemitism.” Canadian Prime Minister Mark Carney and Ontario Premier Doug Ford both condemned the attacks. The Canadian Press via AP Then, early on Monday morning, a gunman fired a single shot at the US consulate in central Toronto, before leading police on a high-speed chase. Police ultimately broke off the pursuit. Deputy police chief Frank Barredo said an officer stationed outside the consulate heard a gunshot at 4.46am, before witnessing a white Honda Accord with no licence plate speeding away from the scene.



Toronto Mayor Olivia Chow called it a “brazen attack” and vowed to work with authorities to “remove the illegal American guns off our streets”. There were no injuries from any of the three incidents. It was the second time the US consulate in Toronto was shot at this year, after a similar incident in March. Police have said young people are being paid to carry out attacks on synagogues and other targets. Sammy Kogan/The Canadian Press via AP Last month, Toronto police said young people were being hired over encrypted messaging services to carry out targeted and connected shootings, including at Jewish schools and synagogues.



“In order to get paid, they are required to film their attacks,” Toronto police chief Myron Demkiw said at the time. “Who is paying for this? This is what we’re trying to determine.” An operation in June recovered two firearms – a 9mm handgun and a 45-calibre pistol – both from the US. Police said the 9mm was linked to at least six shootings and the 45-calibre to at least 21. Two people were arrested in that operation and an officer, Marc Pinizzotto, was killed. A third person, already in custody, faced additional charges over the matter, while a fourth person was subsequently arrested. Ruby Sahota (right) used a speech in Canada’s parliament last month to publicly state that a “foreign entity” was responsible for orchestrating the attacks. Bloomberg Canadian MP Ruby Sahota, the secretary of state for combatting crime, told parliament that the people responsible for firing shots at Toronto synagogues in early March were hired and paid by a “foreign entity”. She did not identify the country.



A late June report from Canada’s Integrated Threat Assessment Centre referred to terrorist activity by the Islamic Movement of the Companions of the Right, an Iran-linked network which claimed responsibility for attacks in Britain, and was recently designated a terrorist group by that country. The report, excerpts of which were obtained by this masthead, also said Canadian authorities had disrupted four terrorist plots inspired by Islamic State since the war between Israel and Hamas began in October 2023. Toronto Mayor Olivia Chow condemned the “brazen attack” while pledging to get American guns off her city’s streets. The Canadian Press via AP In 2024, father and son Ahmed and Mostafa Eldidi were arrested and charged with allegedly plotting an Islamic State-inspired attack in Toronto. They are due to face trial in September. On Monday, police said it was too early to say whether the latest shooting at the US consulate and the violence at the Jewish bagel shops were linked to the aforementioned guns-for-hire scheme.



Shack told this masthead that Islamist terrorism posed a serious threat to Toronto and Canada and “represents a ticking time bomb that needs to be defused”. Related Article Exclusive

Terror charges Why underworld kingpin Kaz Hamad struck a deal with Iran to attack a Melbourne synagogue The alleged criminals-for-hire scheme “follows the pattern that was uncovered in Australia of the Iranian regime hiring criminals to attack the Jewish community with a spate of arson attacks”. “This is a clear tactic that is being used in Australia, in Europe and we believe here in Canada as well,” he said. Shack said Toronto’s Jewish community was shaken by the latest attacks, which “sit squarely in a pattern that’s recognisable to us”.



But the community was also resilient and determined not to let terrorists succeed, he said. Kiva’s Bagel Bar sold out of bagels on Monday, he added. Ontario Premier Doug Ford said he was “totally disgusted” by the shootings and vandalism in Toronto over the preceding 48 hours, and expected those responsible to be punished to the fullest extent of the law. Related Article Crime Berlin Pride van attack suspect shot dead in confrontation with police It comes as authorities in Germany are questioned over their handling of Abdul Ballout, a German-born citizen with Lebanese roots, suspected of driving a van into a crowd at Berlin’s Pride festival, killing one person and injuring 29. Ballout previously sought to join Islamic State, prosecutors said, and was convicted in Berlin of preparing a serious act of violence. But a court released him pending an appeal. He was killed in a confrontation with police responding to the Pride festival attack. Get a note directly from our foreign correspondents on what’s making headlines around the world.

World.title: ASX slides lower, oil prices retreat; Trump pushes for rate cut
World.content:
Updated BusinessMarketsWorld markets ASX slides lower, oil prices retreat; Trump pushes for rate cut Damian Troise and Alex Veiga Updated July 28, 2026 — 10:05am ,first published July 28, 2026 — 5:17am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

The Australian sharemarket has slid lower at the open after a mixed session on Wall Street, while oil prices continued to fall after the US and Iran paused their attacks while work resumed on restarting negotiations to end the war. The S&P/ASX 200 was down 22.8 points, or 0.3 per cent, to 8871.2 in early trade, after jumping by 1.4 per cent on Monday. The Australian dollar was 0.1 per cent lower to US69.86¢. Wall Street has kicked off its week with a mixed session. AP Overnight, the S&P 500 fell 0.2 per cent. The index is coming off two weekly losses in a row. The Dow Jones rose 155 points, or 0.3 per cent. The Nasdaq composite fell 0.4 per cent. Oil prices reversed course from a week ago, when a sharp escalation in fighting between the US and Iran worsened worries about global oil supplies. The price of Brent crude, the international standard, dropped 8.7 per cent to close at $US88.36 a barrel for September delivery. Prices surged to over $US100 a barrel last week before easing.



The war between the US and Iran has sharply curtailed, and at times halted, traffic through the vital Strait of Hormuz. That has had a ripple effect throughout the world’s economy. Gasoline prices have surged and shipping costs for most goods are rising, with businesses typically passing those costs along to households. Related Article Opinion

Aviation Alan Joyce thinks it could’ve been worse Kishor Napier-Raman Senior Business Writer President Donald Trump called on the Federal Reserve to lower interest rates, saying the US should have the lowest interest rate in the world. “Rates should be lowered... We have other countries that are paying less interest rates,” Trump told reporters aboard Air Force One. “We should have the lowest interest rate in the world,” Trump said.



“Kevin is fantastic, but he’s got a board, and the board members are very political,” Trump said, referring to Fed chair Kevin Warsh, adding he knew what Warsh wanted to do. The Federal Reserve will announce its interest rates decision on Thursday (AEST), with markets expecting the central bank to stay on hold. Bond yields fell. The yield on the 10-year Treasury fell to 4.65 per cent from 4.69 per cent late Friday. Technology companies were behind much of the shifts on Wall Street, with gains and declines for a mix of big companies resulting in uncertain trading. Nvidia fell 5 per cent and Micron Technology slumped 2.3 per cent. At the same time, Microsoft rose 1.9 per cent and Apple rose 1.2 per cent. They are all among the most valuable companies in the world and those market values give them more influence over the direction of the broader market. The mix of gains and losses from a variety of those companies had more impact in pushing and pulling the market, even as the majority of companies in the S&P 500 gained ground.



In Asia, Chinese memory chipmaker CXMT soared in its debut in Shanghai. The company jumped to become China’s most valuable listed company with an estimated market capitalisation of 3.3 trillion yuan (nearly $US490 billion). Wall Street has a busy week ahead with several potentially mark-moving updates on the economy and company earnings. Reports are due out on consumer confidence Tuesday and inflation on Thursday. Related Article Opinion

Trade wars Trump’s America is sinking as his war on the world sputters Stephen Bartholomeusz Senior business columnist “This is a week with more than its fair share of potential surprises, good and bad,” said Chris Larkin, managing director, trading and investing, at E-Trade from Morgan Stanley. The big focus will be on the Federal Reserve, which will give an update Wednesday on its interest rate policy. The central bank has been grappling with the impact from rising inflation because of the ongoing US war with Iran. It also has to contend with a fresh round of US-imposed tariffs globally, which could further worsen inflation.



Wall Street anticipates a nearly 36 per cent chance that the Fed will raise interest rates at its meeting this week. Higher rates can help cool inflation by making borrowing more expensive and slowing economic growth. The central bank has been holding rates steady throughout the year as it monitors inflation’s direction and impact, but Wall Street expects at least one rate hike by the end of the year. Stubbornly high inflation has been squeezing households and fuel costs have hit budgets and spending particularly hard. Gasoline costs are taking a bigger chunk out of household budgets, and that could mean tighter spending on other things like clothing and travel. Investors are monitoring the latest round of corporate earnings for signs of consumer stress along with whether the yearlong jump in stock values throughout Wall Street is justified by profits and forecasts for profit growth. Investors also have a heavy round of corporate earnings to review this week. Many of those reports could provide more clues into the health of different areas of the economy. Paint and coatings maker Sherwin-Williams, aircraft maker Boeing and payments processor Visa will report their latest results on Tuesday.



Starbucks and Chipotle will report results on Wednesday. Technology companies are being especially watched because their sharp gains throughout the year have been behind the Wall Street’s record run. Microsoft will report results Wednesday. Amazon, with its growing cloud services business and AI-focus, will report results on Thursday, along with Apple. World.title: Is your dog protection out of sight and out of mind?
World.content:
Sponsored LifestyleHealth & wellnessZoetis Is your dog protection out of sight and out of mind? Sponsored by Zoetis Simon Webster July 28, 2026 — 9:18am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

A lot of people would do anything for their dog. Ask them what they’d sacrifice for their pooch’s health, and it seems there are almost no limits: 46 per cent of Australian dog owners say they would give up takeaway coffee if it meant their dog would never get a parasite, according to a recent survey conducted for animal health company, Zoetis. A consistent health routine helps protect your dog from invisible threats. Image by Alexandrena Parker And when an Australian says they’d give up coffee for someone, that’s true love. Yet our actions don’t always match our words. Many dog owners overlook basic health routines, says vet Dr Chris Ng, a veterinary operations manager at Zoetis Australia. “It is something I witnessed regularly in clinical practice,” Ng says. “Many dog owners come to us with the very best intentions, but life gets busy, and preventative health care is often the first thing to slip when routines are disrupted.”



Part of the problem is that prevention is invisible, he adds. When it works, nothing bad happens, so owners don’t always see the benefit. “There’s also an awareness gap around how frequently parasites and other threats affect dogs, even healthy-looking ones. Cost is a factor, too, but prevention is almost always far less costly – both financially and emotionally – than treating a disease.” For many dog owners, the issue is simply that they don’t have a clear, structured plan to follow. But if you want such a plan, you’ve come to the right place. Here are five simple steps to prevent many problems and catch others early. 1. Prevent parasites What: There are many options for parasite control to suit different dogs, owners and lifestyles, from spot-ons to tasty chewables – like Simparica Trio® – which protects against fleas, ticks and heartworm. “No single product covers every parasite. Your vet can help you understand what different products cover to ensure we don’t leave any gaps. The key is not which options you choose but finding a routine that works for you and doing it consistently,” Ng says.



Why: Parasites can cause harm all year round, Ng says. Fleas can cause skin disease, ticks can cause illness or paralysis and heartworm can be fatal. “Some are zoonotic, meaning humans can also catch them, posing a risk to your whole family,” he says. “Lapsed prevention leaves your dog and household vulnerable.” 2. Keep up with vaccinations What: It’s essential you keep core vaccines (parvovirus, distemper and hepatitis) up to date, plus supplementary vaccines (kennel cough and leptospirosis) where relevant, according to your vet’s advice. Why: “Some of these diseases can be fatal. Parvovirus is a common infection that has a very high mortality rate in unvaccinated dogs. Lapses in vaccination leave your dog at serious risk.” 3. Manage their food and weight



What: Feed a nutritionally complete diet in correct portions, monitor your dog’s body condition score regularly, and discuss any dietary concerns with your vet, Ng advises. Weight checks can be done at home or during vet visits. Why: “Obesity significantly increases the risk of osteoarthritis, diabetes, heart disease and cancer, and shortens life expectancy. I have seen many dogs whose quality of life improved dramatically once their weight was managed.” 4. Don’t forget dental hygiene What: Ng recommends brushing your dog’s teeth with a soft brush and a dog-specific toothpaste (not a human one) once or twice a day. You can also give them dental chews for dogs (follow your vet’s advice regarding these), and ask your vet to conduct a dental inspection when you take your dog in for a general check-up (see below). Why: “Dental disease causes pain and tooth loss, and untreated oral bacteria can damage the heart, kidneys and liver. Dogs rarely show obvious signs of dental pain.”



5. Take them for regular health checks What: Take your dog to the vet at least once a year (twice a year for older dogs), for a physical exam covering eyes, teeth, heart, joints and overall wellbeing, Ng tips. Why: “Dogs are stoic creatures and often early signs of disease are subtle. Conditions like osteoarthritis, skin conditions and dental disease are far easier to manage when caught early. Skipping health checks at the vet means problems are often only discovered once advanced and more costly to treat.” A good preventive health routine doesn’t need to be complicated. It just needs to be consistent. According to Ng, tailoring the right plan to your furry best friend’s age, breed and lifestyle is essential to saving lives and avoiding costly medical treatments before problems arise — a strategy supported by the entire veterinary community.



Ready to winter-proof your pet’s health? Fieldwork was undertaken online between March 13 and 18, 2026. The figures have been weighted and are representative of all Australian dog owners aged 18 and over.
